questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which nerve is most commonly injured during indirect inguinal hernia surgery?
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve is the most frequently injured nerve during open inguinal hernia repair. It typically runs on the surface of the spermatic cord, just beneath the external oblique aponeurosis. During the dissection of the inguinal canal to treat an indirect hernia, the nerve can be accidentally entrapped in sutures, crushed by forceps, or severed. Injury leads to numbness or chronic pain (neuralgia) in the inguinal region and the base of the scrotum or labia majora. The genitofemoral nerve (Option B), specifically its genital branch, is also at risk, but injury is less common than with the ilioinguinal. The femoral nerve (Option A) and obturator nerve (Option C) are located much deeper and more laterally or medially, respectively, and are rarely involved in standard anterior inguinal hernia repairs unless severe complications or deep stitch placement occur. Surgeons often routinely identify and protect the ilioinguinal nerve to prevent postoperative chronic groin pain
questions.learning: The ilioinguinal nerve is the most frequently injured nerve during open inguinal hernia repair. It typically runs on the surface of the spermatic cord, just beneath the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies.

Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa. The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

Other options:

B) Leprosy: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous lesions, without much bacilli. Hence called paucibacillary leprosy. Lepromatous lesions contain large aggregates of lipid-laden macrophages (lepra cells), often filled with masses (globi) of acid-fast bacilli. Because of the presence of abundant bacteria, it is also called as multibacillary.

Given below are the images that depict lepromatous lesion showing foamy macrophages with globi of pink/red acid-fast bacilli and tuberculoid leprosy showing granulomatous lesions, respectively.

C) Mycosis fungoides: Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characterized by polymorphic patches and plaques with fine scaling usually present on the limbs, breast, and buttocks. The lesions may be pruritic or even asymptomatic.  Histological hallmarks include: 1. Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/ hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane), 2. Pautrier's microabscesses - tumor cells invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters, forming a collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis and 3. Epidermotropism - pronounced invasion of the tumor cells into the epidermis.

Given below is the image of Sezary-Lutzner cells.

Given below is the arrow pointing at Paurtier's microabcess.

D) Visceral leishmaniasis: In visceral leishmaniasis, parasites invade and activate the macrophages throughout the mononuclear phagocyte system. Hence, these phagocytic cells are enlarged and filled with leishmania species; many plasma cells are also present.

The given slide shows macrophages infested with intracellular Leishmania donovani bodies (arrows) characterized by a kinetoplast and characteristic double dot appearance (Leishman stain).
questions.learning: Pemphigus vulgaris — The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension,palpitations and sweating. His catecholamine and aldosterone levels were found to be elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The clinical vignette of hypertension, sweating and palpitation with elevated catecholamine levels point towards pheochromocytoma.

Pearl PF0334: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The recommended dose of cotrimoxazole for treatment of pneumonia in a child weighing 16 kg is:
options: One paediatric tablet twice a day
Two paediatric tablets twice a day
Three paediatric tablets twice a day
Four paediatric tablets twice a day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two paediatric tablets twice a day

Under the IMNCI/F-IMNCI guidelines, cotrimoxazole was recommended for the treatment of non-severe pneumonia in children. The dose is based on body weight (or age).

For a child weighing 16 kg, the recommended dose is:

• Two paediatric tablets twice daily for 5 days

Hence, the correct answer is B. Two paediatric tablets twice a day.

Note: Current WHO and Indian guidelines now recommend oral amoxicillin as the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated childhood pneumonia. Cotrimoxazole is of historical importance and may still appear in older examination questions.
questions.learning: Two paediatric tablets twice a day Under the IMNCI/F-IMNCI guidelines, cotrimoxazole was recommended for the treatment of non-severe pneumonia in children.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following are features of third cranial nerve palsy except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Limited abduction

Limited abduction is not a feature of third cranial nerve palsy.

Abduction is carried out by the lateral rectus, which is supplied by the abducens (sixth) nerve.

Third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy presents with:

• Profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle
• Limited adduction due to medial rectus weakness
• Limited elevation due to the weakness of the superior rectus and inferior oblique
• Abduction and depression in the primary position ("down and out")
questions.learning: Limited abduction Limited abduction is not a feature of third cranial nerve palsy. Abduction is carried out by the lateral rectus, which is supplied by the abducens (sixth) nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Level of posterior superior iliac spine:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S2

The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) is an important surface anatomical landmark on the posterior pelvis. It is visible externally as the “dimples of Venus” in the lower back.

The PSIS corresponds approximately to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2).

The S2 vertebral level is important because it corresponds to:

• Termination of the dural sac
• End of the subarachnoid space
• A landmark used in caudal epidural anesthesia

Other related landmarks:

• Iliac crest line (Tuffier’s line) → level of L4 vertebra
• Sacral hiatus → around S4
questions.learning: S2 The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) is an important surface anatomical landmark on the posterior pelvis. It is visible externally as the “dimples of Venus” in the lower back.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A patient presents with vertigo associated with horizontal nystagmus. The slow component is towards the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?

BPPV- Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left hypoactive labyrinth

The most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with horizontal nystagmus and fast component towards the right (slow component towards the left) is left hypoactive labyrinth.

Nystagmus is an involuntary oscillatory movement of the eyes, which can occur in horizontal, vertical, or torsional directions. The direction of nystagmus is determined by the fast component.

In horizontal nystagmus, the direction of nystagmus (fast phase) is always away from the hypoactive lesions and towards the active or hyperactive lesions of the labyrinth. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a hyperactive disease while vestibular neuronitis and vestibular Schwanomma are hypoactive diseases.

The involvement of the vertical semicircular canals (superior and posterior) leads to vertical or mixed vertical-torsional nystagmus, ruling out posterior canal BPPV (Option A) and superior canal BPPV (Option B).

Alternatively, if the right hypoactive labyrinth was one of the options, it could be considered as a differential for horizontal nystagmus with the slow component towards the right.

BPPV is a condition characterized by recurrent episodes of transient vertigo (<1 min) triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity. It is caused by dislodged calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) from the utricular macula into one of the semicircular canals, usually the posterior semicircular canal. A diagnosis of BPPV can be made by Dix-Hallpike test and the condition is treated by repositioning maneuvers for the otoconia such as the Epley maneuver.
questions.learning: Left hypoactive labyrinth — The most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with horizontal nystagmus and fast component towards the right (slow component towards the left) is left hypoactive labyrinth.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient came with complaints of palpitations, sweating, and restlessness. He has a complaint of sweaty palms. Clinical findings are depicted in the image given below. What is the diagnostic finding seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid receptor antibody

Based on the clinical findings the most likely diagnosis is Graves' disease. Elevated levels of thyroid receptor–stimulating antibodies are diagnostic of Graves' disease.

The hyperthyroidism of Graves’ disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) that are synthesized in the thyroid gland as well as in bone marrow and lymph nodes. TSI cause stimulation of the thyroid gland causing features of hyperthyroidism in the presence of low TSH levels.

Clinical features of Graves' disease:

• Hyperthyroid features like hyperactivity, irritability, dysphoria, heat intolerance and sweating palpitations, fatigue, and weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhea, polyuria, oligomenorrhea, loss of libido, tachycardia
• Eye signs as mentioned in Graves' ophthalmopathy.
• Graves ophthalmopathy: It is due to increased volume of the retroorbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles because of marked lymphocytic infiltration of the retro-orbital space, accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate, and increased numbers of adipocytes (fatty infiltration). Corneal exposure, lid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, conjunctival injection, restriction of gaze, diplopia, and visual loss from optic nerve compression are cardinal symptoms.

Histopathology shows follicular hyperplasia with scalloped margins on biopsy.

Management involves

• Propylthiouracil is the mainstay of treatment for Graves' disease but it does not affect Graves' ophthalmopathy.
• Radioactive Iodine is also used as a treatment modality for hyperthyroidism in suitable patients but does not affect Grave's ophthalmopathy.

Other options:

Levels of anti-thyroid peroxidase (Option B) and anti-thyroglobulin (Option A) are elevated in autoimmune hypothyroidism which is characterized by features of dry skin, cold intolerance, tiredness, weakness, feeling tired, weight gain, etc.

Option D: Ultrasensitive thyrotropin level (TSH) is elevated in primary hypothyroidism.
questions.learning: Thyroid receptor antibody — Based on the clinical findings the most likely diagnosis is Graves' disease. Elevated levels of thyroid receptor–stimulating antibodies are diagnostic of Graves' disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child accidentally took a bottle full of iron tablets. Which drug is used as antidote for poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deferoxamine

The antidote used for iron chelation is deferoxamine.

Deferoxamine, a potent iron-chelating compound, can be given intravenously to bind iron that has already been absorbed and to promote its excretion in urine and feces.

Other options:

Luspatercept is a first-in-class erythroid maturation agent, is recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of anemia in adult patients with beta-thalassemia who require regular red blood cell transfusions.

Deferiprone and deferasirox are both oral drugs and can be given in transfusion-related siderosis but are less effective than desferrioxamine but can be preferred because of the ease of administration through the oral route and multiple transfusions required for beta-thalassemia patients.

DMSA is the oral agent of choice in lead poisoning.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with the following lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyoderma gangrenosum

The given image along with the history of Inflammatory bowel disease is most likely pyoderma gangrenosum.

Pyoderma gangrenosum:

* dermatological extraintestinal manifestation of IBD (inflammatory bowel disease).

* begins as a pustule and progresses to an ulcer with necrotic tissue and exudates.

* may occur years before the onset of bowel symptoms and is usually associated with severe disease.

* Lesions are commonly found on the dorsal surface of the feet and legs but may occur on the arms, chest, and even the face.

* very difficult to treat and often requires IV antibiotics and IV glucocorticoids.

* Other drugs used in its management include dapsone, IV cyclosporine, and infliximab.

Note:

Other dermatological manifestations associated with IBD include erythema nodosum, Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis), perianal skin tags, psoriasis, and metastatic Crohn's disease (cutaneous granulomas).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a child who has persistently poor mathematical abilities despite having a normal IQ and otherwise age- appropriate learning skills, and who shows no improvement even after one year of specialized mathematics tutoring?
questions.explanation: This child’s persistent difficulty with mathematics despite normal intelligence and adequate educational interventions is diagnostic of a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD). Under DSM-5, this term covers impairments in reading, writing, and mathematics (dyscalculia). ADHD (Option A) causes academic issues through inattention or impulsivity rather than a specific skill deficit. Mathematics Learning Disorder (Option B) is the specific description, but "Specific Learning Disorder" is the broader and clinically preferred diagnostic term in standardized examinations. Asperger’s Syndrome (Option C) involves social communication deficits; children with this condition often excel in mathematics. Given the persistence of the mathematical deficit despite tutoring, SLD is the most accurate over arching diagnosis. **************
questions.learning: This child’s persistent difficulty with mathematics despite normal intelligence and adequate educational interventions is diagnostic of a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man is brought to ER after a car accident. He had multiple injuries and a femoral shaft fracture. He was treated and stabilized. But 48 hours later, he suddenly develops breathing difficulty, increased heart rate and petechial rashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

History of sudden onset breathlessness and rashes on 3rd day of admission after femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

Fat embolism is the presence of fat globules in vital organs and peripheral circulation after fracture of the long bone or other major trauma.

Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules.

Clinical features:

* Early signs are fever and tachycardia

* Presenting features are of 2 types- Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation or Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia

* Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva

The classical clinical triad consists of respiratory distress, neurological abnormalities, and petechial haemorrhages

Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive:

* Respiratory support (oxygen)

* Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity)

* Intravenous low molecular weight dextran

* Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis

* Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures

Other Options:

Option A: Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds) is seen in cardiac tamponade.

Option B: Pneumothorax can cause sudden, sharp chest pain and difficulty breathing, but it often presents with hyper-resonant percussion (tapping on the chest) and decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

Option C: Sudden onset dyspnoea and bilateral fine basal crackles are signs of Pulmonary edema.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.
questions.learning: Fat embolism History of sudden onset breathlessness and rashes on 3rd day of admission after femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image depicts a carbuncle (Option D), which is a deep-seated bacterial infection of a cluster of hair follicles. It is characteristically formed by several interconnected furuncles (boils) and is identified by its multiple draining sinus tracts on the skin surface, often referred to as a "sieve-like" appearance. These are most common in areas with thick skin, like the back of the neck or the back. Botryomycosis (Option A) is a rare chronic granulomatous bacterial infection that mimics fungal lesions. Erysipelas (Option B) is a superficial cellulitis with well-defined, raised borders and intense erythema. Ecthyma (Option C) is an ulcerative form of impetigo that extends into the dermis, resulting in "punched-out" ulcers. Carbuncles are frequently associated with underlying immunosuppression or diabetes mellitus. Treatment requires incision and drainage along with systemic antibiotics to manage the extensive staphylococcal infection

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 26-year male presented to OPD with a deformity of the left hand. He had a past history of RTA in which he had injured the same limb 6 months back. There was hypothenar muscle atrophy and a fixed deformity where on opening his hand he is not able to extend the medial two fingers. Which of the following nerves is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given description is of a claw hand with hypothenar muscle atrophy classically seen in case of an ulnar nerve injury.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles in the hand. The lumbricals are primarily responsible for the extension at the interphalangeal joints. Therefore, in ulnar nerve palsy, there is clawing of the medial two fingers.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book between the thumb and index finger while the examiner attempt to pull it forcefully. In case of an ulnar nerve injury, the adductor pollicis is paralyzed and the patient attempts to hold the book with the flexor pollicis longus muscle supplied by the median nerve.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, the examiner can pull out the card with ease.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with a wrist drop due to paralyzed wrist extensors. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to ape thumb deformity. A pointing finger deformity can also be seen due to paralyzed flexors of the fingers.

Option D - Long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle. Patients with injury to this nerve present with winging of the scapula.

Pearl PF1196: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

1. Neurapraxia
2. Axonotmesis
3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis:

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis:

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic gout presents with an acute flare characterized by severe pain, swelling, and tenderness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. His serum uric acid level is elevated. Following resolution of the acute attack, which is the best drug for long-term use in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Allopurinol

Allopurinol is the first-line urate-lowering therapy for the long-term management of chronic gout. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby reducing serum urate levels and preventing recurrent gout attacks, tophi formation, and uric acid nephrolithiasis. Urate-lowering therapy should be initiated only after the acute gout attack has resolved, as starting it during an acute flare may worsen or prolong symptoms.

Why not the other options?

• B. Colchicine: Used for acute gout attacks and as prophylaxis when initiating urate-lowering therapy, but it does not reduce serum uric acid and is not the primary long-term urate-lowering drug.
• C. Rasburicase: Converts uric acid to allantoin and is mainly used for tumor lysis syndrome, not chronic gout.
• D. Indomethacin: An NSAID used for symptomatic treatment of acute gout, but it has no role in long-term urate reduction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which is the drug used for refractory intractable rheumatic chorea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sodium valproate

The drug used for refractory intractable rheumatic chorea is sodium valproate, as it doesn't have extrapyramidal side effects.

Sydenham's chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements which mainly affect the head and upper limbs. In the tongue, it is visible as the characteristic darting movements.

Medications used to treat Sydenham chorea are:

• Mild cases - Providing a calm environment.
• Severe cases:

• Dopamine antagonists - haloperidol, pimozide
• Antiepileptic medications - sodium valproate, carbamazepine.

• Severe, refractory cases - Steroids (thought to be immune-mediated)
• IV immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis - limited studies, decreased efficacy (not currently recommended)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The type of knot seen in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reef knot

The given image shows the suture material exiting the knot is on the same side as the entry i.e no cross-over is seen. This is seen in a reef knot.

A knot is a fastening made of threads intertwined together or on themselves. Each knot consists of- 2 half-hitches placed in sequential throws. Squaring refers to tightening the knot/half-hitch in a manner that the threads lay flat due to the alternating direction of half-hitches in adjacent layers.

Types of knots:

1. Granny knot: half-hitch over a half-hitch in the same direction. It has better-holding power than half-hitch
2. Reef knot: half-hitch followed by a second half-hitch after squaring.
3. Triple throw knot: Reef knot with another half-hitch knot for added security. Knots made with prolene sutures require 6-8 throws to prevent slippage.
4. Surgeon’s knot: Modification of the reef knot with two half-hitches in the first layer.
5. Slip knot: Modification of either granny/reef knot formed when one end of the thread is kept taut while tightening the knot.
questions.learning: Reef knot — The given image shows the suture material exiting the knot is on the same side as the entry i.e no cross-over is seen. A knot is a fastening made of threads intertwined together or on themselves.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The mother of a 12-year-old girl was worried that her daughter is shorter when compared with her classmates. On examination, the child had a webbed neck, low hairline, and shield chest. A provisional diagnosis of Turner's syndrome was made. Which of the following is a likely finding to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bilateral small streak ovaries

The likely finding seen in a patient with Turner syndrome is bilateral small streak ovaries.

Turner syndrome results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome. It is characterized by hypogonadism in phenotypic females. It is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females. Three types of karyotypic abnormalities are seen

• Missing an entire X chromosome - this results in a 45X karyotype.
• Structural abnormalities of the X chromosomes - isochromosome of the long arm and loss of the short arm, 46X,i(X)(q10), deletion of portions of both long and short arms that lead to the formation of a ring chromosome, 46X,r(X), deletion of portions of the short or long arm, 46X,del(Xq) or 46X,del(Xp).
• Mosaics - they will have 45X along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal cell types. Examples are 45X/46XX, 45X/46XY, 45X/47XXX, 45X/46X,i(X)(q10).

Important features associated with Turner's syndrome:

• Short stature
• Webbing of neck
• Broad chest and widely spaced nipples
• Cubitus valgus
• Streak ovaries
• Infertility, amenorrhea
• Peripheral lymphedema at birth
• Low posterior hairline
• Broad chest and widely spaced nipples
• Pigmented nevi
• Coarctation of aorta

There is failure to develop normal secondary sex characteristics at puberty. The genitalia remain infantile, breast development is inadequate, and there is little pubic hair. Short stature and amenorrhea are of particular importance in establishing the diagnosis in an adult.

Other options:

Aortic dissection, subluxation of lens, and mitral valve prolapse are seen in Marfan syndrome.
questions.learning: Bilateral small streak ovaries — The likely finding seen in a patient with Turner syndrome is bilateral small streak ovaries. Turner syndrome results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is beneficial in reducing the painful crisis of sickle cell anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxyurea

Hydroxyurea is beneficial in reducing the painful vasoocclusive crisis of sickle cell anemia.
Hydroxyurea is a myelosuppressive agent that is effective in reducing the frequency of painful episodes like dactylitis and acute chest syndrome, decreasing the rate of hospitalization, and requirement for blood transfusion. It is safe and well-tolerated in children and infants. Hydroxyurea is approved for long-term maintenance of sickle cell disease, and is recommended for patients of all ages regardless of symptoms.

Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin levels by an unknown mechanism and interferes with the polymerization of abnormal HbS.

Newer drugs for management of acute painful crisis of sickle cell anemia include L-glutamine and crizanlizumab. For individuals >5 years of age with sickle cell disease who have pain despite hydroxyurea (or who cannot tolerate hydroxyurea), L-glutamine is recommended, regardless of whether they are receiving hydroxyurea. The mechanism of action of this drug, is that it reduces oxidative stress in sickle erythrocytes. Crizanlizumab is a P-selectin-blocking monoclonal antibody which is given intravenously every month to reduce acute painful episodes.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis. Sickle cell disease causes hemolytic anemia due to increased erythrocyte destruction. The anemia is generally well compensated. Complications occur due to abnormal erythrocyte configurations that increase hemoglobin polymerization leading to a painful vaso-occlusive state.

Clinical features of sickle cell anemia :

- Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
- Painful bone crisis : hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.
- Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.
- Hyposthenuria : inability to concentrate urine.
- Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
- Spleen : In children, splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion. In adolescence or early adulthood, autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
- Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.
- Other clinical features include priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

Other options :
Option B : Methotrexate interferes with folate metabolism by acting as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase. This starves cells for tetrahydrofolate and makes them unable to synthesize purines and thymidine monophosphate. It does not treat painful crisis of sickle cell anemia.

Option C : Methionine is an essential amino acid involved in the synthesis of folate and vitamin B12. It is not used in the management of sickle cell anemia.
Option D : Eltrombopag is a thrombopoetin analog used to treat immune thrombocytopenia. It is not used in the treatment of painful sickle cell crisis.
questions.learning: Hydroxyurea Hydroxyurea is beneficial in reducing the painful vasoocclusive crisis of sickle cell anemia. Hydroxyurea is a myelosuppressive agent that is effective in reducing the frequency of painful episodes like dactylitis and acute chest syndrome,…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presents with eye pain, photophobia, and redness a few days after a minor injury while climbing a tree. Slit-lamp examination reveals distinct lesions surrounding a central focus of infection. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: The history of ocular trauma involving vegetative matter (climbing a tree) followed by a painful corneal infection is a classic clinical clue for fungal keratitis. The hallmark slit-lamp finding described—"distinct lesions surrounding a central infection site"—refers to satellite lesions. These are smaller infiltrates located away from the main primary ulcer, representing the outward spread of fungal hyphae through the corneal stroma. A reverse hypopyon (Option A) refers to emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. A dendritic ulcer (Option B) is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and has a branching tree-like pattern. A ring abscess (Option C) can occur in advanced Pseudomonas or Bacillus keratitis but is not the specific "surrounding lesion" pattern described here. Fungal ulcers are often dry in appearance with feathery margins. Therefore, satellite lesions are the definitive finding confirming a fungal etiology in this patient. Treatment involves topical antifungals like natamycin
questions.learning: The history of ocular trauma involving vegetative matter (climbing a tree) followed by a painful corneal infection is a classic clinical clue for fungal keratitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is characterized by the absence of P waves?
questions.explanation: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) is an irregularly irregular rhythm characterized by the complete absence of distinct P waves on the ECG. Instead of organized atrial contraction (represented by a P wave), the atria undergo chaotic "fibrillatory" activity, often seen as a wavy baseline. Ventricular tachycardia (Option A) is a regular wide-complex rhythm where P waves are usually buried or absent, but AF is the classic "absent P wave" diagnosis taught in basic rhythm analysis. Focal atrial tachycardia (Option B) involves a specific ectopic focus and does produce a recognizable, albeit abnormal, P wave. Ventricular fibrillation (Option C) is a pulseless, chaotic rhythm where all complexes (P, QRS, T) are absent, making AF the more specific answer for a rhythm that maintains recognizable QRS complexes without P waves. Therefore, AF is the definitive choice for this clinical hallmark
questions.learning: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) is an irregularly irregular rhythm characterized by the complete absence of distinct P waves on the ECG. Instead of organized atrial contraction (represented by a P wave), the atria undergo chaotic "fibrillatory" activity, often…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which vaccines should healthcare workers receive?
questions.explanation: Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at significant occupational risk for blood-borne infections. Vaccination against Hepatitis B is the most critical and universally recommended immunization for all HCWs who may come into contact with blood or body fluids. The Hepatitis B vaccine is highly effective and prevents a leading cause of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis among medical professionals. Cholera (Option A) and Rabies (Option D) vaccines are generally only recommended for specialized workers, such as those in labs or endemic travel regions, rather than for general HCWs. HPV (Option B) is a routine vaccine for adolescents but is not an occupational requirement for HCWs. In addition to Hepatitis B, HCWs should ideally be immune to influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella. Occupational safety standards mandate that employers provide the Hepatitis B vaccine free of charge to at-risk staff. This protective measure is fundamental to reducing the risk of workplace-acquired infections and ensuring the long-term health of the medical workforce
questions.learning: Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at significant occupational risk for blood-borne infections. Vaccination against Hepatitis B is the most critical and universally recommended immunization for all HCWs who may come into contact with blood or body fluids.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic sun exposure presents to the outpatient clinic with brownish pigmentation, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates Melasma, a common acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetrical, patchy, brownish macules on sun-exposed areas of the face, such as the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip. It is most prevalent in women and is strongly associated with chronic UV exposure, hormonal changes (e.g., pregnancy or oral contraceptives), and genetic predisposition. Freckles (Option B) are much smaller, discrete tan spots that darken with sun exposure. Melanoma (Option C) is a malignant pigment-cell tumor that typically presents as an asymmetric, irregular mole rather than a broad, symmetrical patch. Basal cell carcinoma (Option D) usually presents as a slow-growing, pearly nodule with telangiectasia. Management of melasma involves strict sun protection, the use of broad-spectrum sunscreens, and topical lightening agents like hydroquinone, tretinoin, and corticosteroids (Kligman's formula). It is often a chronic condition that requires long-term maintenance to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: The image illustrates Melasma, a common acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetrical, patchy, brownish macules on sun-exposed areas of the face, such as the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, constipation, and fatigue and is subsequently diagnosed with lead poisoning. Which enzyme defect is most likely responsible for the manifestations of lead toxicity in this patient?
questions.explanation: Lead poisoning interferes with several enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway, but its most characteristic and potent effect is the inhibition of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase. This enzyme (also known as porphobilinogen synthase) catalyzes the second step of the pathway, converting two molecules of ALA into one molecule of porphobilinogen. Lead also inhibits ferrochelatase (Heme synthase, Option C), which is responsible for the final step of inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX. Inhibition of ALA dehydratase leads to an accumulation of ALA in the blood and urine, which is thought to contribute to the neurological symptoms and abdominal pain seen in lead toxicity. ALA synthase (Option A) is the rate-limiting enzyme but is not the primary target of lead. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase (Option D) is another pathway enzyme but is less sensitive to lead than ALA dehydratase. Clinically, lead poisoning is often identified by "basophilic stippling" on a blood smear and elevated blood lead levels. Management focuses on removing the source of lead and using chelation therapy in severe cases
questions.learning: Lead poisoning interferes with several enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway, but its most characteristic and potent effect is the inhibition of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-month-old infant has clusters of flexor spasms on awakening. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Vigabatrin is started. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase, increasing GABA levels
Positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase, increasing GABA levels

Vigabatrin is an antiepileptic drug that acts by irreversibly inhibiting GABA transaminase (GABA-T), the enzyme responsible for GABA degradation. This results in increased GABA concentrations in the brain, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission and suppressing seizures.

It is particularly effective in infantile spasms (West syndrome), especially those associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. The infant has:

• Clusters of flexor spasms
• Occurring on awakening
• Hypsarrhythmia on EEG

This is the classic triad of West syndrome (infantile spasms), for which vigabatrin is a first-line therapy. Its mechanism is irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase.

Why not the other options?

• B. Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels: Mechanism of phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and lacosamide.
• C. Inhibition of T-type calcium channels: Mechanism of ethosuximide, used for absence seizures.
• D. Positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors: Mechanism of benzodiazepines and barbiturates.
questions.learning: Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase, increasing GABA levels Vigabatrin is an antiepileptic drug that acts by irreversibly inhibiting GABA transaminase (GABA-T), the enzyme responsible for GABA degradation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male develops tightness in the chest, associated with breathlessness and altered sensorium during his trek towards a mountain peak. The drug prescribed for symptomatic relief acts of which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proximal convoluted tubule

The symptoms are suggestive of acute mountain sickness and acetazolamide can be given for symptomatic relief. It acts on the proximal convoluted tubule.

Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, acts on the enzyme in epithelial cells of the proximal convoluted tubule. By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, HCO3- reabsorption is blocked and diuresis occurs.

Acetazolamide (125–250 mg twice a day), administered for 1 day before ascent and continued for 2 or 3 days is very effective. It can also be used for prophylaxis. Paresthesia and a tingling sensation are common side effects of acetazolamide. Bone marrow depression is rare but a serious side effect. It is contraindicated in liver disease.

Acute mountain sickness:

When individuals arrive first at a high, altitude, many develop transient 'mountain sickness'. This syndrome develops 8-24 hours after arrival at altitude and lasts 4-8 days.

Characterized by:

* Headache

* Irritation

* Insomnia

* Breathlessness

* Nausea and vomiting

Cause: Appears to be associated with cerebral edema

The low PO2 at high altitudes causes arteriolar dilation, and if cerebral autoregulation does not compensate, there is an increase in capillary pressure that favours increased transudation of fluid into brain tissue leading to cerebral edema. In high-altitude cerebral edema, the capillary leakage in mountain sickness progresses to frank brain swelling, with ataxia, disorientation, and in some cases coma and death due to herniation of the brain through the tentorium.

Treatment:

* Descent to a lower altitude

* Diuretics like acetazolamide: inhibits carbonic acid anhydrase, and results in stimulated respiration, increased PaCO2, and reduced formation of CSF

* Glucocorticoids are administered as well. Their mechanism of action is not clear.
questions.learning: Proximal convoluted tubule — The symptoms are suggestive of acute mountain sickness and acetazolamide can be given for symptomatic relief. It acts on the proximal convoluted tubule.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the principal constituent of serum osmolality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium

The principal constituent of serum osmolality is sodium.

Serum osmolality = 2 sodium + (glucose/18) + (BUN/2.8).

The principal determinants of the osmolality of serum are the concentrations of sodium, glucose and urea (blood urea nitrogen or BUN).

Osmolality is defined as a measure of the osmoles (Osm) of solute per kilogram of solvent (osmol/kg or Osm/kg). The osmolality of the intracellular and extracellular fluids is maintained between 290 and 310 mOsm in each compartment.

An increase in plasma sodium (plasma osmolality) attracts water out of the cell. This leads to shrinkage of the intracellular volume. Hyponatremia (decreased plasma osmolality) allows the flow of water into the cell and expands intracellular volume.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycythemia vera

Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2.

A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.

It is characterized by :

• Increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis)
• Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit
• Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding.
• Headache, dizziness, hypertension, dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke.
• Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus
• Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia
• 15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis,
• PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients.

Primary myelofibrosis

• Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen.
• Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL.
• Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes, which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) and TGF-β.
• Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow.
• So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice, which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow, abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids.
• Blood shows mild leukocytosis, decreased Hb and hematocrit levels, and elevated LAP scores.
• Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20% of cases.

Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2, MPL, or CALR mutations.

• Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases) or MPL (5% to 10% of cases), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin.
• In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm. Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive, it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown.

CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]).

PV, PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor.
questions.learning: Polycythemia vera Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a distorted or irregularly shaped eye following delayed healing of a corneal ulcer, despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. Based on the clinical features and examination findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anterior staphyloma is a condition characterized by a bulging, ectatic scar of the cornea that is lined internally by uveal tissue (iris). It typically occurs as a late complication of a perforated corneal ulcer. When an ulcer heals with a thin, weak scar (pseudocornea), the intraocular pressure causes this weak area to protrude outward. The "deformed" and "dark" appearance mentioned comes from the iris pigment visible through the thin scar tissue. Option A (Megalocornea) is a non-progressive congenital enlargement of a clear cornea. Option B (Conjunctivitis) is a superficial inflammation and would not cause eye deformity. Option C (Buphthalmos) is an enlargement of the entire globe due to congenital glaucoma in neonates. Treatment for a large anterior staphyloma is often cosmetic (staphylomectomy or enucleation), as the eye is typically blind. This case emphasizes the importance of managing corneal ulcers aggressively to prevent perforation
questions.learning: Anterior staphyloma is a condition characterized by a bulging, ectatic scar of the cornea that is lined internally by uveal tissue (iris). It typically occurs as a late complication of a perforated corneal ulcer.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oculomotor nerve palsy

Causes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with delayed wound healing, dermatitis, recurrent diarrhea, and alopecia. This combination of symptoms indicates a deficiency of an essential dietary mineral involved in skin maintenance, immune function, and gastrointestinal health. Which mineral deficiency is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of alopecia, dermatitis (often perioral and acral), diarrhea, and impaired wound healing are the classic presentation of Zinc deficiency. Zinc is a critical trace mineral that serves as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes, including those involved in DNA synthesis, protein metabolism, and immune function. Severe congenital zinc deficiency is known as acrodermatitis enteropathica. Iron deficiency (Option A) primarily results in microcytic anemia, fatigue, and pica. Calcium deficiency (Option B) leads to muscle cramps, tetany, and osteoporosis. Magnesium deficiency (Option C) can cause neuromuscular irritability, tremors, and cardiac arrhythmias. Zinc's role in epithelial health and cell division explains why its lack so profoundly affects the skin and gastrointestinal tract. Supplementation typically leads to a rapid improvement in symptoms. Clinicians should consider zinc deficiency in patients with malabsorption syndromes, chronic alcoholism, or those on long-term parenteral nutrition without adequate mineral replacement
questions.learning: The symptoms of alopecia, dermatitis (often perioral and acral), diarrhea, and impaired wound healing are the classic presentation of Zinc deficiency.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which among the following is not used in post laryngectomy rehabilitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Super supraglottic swallow

Super supraglottic swallow is not used in post-laryngectomy rehabilitation.

Super-supraglottic swallow is a maneuver that prevents the aspiration of food or liquid by closing the airway before swallowing. It is used in the management of dysphagia. This method involves holding one’s breath to close the airway prior to swallowing, followed by coughing voluntarily immediately after swallowing to clear any residual food or liquid from the airway entrance. It is an effortful breath-holding technique, which not only results in Valsalva and subsequent leakage of bolus but can also result in arrhythmias.

Other options:

Option A: A tracheoesophageal prosthesis(TEP) involves a one-way valve that is inserted through a previously-created tracheoesophageal puncture. When the patient occludes the stoma, the exhaled air is shunted through the TEP into the oesophagus, where it induces vibration of the upper oesophagal sphincter, which is responsible for phonation. It generates the most intelligible, fluent, natural-sounding voice in contrast to other laryngeal speech methods.

Option B: Oesophagal speech also involves vibration of the upper oesophagal sphincter and subsequent phonation.

Option C: Polite yawning also called the nasal airflow-inducing maneuver is an important olfaction rehabilitation tool after a laryngectomy.

Electrolarynx produces vibrations that are transmitted through the skin toward the throat. The sound generated is converted into low-pitch speech by the vocal tract—palate, tongue, and teeth. The advantages are that is easy and quick to learn, while the disadvantages are that the voice is monotonous and the constant occupation of one hand.
questions.learning: Super supraglottic swallow Super supraglottic swallow is not used in post-laryngectomy rehabilitation. Super-supraglottic swallow is a maneuver that prevents the aspiration of food or liquid by closing the airway before swallowing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most commonly seen pattern in chest CT of patients affected with COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ground glass opacity

Ground glass opacity (GGO) is the most commonly seen pattern in chest CT of patients with COVID-19.

Some of the typical features seen in the CT scans of COVID-19 patients include:

* Ground glass opacities

* Consolidation

* Air bronchograms

* Interlobular septal thickenings

* Visible intralobular lines (crazy-paving pattern)

* Reversed halo sign

The image given below shows an axial CT scan with multiple patchy areas of pure ground-glass opacities bilaterally. GGO are hazy areas with slightly increased density in lungs without obscuration of underlying bronchial and vascular margins.

The image given below shows a CT scan with bilateral GGO in the lower lobe (red frames) and air bronchogram (white arrow) in the left subpleural area. Air bronchograms appear like air-filled bronchi within a highly attenuated parenchymal background. These are dilated bronchi filled with mucus plugs and do not truly contain air.

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple consolidation areas and interlobular septal thickening (arrows) in both the lungs. The pulmonary interstitial structures such as interlobular septa and intralobular lines can thicken and manifest as small linear opacities.

The image given below shows a CT scan with crazy-paving pattern (black circled areas). It is defined as the presence of GGOs with superimposed interlobular septal thickening giving the appearance of irregular paving stones.

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple lesions with reversed halo sign(arrows). The reversed halo sign or atoll sign is the presence of a ring-like area of consolidation with a superimposed rounded GGO.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the seeds shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nigella sativa

The seeds shown in the given image are of the plant Nigella sativa. These are also known as black cumin or kalonji.

The seeds are the most commonly used parts of the plant in traditional medicine. Seeds have a pungent and bitter taste with a considerable amount of oil inside. The seeds are used as a spice in cooking. They are also used as a food preservative and the most often used therapeutic agent is its oil.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Reinke crystals are seen in which of the following gonadal tumours:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Leydig cell tumor

Reinke crystals are rod-shaped, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions characteristic of Leydig cell tumors. They are composed of crystallized proteins related to steroidogenesis.

Leydig cell tumors arise from testicular interstitial cells and often produce androgens.

Seminoma, yolk sac tumor, and Sertoli cell tumor do not show Reinke crystals.

Because Leydig cells produce androgens, hormonal effects occur.

| Age group | Presentation

| --------- | ------------

| Children | Precocious puberty

| Adults | Gynecomastia or infertility

Gynecomastia occurs due to peripheral conversion of testosterone to estrogen.

| Tumor | Characteristic Feature

| ----- | ----------------------

| Leydig cell tumor | Reinke crystals

| Yolk sac tumor | Schiller–Duval bodies

| Granulosa cell tumor | Call–Exner bodies

| Dysgerminoma | Fried egg cells
questions.learning: Leydig cell tumor Reinke crystals are rod-shaped, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions characteristic of Leydig cell tumors. They are composed of crystallized proteins related to steroidogenesis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the following instrument commonly used in obstetrics.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Episiotomy scissors

The instrument given in the picture is episiotomy scissors. The angulation in the scissor is to prevent the extension of pelvic tears into the anal margins and obstetric anal sphincter injuries / complete perineal tears.

Complications of episiotomy:

They can be immediate or remote.

Immediate complications include an extension of the incision into the rectum, vulval hematoma, wound dehiscence and injury to anal sphincter.

Remote complications include dyspareunia, chances of perineal lacerations in subsequent labor and scar endometriosis (rare).

Mayo scissors are long and stout scissors. They can be blunt-tipped/pointed tip/straight or curved. Straight mayo scissors are designed for cutting body tissues near the surface of a wound. They are also used to cut sutures and are also known as suture-cutting scissors.

Curved mayo scissors allow much deeper penetration into the wound and are used to cut thick tissues such as those found in the uterus, muscles, breast, and foot. Mayo scissors used for dissection are placed in tissue with the tips closed. The scissors are then opened so that the tips open and spread out the tissue during the dissection process.
questions.learning: Episiotomy scissors — The instrument given in the picture is episiotomy scissors. The angulation in the scissor is to prevent the extension of pelvic tears into the anal margins and obstetric anal sphincter injuries / complete perineal tears.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child came to the casualty with difficulty in walking and pain in the perianal region. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, it produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals with picric acid. What is the test done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Barberio test

The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test.

Barberio is used to detect seminal fluid. When a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate are produced.

Other options:

Option B: Florence test is used to detect semen. If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately

Option C: The Teichmann test (hemin crystal test) is used to detect bloodstains. If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish-red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of hemin or hematin chloride appear. When hydrogen peroxide is added, the hematin crystals give bubbles of gas.

Option D: The acid phosphatase test is a quantitative test for the presence of acid phosphatase enzyme in the semen. High levels of acid phosphatase from prostatic secretions are present in seminal stains (Normal vaginal secretions have low levels of acid phosphatase). Positive reactions are found till 36 hours after which the enzyme levels fall and disappear within 72 hours. In the absence of demonstrable sperm or aspermia, this test can be considered conclusive.
questions.learning: Barberio test — The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test. Barberio is used to detect seminal fluid.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: New Cholera which is a notifiable disease, should be reported to World Health Organisation within ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 24 hours

Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence.

The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.

An area is declared free of cholera when twice the incubation period, 10 days, has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case.
questions.learning: 24 hours Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence. The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A hemicolectomy specimen biopsy shows adenocarcinoma invading the subserosa with deposits in the mesentery but no lymph node involvement or distant spread. What is the tumor stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3 N1c M0

In colon cancer staging, two findings are crucial: depth of invasion (T stage) and presence of nodal disease or tumor deposits (N stage).

• A tumor that invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/pericolic tissue is staged as T3 (it has not penetrated the serosal surface, which would make it T4a).

• Tumor deposits are discrete cancer nodules in the mesocolic/mesenteric fat that lack identifiable lymph node tissue. Importantly, when tumor deposits are present but no regional lymph nodes are involved, the nodal stage is classified as N1c (even if all lymph nodes are negative).

• Absence of distant spread corresponds to M0.

Therefore, adenocarcinoma invading subserosa with mesenteric tumor deposits, no lymph node involvement, and no metastasis = T3 N1c M0.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Outlet forceps are applied at which station?
questions.explanation: According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), outlet forceps application requires that the fetal scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia. Specifically, the fetal skull has reached the pelvic floor/perineum, and the sagittal suture is in the direct anteroposterior diameter or a slight oblique position. Station +2 (Option C) is classified as a "mid-forceps" delivery if the head is above +2 but engaged, or a "low-forceps" delivery if the leading point is at station +2 or lower but not on the perineum. Station 0 (Option B) is engagement at the level of the ischial spines. Option A (1/5th palpable) refers to the abdominal descent of the head and is not a criteria for outlet forceps. Outlet forceps are considered the safest instrumental delivery type because the fetal head is at the lowest possible point in the birth canal
questions.learning: According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), outlet forceps application requires that the fetal scalp is visible at the introitus without separating the labia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A young male came to the hospital with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding. The patient received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago. What is the best management for this patient?
options: Human tetanus immunoglobulin and full course of vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Single-dose tetanus toxoid

The patient with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding, who received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago, should be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine and appropriate wound care.

Wound management involves cleaning the wound thoroughly to remove soil, foreign bodies, and necrotic tissue.

Note: In cases where combined immunization is necessary, the patient is given 250 units of human tetanus immunoglobulin in one arm and 0.5 mL of adsorbed tetanus toxoid (PTAP or APT) in the other arm or gluteal region. The antitoxin is given for immediate temporary protection, and the tetanus toxoid is given for long-lasting protection.
questions.learning: Single-dose tetanus toxoid — The patient with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding, who received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago, should be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine and appropriate wound care.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
A child presents with a dog bite from a street dog. On examination, an abrasion of 1.5 cm is present, with slight oozing. Which of the following statements are correct?

1. Category 3 wound
2. Wash the wound with normal tap water for 15-20 minutes
3. Clean the wound with spirit
4. Loose suturing of the wound with a proper dressing
5. Equine immunoglobin is given at a dose of 40 IU/kg of body weight, twice
6. Intra-dermal vaccine is administered on days 0, 3, 7, 28
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 6

A child presenting with abrasion with slight oozing after a dog bite comes under category III. The correct statements are 1, 2, 3, and 6.

The following measures should be taken immediately to stop the contraction of rabies:

• Cleansing: The most important step in the prevention of rabies is washing the affected area with plenty of soap and water under a running tap for 15 minutes. This is a standard procedure that minimizes the contraction of rabies.
• Chemical treatment: After washing and drying the wound, disinfectants like povidone-iodine and spirit can be applied.
• Suturing: Bite wounds are not sutured generally. If suturing is unavoidable, rabies immunoglobulin should be infiltrated in the depth and around the wound, and suturing should be delayed by a few hours.
• In unavoidable situations, minimal loose sutures may be applied to arrest bleeding.
• Other measures: Local antibiotics and tetanus toxoids should be given.

Different wound categories for post-exposure prophylaxis:

Categories of wound
Post-exposure prophylaxis

Category I - touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin
None

Category II - nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches, or abrasions
without bleeding
Immediate vaccination and
local treatment of the wound

Category III- single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin contacts with bats
Immediate vaccination and
administration of rabies
immunoglobulin; local
treatment of the wound

Post-exposure prophylaxis regimen for rabies:

Intramuscular regimen: In this regimen, 1 ml or 0.5 ml of vaccine is injected into the deltoid in patients with category II and III wounds.

• Essen regimen: A 5-dose regimen in which 1 dose of vaccine is given on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28.
• Zagreb regimen: A 4-dose multisite regimen in which 2 doses of vaccine are given on day 0, followed by 1 dose on days 7 and 21.

Intradermal regimen: In this regimen, 0.1 ml of injection is given at 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, and 28.

Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin at a dose of 40 IU/kg (a maximum of 3000 IU) body weight is given once. It is given to all Category III bites and also Category II bites in the case of immune-compromised persons.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 6 A child presenting with abrasion with slight oozing after a dog bite comes under category III. The correct statements are 1, 2, 3, and 6.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the ICDS program in India, what is the calorie and protein supplementation provided to a child aged 6-72 months?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 500 kcal, 12-15 grams

Under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, children aged 6–72 months receive supplementary nutrition providing 500 kcal and 12–15 g of protein per day for approximately 300 days per year to bridge the gap between dietary intake and nutritional requirements, thereby preventing protein-energy malnutrition.

Why not the other options?

• A. 200 kcal, 6–8 g: Inadequate for the ICDS recommendation for children aged 6–72 months.
• B. 300 kcal, 8–10 g: Lower than the recommended supplementary nutrition under ICDS.
• D. 600 kcal, 18–20 g: Exceeds the routine supplementation provided to normal children under ICDS.

The supplementation values for each group under ICDS Program:

| Beneficiary | Calories | Protein

| ----------- | -------- | -------

| Child 6–72 months (normal) | 500 kcal | 12–15 grams

| Malnourished children | 800 kcal | 20–25 grams

| Pregnant and lactating mother | 600 kcal | 18–20 grams
