questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following investigations provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dobutamine stress echocardiography

Among the given investigations, dobutamine stress echocardiography provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications.

Preoperative cardiac stress testing can help identify the presence and severity of preexisting CAD. The prognostic performance of these tests is better assessed based on positive and negative likelihood ratios. Among all the given options, dobutamine stress echocardiography has the maximum positive likelihood ratio and hence provides the most accurate prognostic information.

Even though coronary angiography is considered the gold standard, it may not absolutely risk-stratify patients because many perioperative cardiac events may be related to noncritical coronary lesions.
questions.learning: Dobutamine stress echocardiography Among the given investigations, dobutamine stress echocardiography provides the most accurate prognostic information with respect to predicting risks of perioperative cardiac complications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Water hammer pulse is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic regurgitation

Water hammer pulse, also known as Corrigan’s pulse, is characterized by a sharp rise and a rapid fall-off and is seen in aortic regurgitation (AR) due to the fact that arterial pressure falls rapidly in late systole and early diastole.

In AR, the pulse pressure is widened due to systolic hypertension and decreased diastolic pressure. The diastolic pressure is measured at Korotkoff phase IV. In certain patients with AR or a combination of aortic stenosis (AS) and AR, the carotid arterial pulse may exhibit a bisferiens pattern, characterized by two systolic waves separated by a trough.

The apical impulse is heaving and displaced inferiorly. A diastolic thrill may be palpable along the left sternal border.

A2 is usually absent in AR. An early diastolic murmur can be auscultated in chronic AR. It is best heard in the third intercostal space along the left sternal edge.

Severe AS (Option A) would show pulsus parvus et tardus, characterized by the carotid pulse rising slowly to a delayed peak.

Chronic mitral regurgitation (Option D) shows a sharp, low volume upstroke due to reduced cardiac output and acute mitral regurgitation demonstrates narrow pulse pressure.
questions.learning: Aortic regurgitation Water hammer pulse, also known as Corrigan’s pulse, is characterized by a sharp rise and a rapid fall-off and is seen in aortic regurgitation (AR) due to the fact that arterial pressure falls rapidly in late systole and early diastole.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16 year old girl presents to the OPD with a history of primary amenorrhoea and cyclical pain. Perineal examination reveals a bulge protruding from the vagina and is shown as below. Identify the cause of this presentation:
options: Transverse septum in the proximal vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

A history of cyclical abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea and a bulging vaginal membrane suggest cryptomenorrhoea caused by an imperforate hymen.

In addition to this, retention of urine and a palpable abdominal mass may be present. An ultrasound scan of the pelvis confirms the diagnosis. The condition is treated by making a cruciate incision on the hymen. This would resume a normal reproductive function in her.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — A history of cyclical abdominal pain, primary amenorrhea and a bulging vaginal membrane suggest cryptomenorrhoea caused by an imperforate hymen.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 30 year old female is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks. When asked questions she becomes irritable and angry. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Bipolar I disorder with manic episode
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bipolar I disorder with manic episode

This question describes a female who has mania as she is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks.

Bipolar disorder manifests in two primary types:

* Bipolar I: This type is characterized by at least one lifetime episode of mania. Episodes of major depressive disorder may or may not be present.

* Bipolar II: This type involves episodes of hypomania alongside episodes of major depressive disorder. A key diagnostic criterion is the absence of any history of a manic episode.

Mania is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, elated, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy, lasting at least 1 week.

Other options:

Option A: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterised by repetitive intrusive thoughts, impulses or images which are not associated with compulsive acts.

Option C: Hypomania is a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated/irritable mood, abnormally and persistently increased activity/energy, lasting for at least 4 days. It is similar to a manic episode wherein the patients can portray all of the above-mentioned symptoms but it is not severe enough to cause impairment in social or occupational functioning.

Option D: Cyclothymia is a chronic, fluctuating mood disturbance with many periods of hypomania and of depression.

Pearl PF1511: Bipolar disorder

Bipolar & related disorders

Manic episode

• Symptoms more severe
• 1 week unless hospitalized
• Marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or hospitalization necessary
• May have psychotic features; makes episode manic by definition

Hypomanic episode

• Symptoms less severe
• 4 days to less than 7 days
• Unequivocal, observable change in functioning from patient's baseline
• Symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment or necessitate hospitalization
• No psychotic features

Bipolar I

• Manic episode(s)
• Depressive episodes common (but not required for diagnosis)

Bipolar II

• Hypomanic episode(s)
• Major depressive episodes (required for diagnosis)

Cyclothymic disorder

• At least 2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms that
do not meet criteria for hypomanic episodes or major depressive episodes
questions.learning: Bipolar I disorder with manic episode — This question describes a female who has mania as she is very talkative, hyperactive, doesn't sleep well and spends a lot of money shopping for the past 2 weeks.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the causative organism of "bull neck"?
questions.explanation: "Bull neck" is a classic clinical description used to characterize the massive swelling of the neck seen in severe cases of diphtheria. This appearance results from extensive cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue edema. It is caused by the exotoxin-producing strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Corynebacterium ulcerans (Option B) can cause a similar diphtheria-like illness but is rarer and often linked to raw milk. Corynebacterium minutissimum (Option C) causes erythrasma, a superficial skin infection. Corynebacterium tenuis (Option D) is associated with trichomycosis axillaris. Along with the bull neck, patients typically have a thick, adherent, greyish-white "pseudomembrane" on the tonsils and pharynx. Diphtheria is a medical emergency requiring urgent administration of diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics (like penicillin or erythromycin). The "bull neck" is an ominous prognostic sign indicating a high toxic load and potential for airway obstruction or myocarditis
questions.learning: "Bull neck" is a classic clinical description used to characterize the massive swelling of the neck seen in severe cases of diphtheria. This appearance results from extensive cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue edema.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with cleft lip, cleft palate and mental retardation. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patau syndrome

The given findings of cleft lip, cleft palate with mental retardation in a child are consistent with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).

Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities. Patients can develop holoprosencephaly, which is characterized by fused frontal lobes and a single ventricle. Olfactory bulbs are also absent. The midline facial abnormalities seen with trisomy 13 include cleft lip, cleft palate, mental retardation, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, renal defects, and congenital heart diseases.

The image below shows some facial features of Patau syndrome:

Other options:

Option A: Prader-Willi syndrome occurs due to the deletion of band 15q12 on the paternal chromosome and the silencing of the same set of genes derived from maternal chromosomes. It is characterized by mental retardation, obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism, short stature, small hands and feet.

Option C: Angelman syndrome is characterized by the deletion of the ubiquitin ligase gene (UBE3A) on maternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the paternal chromosomal counterpart. It is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter. Due to inappropriate laughter and ataxia, they are also known as happy puppets.

Option D: Trisomy 18 or Edwards syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart diseases. The most characteristic finding is a clenched fist with overlapping fingers: the index finger overlies the third and fourth fingers, while the fifth finger overlaps the fourth. It is also associated with polyhydramnios and a single umbilical artery.
questions.learning: Patau syndrome — The given findings of cleft lip, cleft palate with mental retardation in a child are consistent with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with bowing of the legs, and an X-ray of the wrist shows characteristic abnormalities. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of bow legs (genu varum) combined with the classic radiological findings of metaphyseal fraying, cupping, and splaying at the wrist is diagnostic of Rickets. Rickets is caused by Vitamin D deficiency, which leads to defective mineralization of the growing bone matrix. Regarding the distractors, scurvy (Option B) presents with different X-ray features such as the "white line of Frankel," "Pelkan spurs," and "Wimberger’s ring" of the epiphysis, typically without the wide cupped metaphysis. While hypophosphatemia (Option C) can cause rickets-like bone changes, it is a metabolic cause and is less common than nutritional Vitamin D deficiency in India. The absence of "none" (Option D) is confirmed by the presence of these definitive signs. Thus, the specific "frayed and cupped" appearance of the radius and ulna on the X-ray confirms Rickets
questions.learning: The clinical finding of bow legs (genu varum) combined with the classic radiological findings of metaphyseal fraying, cupping, and splaying at the wrist is diagnostic of Rickets.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A senior resident in the hospital is performing the following clinical examination as shown in the image below. Which of the following structures will not be visible to him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arytenoids

The senior resident would not be visualizing the arytenoids as he is performing a posterior rhinoscopy indicated by the post-nasal mirror that he is holding.

The posterior rhinoscopy mirror (St. Clair Thompson mirror) has two bends in the shaft and is bayonet shaped.

The structures seen in the posterior rhinoscopy are:

• Adenoids
• Posterior ends of nasal turbinates
• Opening of the Eustachian tube
• The posterior border of the nasal septum
• Fossa of Rosenmuller
• Torus tubarius
• The upper surface of the soft palate

The images below show the posterior rhinoscopy mirror and structures seen in the posterior rhinoscopy:

Indirect laryngoscopy is done using a laryngeal mirror. It is straight without any bends with a mirror at the end.

Structures seen during indirect laryngoscopy (in order):

• Oropharynx: Base of the tongue, lingual tonsils, valleculae, medial and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
• Laryngopharynx: Both piriform fossae, post cricoid region, posterior wall of laryngopharynx.
• Larynx: Epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, cuneiform and corniculate cartilages, glossoepiglottic folds, pharyngoepiglottic folds, aryepiglottic fold, true and false vocal cords, anterior commissure, posterior commissure, subglottis and rings of the trachea.

The images below show the laryngeal mirror and structures seen during indirect laryngoscopy:

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following comes under ASA grade 1?
questions.explanation: The ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative physical condition and predict perioperative risk. ASA Grade 1 refers to a completely healthy patient with no systemic disease and no functional limitations. Such individuals are physically fit, have no underlying medical conditions, and are considered to have the lowest anesthetic risk. Examples include a young adult undergoing elective surgery like hernia repair or a child scheduled for tonsillectomy without any comorbidities. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Mild disease: This corresponds to ASA Grade 2, which includes patients with mild systemic illness such as controlled hypertension or diabetes without complications. (C) Moderate disease: This falls under ASA Grade 3, where there is significant systemic disease causing functional limitation, such as poorly controlled hypertension or stable angina. (D) Morbid patient: This corresponds to ASA Grade 4 or 5, indicating severe systemic disease that is life-threatening or a moribund state. Thus, ASA Grade 1 clearly represents a healthy patient
questions.learning: The ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification is used to assess a patient’s preoperative physical condition and predict perioperative risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presented with high-grade fever, and purpuric rash as shown in the image below. CSF sample showed gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria meningitidis

The above image shows a purpuric rash seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial haemorrhages.

Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.
questions.learning: Neisseria meningitidis — The above image shows a purpuric rash seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with mental retardation and an inability to walk. The funduscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates the most likely diagnosis to be Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Other options:

Options B - Hunter disease (mucopolysaccharidosis II) is an X-linked disorder that arises due to the deficiency of iduronate 2-sulfatase. Short stature, joint stiffness, and intellectual disability are the features.

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.
questions.learning: Tay-Sachs disease — The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates the most likely diagnosis to be Tay-Sachs disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a group of 60 patients diagnosed with COVID-19, 12 deaths were recorded. What is the case fatality rate in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a proportion used to measure the severity or virulence of a disease. It is calculated as the ratio of the total number of deaths from a disease to the total number of diagnosed cases of that same disease, expressed as a percentage. Formula: CFR = (Number of deaths / Total diagnosed cases) x 100. Substituting the provided values: CFR = (12 deaths / 60 cases) x 100 = 0.2 x 100 = 20%. CFR is useful for measuring the risk of death in acute infectious diseases like COVID-19 or cholera. It can vary between different epidemics based on host health, medical care quality, and the pathogen's strain. The Case Survival Rate (CSR) would be 100 minus the CFR, which in this case is 80%. Options B, C, and D are incorrect mathematical results
questions.learning: The Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a proportion used to measure the severity or virulence of a disease. It is calculated as the ratio of the total number of deaths from a disease to the total number of diagnosed cases of that same disease, expressed as a…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is suggested in a young boy presenting with a fissured tongue, cracked lips, lesions at the angles of the mouth, and reduced red blood cell glutathione reductase activity on investigation?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of glossitis (fissured tongue), cheilosis (fissured lips), and angular stomatitis (lesions at the corners of the mouth) is highly suggestive of Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency. The biochemical hallmark of this deficiency is decreased erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, as flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), a derivative of B2, is an essential cofactor for this enzyme. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option A) leads to megaloblastic anemia and neurological issues. Vitamin B3 deficiency (Option B) causes pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds" (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Biotin deficiency (Option C) typically presents with dermatitis and hair loss. Because the biochemical test mentioned is the specific gold standard for assessing riboflavin status, Riboflavin is the definitive diagnosis. Early identification is crucial, as these mucocutaneous symptoms are reversible with oral supplementation
questions.learning: The clinical triad of glossitis (fissured tongue), cheilosis (fissured lips), and angular stomatitis (lesions at the corners of the mouth) is highly suggestive of Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Obliteration of right cardiac border on chest X-Ray indicates pathology involving which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right middle lobe

Right middle lobe pathology causes obliteration of right cardiac border.

The silhouette sign is the loss of clear demarcation between normal lung and soft tissue (e.g., heart, diaphragm). This occurs when the lung parenchyma is no longer filled with air and the contrast between air and soft tissue is lost.

A silhouette in a chest radiograph is the outline of a particular structure that is formed at the interface of two tissues with different tissue densities eg. cardiac silhouette between the heart and the lung. Blurring/obliteration of these normal silhouettes due to disease pathologies is known as the silhouette sign.

The silhouette can be obscured only by a pathology that is in direct anatomical contact, eg. right cardiac border will be obscured when there is right middle lobe pneumonia. Hence, the silhouette sign helps us in localizing the site of pathology.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following are recognized local side effects associated with the use of topical corticosteroids? (INICET MAY 2025) 1. Blue grey discolouration of skin 2. Atrophy 3. Acneiform eruption 4. Hypertrichosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4 only

Topical corticosteroids commonly cause local cutaneous adverse effects due to their anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive actions on skin.

Recognized local side effects:

• Skin atrophy → thinning, wrinkling, telangiectasia (most important)
• Acneiform eruptions → steroid acne, folliculitis
• Hypertrichosis → excessive hair growth

Not typical:

• Blue-grey discoloration → seen in conditions like drug-induced pigmentation (e.g., minocycline), not a steroid effect
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 only Topical corticosteroids commonly cause local cutaneous adverse effects due to their anti-proliferative and immunosuppressive actions on skin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old presents on postpartum day 10 with high-grade fever, malaise and pain in her left breast. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her child. She had presented to the OPD a few days back with mild pain and congestion of the breast and was prescribed oral analgesics and antibiotics. On examination, the left breast appears engorged and a fluctuant swelling is present. Ultrasound showed fluid collection. What is the next most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Breast abscess

A lactational mother with high-grade fever and fluctuant swelling which did not resolve with analgesics and antibiotics points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess.

The most common aetiology of breast abscess is Staph. aureus and occurs commonly in lactational mothers. It occurs due to the colonisation of obstructed lactiferous ducts. It is commoner in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Signs and symptoms: Fever and malaise, localized pain and tenderness, redness and swelling of the affected breast, fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed. In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspiration and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage are performed. The conditions include:

* Presence of thick pus

* Bacteria resistant to antibiotics

* If just a superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess

Other options:

Option B: Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of the lactiferous duct due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to a retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscesses.

In Iron deficiency Anaemia, Total Iron Binding Capacity(TIBC) is increased in order to compensate to the deficient state.

• Increased total iron-binding capacity

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The below image is of a femur bone.Which of the following muscles is attached to "A"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iliopsoas

The image shows the posterior surface of the right femur and the structure marked "A" is the lesser trochanter where the iliopsoas muscle is attached.

The Iliopsoas comprises of Psoas major and Iliacus. They arise from the lumbar spine and the inner surface of the ilium bone respectively, and insert on the lesser trochanter. The iliopsoas cause flexion of the hip.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur, shaft, and distal femur.

* The proximal femur consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface. The lesser trochanter is the posteromedial projection of the femur arising posteroinferiorly from the neck-shaft junction.

* The shaft of the femur consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line.

* The distal femur consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman presents with a progressively enlarging fleshy growth on the sclera that is extending onto the cornea toward the pupillary area, causing discomfort and visual disturbance. What is the most appropriate management for this progressive pterygium?
questions.explanation: A pterygium is a benign, wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of the bulbar conjunctiva that can invade the cornea. When the pterygium is progressive and begins encroaching on the visual axis (pupil) or causing significant astigmatism, surgical intervention is mandatory. The current gold standard management is surgical excision followed by a conjunctival autograft (CAG). This technique involves covering the bare sclera with a piece of the patient's own healthy conjunctiva, which significantly reduces the high rate of recurrence compared to simple excision alone. Keratoplasty (Option A) is only indicated for severe scarring after removal. Observation (Option C) is inappropriate for a growth that is actively threatening vision. Beta-radiation (Option D) is an older technique used to prevent recurrence but has been largely replaced by autografting due to potential long-term scleral melting. Thus, excision with autograft is the definitive treatment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with gradual hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus in her right ear. Examination reveals a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane, an audible mastoid bruit, and a negative Rinne test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of pulsatile tinnitus (hearing one's own heartbeat), conductive hearing loss (negative Rinne test), and a reddish-blue mass visible behind the tympanic membrane is the pathognomonic clinical presentation for a Glomus tumor (specifically Glomus jugulare or tympanicum). The presence of an audible bruit over the mastoid further confirms the highly vascular nature of this benign paraganglioma. CSOM (Option A) and ASOM (Option B) involve infection, presenting with discharge and pain respectively, rather than a pulsatile vascular mass. Mastoiditis (Option C) is a complication of infection involving retroauricular swelling and systemic fever, not a vascular neoplasm. Glomus tumors often present with the "rising sun" sign behind the drum. Diagnosis is typically supported by imaging (CT/MRI) showing a "salt and pepper" appearance. Therefore, given the specific vascular symptoms and auscultatory findings, glomus tumor is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment usually involves surgical resection or embolization depending on the extent of the tumor

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During the inflammatory response, which molecule is responsible for promoting the adhesion of leukocytes to the vascular endothelium?
questions.explanation: During inflammation, leukocyte recruitment to the site of injury occurs in steps: rolling → adhesion → transmigration. The initial interaction (rolling) of leukocytes along the vascular endothelium is mediated by selectins, especially P-selectin. P-selectin is expressed on activated endothelial cells and platelets. It binds to carbohydrate ligands (like sialyl Lewis X) on leukocytes, causing them to slow down and roll along the vessel wall. This rolling is crucial because it allows leukocytes to come into close contact with the endothelium, preparing them for firm adhesion. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Platelet-activating factor (PAF) : Involved in leukocyte activation and chemotaxis, not primary adhesion (C) VCAM-1 : Mediates firm adhesion (via integrins), not the initial adhesion/rolling (D) Complement : Plays a role in opsonization and chemotaxis, not adhesion
questions.learning: During inflammation, leukocyte recruitment to the site of injury occurs in steps: rolling → adhesion → transmigration. The initial interaction (rolling) of leukocytes along the vascular endothelium is mediated by selectins, especially P-selectin.

questions.text: As per the WHO expert group, the cutoff point of haemoglobin in venous blood for the diagnosis of anaemia in adult males is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 13 g/dL

According to the WHO criteria, anemia in an adult male is diagnosed when the hemoglobin concentration is <13 g/dL in venous blood.

• Adult male: Hb <13 g/dL → Anemia
• Adult non-pregnant female: Hb <12 g/dL → Anemia
• Pregnancy: Hb <11 g/dL → Anemia

Therefore, the correct cutoff is 13 g/dL.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Diphtheria vaccine is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxoid

Diptheria vaccine is a toxoid.

Toxoids: Certain organisms like diphtheria and tetanus bacilli produce exotoxins. The toxins produced by these organisms are detoxicated and used in the preparation of vaccines. The antibodies produced to neutralize the toxic moiety produced during infection, rather than acting upon the organisms. In general, toxoid preparations are highly efficacious and safe immunizing agents.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with fatigue and tingling sensation in the arms, weight loss and h/o polyuria. The following findings were detected on bone marrow biopsy. What is probable cause ?
options: Subacute combined degeneration due to cobalamin deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multiple myeloma

The given clinical scenario and marrow aspirate with plasma cells suggest multiple myeloma. The clinical features of fatigue, tingling sensation in the arms, weight loss, and polyuria are due to hypercalcemia.

Plasma cell dyscrasias are B-cell proliferations that contain neoplastic plasma cells that secrete a monoclonal Ig or Ig fragment. Multiple myeloma is a malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine. It is a disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years.

Signs and symptoms include hypercalcemia, fractures/ lytic bone lesions, renal failure and anaemia.

Investigations reveal:

• Radiography - Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray
• Electrophoresis - Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin
• Urinalysis - Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)
• Bone marrow biopsy - 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%)
• Peripheral smear - Rouleaux formation. A high level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.

Plasma cell tumours are positive for CD138.

Morphology:

Myeloma cell size varies from small differentiated cells to large immature and undifferentiated cells. Plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate. Other cytologic variants include flame cells and Mott cells.

Flame cells have fiery red cytoplasm, and Mott cells are with multiple grape-like cytoplasmic droplets. Other inclusions include fibrils, crystalline rods, and globules.

Image showing Mott cell:

The globular inclusions are Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear). Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific.

Image showing Russell and Dutcher bodies:

Other options:

Options A and D: Megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration(SACD) occur due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Patients with SACD present with loss of vibration sense and proprioception, paresthesia, unsteady gait, loss of deep tendon reflexes, peripheral neuropathy, and optic neuropathy.

Option C: Diabetes does not lead to subacute degeneration.
questions.learning: Multiple myeloma — The given clinical scenario and marrow aspirate with plasma cells suggest multiple myeloma. The clinical features of fatigue, tingling sensation in the arms, weight loss, and polyuria are due to hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the medical term for a person who has a fear of tall buildings and looking down from heights?
questions.explanation: The specific, intense fear of heights, including looking down from tall buildings, is called Acrophobia. Agoraphobia (Option A) is the fear of being in situations or places (like open spaces or crowds) where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during a panic attack. Claustrophobia (Option C) is the fear of enclosed or small spaces. Nomophobia (Option D) is the fear of being without a mobile phone or being out of cellular contact. Acrophobia is one of the most common specific phobias and can cause significant distress or avoidance behavior. Patients may experience dizziness, sweating, or a sense of "pulling" toward the edge when exposed to heights. Treatment usually involves Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), specifically exposure therapy, where the person is gradually and systematically exposed to feared heights in a safe environment to reduce the anxiety response

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Defective Tyrosine transaminase is associated with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2 Tyrosinemia

Defective Tyrosine transaminase is associated with type II tyrosinemia, known as Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia.

There are three types of tyrosinemias:

* Type 1 tyrosinemia: also known as hepatorenal tyrosinemia is an autosomal recessive condition. The defective enzyme is fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase. Clinical features are liver failure, hypoglycemia, boiled cabbage odor in the urine, and mental retardation.

* Type 2 is known as oculocutaneous tyrosinemia or Richner-Hanhart syndrome. The defective enzyme is tyrosine transaminase. Clinical features are palmoplantar keratosis, painful corneal erosions, photophobia, and mental retardation.

* Type 3 is known as neonatal tyrosinemia. It is due to the deficiency of 4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate hydroxylase. Clinical features include normal liver function, developmental delay, seizures, and intermittent ataxia.

Alkaptonuria is an inborn error of metabolism due to the deficiency of an enzyme homogentisate oxidase, leading to the accumulation of homogentisic acid in connective tissue resulting in ochronosis. Due to the oxidation and polymerization of homogenetic acid, it shows a characteristic blackening of urine on standing for a long time or black stain in diapers. They often present in the third to the fourth decade of life.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drug binds to CD4 receptors and is used for both CCR-5 as well as CXCR-4 tropic HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ibalizumab

Ibalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds the CD4 receptor post-attachment and blocks HIV entry. Because it targets CD4 rather than the co-receptor, it is effective against both CCR5- and CXCR4-tropic HIV strains. Maraviroc blocks only CCR5, not CXCR4 virus. CD4-directed entry inhibition is the key distinguishing feature.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy rapidly develops hypoglycemia after moderate activity. Blood examination reveals raised levels of ketone bodies, lactic acid, and triglycerides. On examination, the liver and kidneys are found to be enlarged. Histopathology of the liver shows deposits of glycogen in an excess amount. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. von Gierke’s disease

The given features are consistent with von Gierke's disease. It is the most common glycogen storage disease.

Enzyme deficient in this condition is glucose-6-phosphatase (common to both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis). Inheritance is autosomal recessive.

Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to the deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas the spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

A definitive diagnosis is made using a liver biopsy. Fructose and galactose restriction in the diet is advised.
questions.learning: von Gierke’s disease The given features are consistent with von Gierke's disease. It is the most common glycogen storage disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: From which of the following structure does the saccule develop?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pars inferior

The saccule develops from pars inferior.

The development of the inner ear begins in the 3rd week of fetal life and is completed by the 16th week. The surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon thickens to form otic/auditory placodes, which then invaginate to form the otic vesicle (otocysts).

The cells of the otic vesicle differentiate to form ganglion cells, which later develop into the vestibulocochlear ganglia. Later each otic vesicle divides into a dorsal component called pars superior and a ventral component called pars inferior.

Pars superior gives rise to the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic ducts. Pars inferior gives rise to saccule and cochlear duct. The saccule is connected to the cochlea through a narrow duct called ductus reuniens.
questions.learning: Pars inferior — The saccule develops from pars inferior. The development of the inner ear begins in the 3rd week of fetal life and is completed by the 16th week.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The Anemia Mukt Bharat program aims to reduce anemia across India through targeted interventions. Which statement correctly describes how Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation is administered under this program?
options: IFA is provided during the 2nd trimester of pregnancy and continues during lactation for up to 6 months
IFA supplementation is administered solely during pregnancy
A 100-day course of IFA supplementation is sufficient
Administering IFA during the 1st trimester is adequate.
questions.explanation: The Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy follows a comprehensive "6x6x6" framework to reduce anemia prevalence across the life cycle. For pregnant women, the protocol mandates the administration of one Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) tablet daily, containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid. This starts in the second trimester (after the first 12 weeks of pregnancy) and continues for 180 days throughout the remainder of the pregnancy. Crucially, the supplementation must continue postpartum during lactation for an additional 180 days (6 months). Solely administering it during pregnancy (Option B) is insufficient to replenish maternal iron stores depleted during childbirth. A 100-day course (Option C) was the older standard, now replaced by the 180-day regimen to ensure better clinical outcomes. First-trimester administration (Option D) is generally avoided to prevent aggravating nausea and because the physiological demand for iron increases most rapidly during the second and third trimesters

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought with a gradually enlarging, tender mass in the flank region noticed over the past few weeks. On examination, the child appears otherwise well. The mass is firm, non-fluctuant, non-mobile, and not associated with overlying skin changes or signs of inflammation. No other systemic symptoms are present. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A large, firm, flank mass in a 4-year-old child is the classic presentation for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common primary renal malignancy of childhood. Crucially, the mass in Wilms tumor is typically smooth and characteristically does not cross the midline, which differentiates it from neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma (Option D) often presents in younger children (average age 2), feels "knobby" or irregular, and characteristically crosses the midline. Angiomyolipoma (Option A) is a benign renal tumor rare in early childhood unless associated with tuberous sclerosis. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) is extremely rare in the first decade of life. While Wilms tumor mass is often described as painless, large tumors can cause discomfort or tension in the flank region. Management involves a combination of surgery (nephrectomy) and chemotherapy, with excellent survival rates for localized disease
questions.learning: A large, firm, flank mass in a 4-year-old child is the classic presentation for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common primary renal malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient came with a history of fever, body ache, and joint pain. He was given NSAIDs. A few days later, he developed brownish pigmentation over the nose. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chikungunya

The given history of fever, joint pain, and centrofacial hyperpigmentation points toward a diagnosis of chikungunya. Post chikungunya pigmentation (PCP) usually appears after the fever subsides and persists for about 3-6 months. Hyperpigmentation associated with chikungunya fever is macular and most commonly affects the nose and cheeks.

Another close differential is fixed drug eruptions (FDE). FDE has a shorter latency, usually presents 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure, and recurs at the same location on re-exposure. It presents with hyperpigmented plaques that may be preceded by vesiculobullous lesions.

Hyperpigmentation of the centrofacial region (nose and cheeks) mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

Nose pigmentation is striking in cases of chikungunya fever and is termed chik sign. The image below shows chik sign on the nose:

FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction.  They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation. NSAIDs, paracetamol and co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE. NSAID‐induced FDE mainly affects the genitals and lips.

The image below shows FDE on upper lip area:
questions.learning: Chikungunya — The given history of fever, joint pain, and centrofacial hyperpigmentation points toward a diagnosis of chikungunya. Post chikungunya pigmentation (PCP) usually appears after the fever subsides and persists for about 3-6 months.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On slit-lamp examination, a patient with acute anterior uveitis shows a visible beam of light in the anterior chamber due to light scattering by protein. This optical phenomenon is best explained by which physical principle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tyndall effect

| Option | Status | Reasoning

| ------ | ------ | ---------

| A) Tyndall effect | Correct | Scattering of light by colloidal-sized protein particles suspended in the aqueous — the basis of "flare"

| B) Purkinje shift | Distractor | Relates to shift in peak spectral sensitivity of the eye from photopic to scotopic vision, unrelated

| C) Doppler effect | Distractor | Relates to frequency shift with relative motion; used in retinal/vascular flow studies, not flare

| D) Stokes' law | Distractor | Relates to particle settling velocity in a fluid (physics), not light scattering

Pearl:

• Flare = protein leak (marked in non-granulomatous uveitis).
• Cells = active inflammatory cells (denotes disease activity, guides steroid tapering).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with poor appetite and failure to thrive. On examination, signs of dehydration such as decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes are noted. What is the glucose concentration of the oral rehydration solution used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: The child presents with "poor appetite and failure to thrive" along with signs of dehydration, which in a 10-year-old in a clinical setting often implies severe acute malnutrition (SAM). For the rehydration of children with SAM, a specific solution called ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition) is used. ReSoMal differs from standard ORS; it contains more glucose (125 mmol/L) and less sodium to account for the unique physiological needs and electrolyte imbalances of malnourished children. Standard low-osmolarity ORS contains of glucose. Options A, C, and D do not represent the standard glucose concentrations for these rehydration protocols. Management of dehydration in SAM must be very cautious and slow to prevent heart failure. ReSoMal is administered orally or via a nasogastric tube over a longer period compared to children without SAM. This specific biochemical composition is a critical detail in pediatric nutritional rehabilitation
questions.learning: The child presents with "poor appetite and failure to thrive" along with signs of dehydration, which in a 10-year-old in a clinical setting often implies severe acute malnutrition (SAM).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient weighing 60 kg is on mechanical ventilation for ARDS secondary to urosepsis. The respiratory parameters are as follows: tidal volume- 360 mL; frequency- 30 breaths/min; PEEP- 5 cm of H2O; and FiO2- 90%. The arterial blood gas findings are as follows: paO2- 50 mmHg; paCO2- 38 mmHg; and pH- 7.38. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increase PEEP

Increasing PEEP in this patient would be the next step in ensuring adequate oxygenation. Applying adequate PEEP can improve arterial oxygenation by reducing ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch in areas of atelectasis.

This patient's low paO2 and low paO2/FiO2 ratio are suggestive of impaired oxygenation. The ratio of arterial oxygen partial pressure to the fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) is ≤300 mmHg as assessed on 5 cm H2O of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) or continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). In this patient the ratio is ≤100 mmHg, implying that the PEEP of 5 cm H2O is insufficient and must be increased.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most severe type of acute lung injury characterized by poor oxygenation, pulmonary infiltrates, and acuity of onset. It is associated with capillary endothelial injury and diffuse alveolar damage.

Etiology for ARDS:

• Direct lung injury- pneumonia, aspiration of gastric contents, pulmonary contusion, near-drowning, toxic inhalational injury
• Indirect lung injury- sepsis, severe trauma like multiple bone fractures, flail chest, head trauma, burns, multiple transfusions, drug overdose, pancreatitis, post-cardiopulmonary bypass

ARDS is characterized by the development of dyspnea and hypoxemia, which progressively worsens within 6 to 27 hours of the initial provoking event.

Recommended therapies in ARDS with clinical or supportive evidence:

• The low tidal volume ventilation (LTVV) strategy (4–6 mL/kg of ideal body weight) is recommended to maintain adequate ventilation and avoid ventilator-induced lung injury by barotrauma and volume trauma.
• High positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) or open lung mechanical ventilation
• Prone position
• Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)

Other options:

Option A: Reducing FiO2 will further worsen the patient's arterial oxygen as PaO2/FiO2 is ≤100 mmHg.

Option B: The LTVV strategy recommends a goal of 4–6 mL/kg of ideal body weight. The tidal volume setting in this patient is already at a goal of 6 mL/kg and further increasing it without first recruiting atelectatic lung tissue, would increase the risk of volume trauma.

Option C: Increasing the respiratory rate is an acceptable measure in the event of acute respiratory acidosis. The results of arterial blood gas analysis in this patient do not reflect acidosis. Furthermore, since the respiratory rate is already set at 30 breaths/min, increasing it further can worsen the risk of barotrauma and hyperinflation.
questions.learning: Increase PEEP Increasing PEEP in this patient would be the next step in ensuring adequate oxygenation. Applying adequate PEEP can improve arterial oxygenation by reducing ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch in areas of atelectasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following organizations of importance in the history of international health: 1. The Health Organization of the League of Nations 2. The Pan American Sanitary Bureau 3. The United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration 4. The World Health Organization Which one of the following represents the correct chronological order (from the oldest to the newest) of the establishment of these organizations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 → 1 → 3 → 4

The correct chronological order is:

1. Pan American Sanitary Bureau (PASB) → 1902
2. Health Organization of the League of Nations → 1923
3. United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA) → 1943
4. World Health Organization (WHO) → 1948

Therefore:

1902 → 1923 → 1943 → 1948

→ D. 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
questions.learning: 2 → 1 → 3 → 4 The correct chronological order is: 1. Pan American Sanitary Bureau (PASB) → 1902 2.

questions.text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the hyperacute rejection of renal transplants?
questions.explanation:

Hyperacute graft rejection is an example of type II hypersensitivity reaction.

It is mediated by preformed antibodies. It is a rare event that occurs in kidney transplantation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A newly joined teacher develops rice water stools. The causative agent acts on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GM1 ganglioside receptor

The given clinical scenario of rice-water stools is suggestive of cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The toxin produced by the organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors.

Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility. It has a single polar flagellum. It causes cholera, an acute diarrheal disease. It is marked by painless, profuse, watery diarrhea with flecks of mucus (rice water stools) associated with effortless vomiting. Pulmonary edema and arrhythmias are some of the complications.

Infection is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food and water. The organisms produce an enterotoxin known as cholera toxin (CT). It has 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B subunit (binding units) fixes to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on jejunal epithelial cells. The A subunit dissociates into the A2 fragment, which attaches the A1 fragment to the B subunit. This results in prolonged accumulation of cAMP, which causes an outpouring of large amounts of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Ultimately, it results in profuse watery diarrhea.

In addition to the cholera toxin, additional toxins such as zona occludens toxin and accessory cholera toxin are also produced. The former alters intestinal permeability by its action on intestinal epithelial cells.

The characteristic darting mobility and its hindrance by antiserum can be used for rapid microscopic diagnosis.

Fluid resuscitation by rice-based ORS is recommended. Medical management includes erythromycin or azithromycin.
questions.learning: GM1 ganglioside receptor — The given clinical scenario of rice-water stools is suggestive of cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The toxin produced by the organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme activity decreases in fasting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phosphofructokinase 1

During fasting, there is low insulin, and hence, the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 gets inhibited.

Phosphofructokinase 1 is an enzyme of glycolysis. It is induced by insulin and a well-fed state.

Other options:

Option A: Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored fats in a fasting state.

Option B: Glycogen phosphorylase is active in fasting state so as to produce glucose from glycogen.

Option C: Pyruvate carboxylase is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis. During the fasting state, the liver is flooded with fatty acids mobilized from adipose tissue. The resulting elevated hepatic acetyl CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase. Other enzymes of gluconeogenesis that are elevated in fasting include Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and Glucose-6-phosphatase.
questions.learning: Phosphofructokinase 1 During fasting, there is low insulin, and hence, the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 gets inhibited. Phosphofructokinase 1 is an enzyme of glycolysis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60 year old patient presents with limping gait and left hip pain. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Avascular necrosis

The given scenario of limping gait and left hip pain with radiographic findings of the radiolucency and distorted articular surface is suggestive of avascular necrosis of the head of femur.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) or osteonecrosis is a painful bone condition as a result of diminished blood supply mainly due to trauma or non-traumatic etiologies.

The typical features are pain with movements in or near the joint, click in the joint, joint stiffness, limping gait, and deformity. Restriction of movements is also a feature of this condition.

An x-ray shows reactive new bone formation, increased radiolucency in the subchondral bone, and a distorted articular surface.

MRI is the investigation of choice. It allows the identification of AVN of the femoral head and also determines the exact stage and extent of the pathologic process.

Management is based on Ficat and Arlet Classification:

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculosis of the hip is characterized by painful and restricted movements of the hip. The radiographic findings are not appreciable in the early stages. But late stages show periarticular osteoporosis, hazy, and irregular joint margins with a reduction in the joint space, and wandering acetabulum.

Option B: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is usually seen in females in the 4th to 5th decade. Patients present with symmetrical polyarthritis of the proximal finger joints, tenosynovitis, early morning stiffness and pain. RA of the hip can be bilateral. Radiographic findings such as joint space narrowing due to hyaline cartilage destruction, cyst formation, and acetabular protrusion-type deformity can be seen.

Option C: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the spine and sacroiliac joint. It typically occurs in the age group 15-25 years with a male preponderance. Features include backache, stiffness, sciatica, and fixed flexion contracture. Radiographic findings show erosion of sacroiliac joints, squaring, and bridging of the vertebral body leading to a bamboo spine appearance.
questions.learning: Avascular necrosis — The given scenario of limping gait and left hip pain with radiographic findings of the radiolucency and distorted articular surface is suggestive of avascular necrosis of the head of femur.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is included in co-testing for cervical cancer screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HPV DNA + Pap smear

Co-testing in cervical cancer screening refers to performing a pap smear and HPV DNA testing together.

Cervical cancer screening:

* Pap smear: Screening starts at 21 years and is repeated every 3 years until 29 years. From 30 to 65 years, cytology with HPV co-testing is recommended every 5 years. After 65 years of age, screening may be discontinued if there have been three consecutive negative cytology results or two consecutive negative co-tests within the past 10 years, with the most recent test done within the last 5 years.

* HPV DNA testing: If the result is positive for high-risk HPV, the next step is colposcopy followed by biopsy.
If the result is negative, the smear should be repeated after 5 years.

* Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA): In low-resource settings, a simple screening method is used in which, after exposing the cervix with a speculum, it is painted with 3.5% acetic acid. Any areas that turn white within one minute of application are considered suspicious and should be further evaluated with colposcopy or biopsy.

* Colposcopy: Colposcopy is the direct examination of the cervix using a microscope that provides low magnification, typically between 6 and 16 times. Indications include:

*

* Women whose cytology shows HSIL, ASC-H, or ASCUS with a positive HPV test

* Clinically abnormal cervix, even if cytology is normal

* Women with persistent high-risk HPV DNA positivity

* Abnormal cervical cytology accompanied by a positive HPV test

(HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, ASCUS: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, ASC-H: Atypical Squamous Cells – cannot exclude HSIL)

Incorporating HPV testing with pap smear improves its predictive value and reduces the number of colposcopic evaluations.

Pap smear:  The patient is put in a dorsal position and Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced. The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula. Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush. Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides. The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol and stained with Pap stain.
