questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Orbital varices are abnormal, dilated veins within the orbit that typically present with intermittent proptosis. A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the bulging of the eye increases during maneuvers that raise venous pressure, such as bending down, coughing, or performing the Valsalva maneuver. These lesions are usually unilateral and slowly progressive. Thyroid Eye Disease (Option B) is the most common cause of proptosis but is typically bilateral and does not fluctuate rapidly with head position. Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Option C) presents with painful proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, and systemic signs of infection rather than postural changes. Orbital Cellulitis (Option D) is an acute, painful infection of the orbit featuring redness, swelling, and fever. Diagnosis of orbital varices is aided by CT scans showing dense structures that enlarge during a Valsalva maneuver. Treatment is only needed for severe symptoms or optic nerve compression
questions.learning: Orbital varices are abnormal, dilated veins within the orbit that typically present with intermittent proptosis. A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the bulging of the eye increases during maneuvers that raise venous pressure, such as bending down,…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is oxygen therapy not useful?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Central respiratory depression

Oxygen therapy is not beneficial in central respiratory depression.

High dose oxygen reduces the output of peripheral chemoreceptors. So, if given to patients who already have central respiratory depression, it will indirectly reduce the hypoxic drive to breathe even further, leading to a reduction in respiratory frequency and minute ventilation.

Note: In acute severe asthma, a high concentration of oxygen should be given by face mask to achieve an oxygen saturation of >90%.
questions.learning: Central respiratory depression Oxygen therapy is not beneficial in central respiratory depression. High dose oxygen reduces the output of peripheral chemoreceptors.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of infertility is on treatment with human menopausal gonadotropin. She presented with the following finding in the USG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

The image showing enlarged ovaries with multiple large cysts along with the history of treatment for infertility with human menopausal gonadotropin suggests the diagnosis of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

Human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG) is a medication that is composed of FSH and LH. It is used to stimulate the release of ova in women who do not ovulate spontaneously. It can lead to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is a condition associated with ovarian enlargement due to exogenous gonadotropin therapy. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distention, ascites, gastrointestinal problems, respiratory compromise, oliguria, and thromboembolism. It can occur during ovulation induction or in early pregnancies conceived through exogenous ovarian stimulation.

Predisposing factors for OHSS include multi-follicular ovaries (such as in PCOS), young age, high estradiol levels during ovulation induction, and pregnancy.

Vasoactive substances produced by the corpus luteum, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiotensin II, are believed to contribute to enhanced capillary permeability, resulting in the loss of fluid, protein, and electrolytes into the peritoneal cavity and hemoconcentration.

Sonographic examination reveals enlarged ovaries with numerous follicular cysts and ascites.

Maintaining fluid balance with isotonic fluids like normal saline is crucial. Strategies to prevent OHSS during exogenous ovulation include reducing follicular stimulation (low FSH dose), coasting (withholding FSH administration one or more days prior to the hCG trigger), prophylactic volume expanders, and substituting hCG for FSH towards the end of ovarian stimulation.

Other options:

Option B: Theca lutein cysts are a rare form of follicular cysts characterized by luteinization and hypertrophy of the theca interna layer. Both ovaries are enlarged and cystic. This condition is commonly associated with gestational trophoblastic disease, multifetal gestation, and placentomegaly.

Option C: Polycystic ovarian syndrome shows 12 or more small follicles each 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally (necklace pattern) (shown below). The patient presents with menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne, etc.
questions.learning: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — The image showing enlarged ovaries with multiple large cysts along with the history of treatment for infertility with human menopausal gonadotropin suggests the diagnosis of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9 months old infant is brought for a routine check-up. The infant is able to sit without support and transfer objects. Which of the following developmental milestones is most likely to be present at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Creeps well on hands and knees

At 9 months of age, infants typically achieve gross motor milestones such as sitting without support and beginning to creep or crawl on hands and knees. Fine motor development at this stage includes transferring objects from one hand to another and developing an immature pincer grasp.

• Gross motor: sits without support, creeps/crawls
• Fine motor: hand-to-hand transfer of objects, immature pincer grasp
• Advanced milestones like mature pincer grasp (12 months), running (18–24 months), and hopping (4 years) occur later
questions.learning: Creeps well on hands and knees At 9 months of age, infants typically achieve gross motor milestones such as sitting without support and beginning to creep or crawl on hands and knees.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vertex positions is the least common during childbirth? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left Occipitoposterior (LOP)

The most common fetal vertex position during labor is occipitoanterior, especially Left Occipitoanterior (LOA), because the left oblique diameter of the maternal pelvis is slightly larger and better accommodates fetal descent.

Frequency of vertex positions:

• LOA → most common
• ROA → common
• Occipitoposterior positions → less common
• Left Occipitoposterior (LOP) → least common

Occipitoposterior positions are associated with:

• Prolonged labor
• Increased back pain (“back labor”)
• Higher risk of instrumental delivery or cesarean section

Thus, LOP is considered the least common vertex position during childbirth.
questions.learning: Left Occipitoposterior (LOP) — The most common fetal vertex position during labor is occipitoanterior, especially Left Occipitoanterior (LOA), because the left oblique diameter of the maternal pelvis is slightly larger and better accommodates fetal descent.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: While walking, the suspended leg is supported by which muscle on other side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gluteus medius

The correct answer is Gluteus medius.

During walking, gluteus medius of the stance limb stabilizes the pelvis and prevents dropping of the pelvis on the suspended side.

Paralysis causes a positive Trendelenburg sign with pelvic tilt toward the unsupported limb.

Gluteus maximus extends the hip, tensor fascia lata assists abduction, and quadriceps stabilizes the knee, not pelvic support.
questions.learning: Gluteus medius — The correct answer is Gluteus medius. During walking, gluteus medius of the stance limb stabilizes the pelvis and prevents dropping of the pelvis on the suspended side.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old primigravida at 25 weeks of gestation presents with right upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and generalized edema. Peripheral smear shows evidence of hemolysis. Her vital signs are stable, with a blood pressure of 104/72 mm Hg and pulse rate of 72/min. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocyte count of 10,500/mm³, platelet count of 62,000/mm³, hematocrit of 26%, and elevated AST levels (90 IU/L). Based on this clinical and laboratory profile, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of HELLP syndrome is based on the laboratory triad of Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets. This patient satisfies all criteria: "hemolysis" on peripheral smear (also suggested by low hematocrit), elevated AST (90 IU/L), and a significantly low platelet count (62,000/mm3). Although her blood pressure is currently 104/72 mm Hg, HELLP can occur in the absence of overt hypertension or proteinuria in up to 15-20% of cases. Hepatitis B (Option B) and obstetric cholestasis (Option D) do not cause hemolysis or severe thrombocytopenia. Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP, Option C) is a close differential but typically presents later in the third trimester and is often associated with coagulopathy and hypoglycemia. The right upper quadrant pain is a classic symptom caused by Glisson’s capsule distension. HELLP syndrome is an obstetric emergency requiring stabilization and usually prompt delivery, as it carries high risks of maternal morbidity and fetal mortality
questions.learning: The diagnosis of HELLP syndrome is based on the laboratory triad of Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets. This patient satisfies all criteria: "hemolysis" on peripheral smear (also suggested by low hematocrit), elevated AST (90 IU/L), and a…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Revised A 36-year-old man presented with complaints of bluish-black discolouration of sclera and pinna for last 6 months. Since childhood, his urine turns black on standing as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alkaptonuria

The clinical features along with the blackening of urine on standing are characteristic of alkaptonuria.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/ homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis, which is bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue; generally occurs after the third decade of life and it occurs due to the accumulation of homogentisic acid and its oxidation products like benzoquinone acetic acid in connective tissue.

Arthritis generally begins in the third decade. Arthritis often begins in the spine and resembles ankylosing spondylitis in its large-joint distribution. Radiographs of the spine showing flattened and calcified intervertebral discs are pathognomonic. Other findings include degeneration of the intervertebral discs followed by disc calcification and eventually fusion of the vertebral bodies. Osteophyte formation and calcification of the intervertebral ligaments also occur.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria. The ferric chloride test will be positive.

The images below show pigmentation of the skin and an x-ray of the spine that shows calcification of intervertebral discs.
questions.learning: Alkaptonuria — The clinical features along with the blackening of urine on standing are characteristic of alkaptonuria. Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A microbiology resident is comparing the major diarrheagenic pathotypes of Escherichia coli. One of the following statements incorrectly describes the mechanism of disease. Identify the false statement.
options: Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) produces the heat-stable enterotoxin EAST-1.
Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) infection may be complicated by hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes diarrhea by invading intestinal epithelial cells.
Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is a common cause of traveler's diarrhea.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes diarrhea by invading intestinal epithelial cells.

Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) is non-invasive. It causes diarrhea by producing attaching and effacing (A/E) lesions, leading to:

• Intimate attachment to enterocytes (via intimin)
• Destruction of microvilli
• Formation of actin-rich pedestals
• Malabsorption and watery diarrhea

Unlike Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), EPEC does not invade intestinal epithelial cells.

Why the other options are correct?

• A. EAEC produces heat-stable enterotoxin EAST-1 ✅: Correct. Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC) characteristically exhibits stacked-brick adherence and may produce EAST-1 (Enteroaggregative Heat-Stable Toxin-1), contributing to persistent diarrhea.
• B. EHEC can be complicated by HUS ✅: Correct. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) (e.g., O157:H7) produces Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin), which may lead to:

• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
• Thrombocytopenia
• Acute kidney injury (Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome)

• D. ETEC is a common cause of traveler's diarrhea ✅: Correct. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) produces:

• Heat-labile toxin (LT) → ↑ cAMP
• Heat-stable toxin (ST) → ↑ cGMP

causing secretory watery diarrhea.
questions.learning: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes diarrhea by invading intestinal epithelial cells. Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) is non-invasive.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a palpable lump in the left breast. Mammography suggests malignancy, and tissue diagnosis is required. Which is the preferred biopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Core needle biopsy

• Core needle biopsy (CNB) is the preferred initial biopsy for suspected breast cancer.
• It provides tissue architecture, unlike FNAC which provides only cytology.
• Histology allows assessment of tumor type, grade, ER/PR status, and HER2 expression.
• It guides neoadjuvant therapy and surgical planning.
• FNAC cannot reliably distinguish in situ from invasive carcinoma.
• Excision biopsy is no longer the first-line diagnostic procedure.
• Incisional biopsy is rarely required.
• CNB is usually performed under ultrasound or stereotactic guidance.
• It has high sensitivity and specificity with minimal morbidity.
• Triple assessment = Clinical examination + Imaging + Core needle biopsy.
questions.learning: Core needle biopsy • Core needle biopsy (CNB) is the preferred initial biopsy for suspected breast cancer. • It provides tissue architecture, unlike FNAC which provides only cytology. • Histology allows assessment of tumor type, grade, ER/PR status, and…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown below?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates Condyloma acuminata, commonly known as genital warts. These are caused by infection with low-risk strains of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV), most frequently types 6 and 11. They characteristically appear as fleshy, "cauliflower-like," or filiform exophytic growths on the skin and mucous membranes of the anogenital region. In contrast, condyloma lata (Option A) are a manifestation of secondary syphilis and appear as broad, flat, moist papules that are highly infectious. Molluscum contagiosum (Option C) is caused by a poxvirus and presents as small, discrete, umbilicated pearly papules. Condyloma acuminata is a highly contagious sexually transmitted infection. Management includes topical therapies like podophyllin or imiquimod, or destructive methods such as cryotherapy, electrocautery, or laser excision. Prevention is primarily through the HPV vaccine, which covers these common low-risk strains. Accurate clinical differentiation between these conditions is essential, as the underlying etiologies and necessary pharmacological treatments (antivirals/cryotherapy vs. penicillin for syphilis) differ significantly
questions.learning: The image illustrates Condyloma acuminata, commonly known as genital warts. These are caused by infection with low-risk strains of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV), most frequently types 6 and 11.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child is brought to the casualty with a history of dyspnea. His mother gives a history of foreign body aspiration. What is the first investigation to be done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xray

The first investigation in a child with suspicion of foreign body aspiration is Xray.

Food items (nuts, seeds hard candy, gum, bones raw fruits, and vegetables) account for the majority of choking cases in children. The most common site of foreign body lodging is the bronchus. Foreign body aspiration into the airway has three stages: immediate symptoms of coughing and choking, an asymptomatic interval, and later complications such as fever, atelectasis, and pneumonia.

When a child presents with a history of choking, detailed history taking and physical examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx, neck, and lungs are necessary.

The next step for suspected foreign body aspiration is to obtain a chest X-ray, including the abdomen, despite most foreign bodies being radiolucent. Secondary findings on the X-ray can indicate foreign body involvement, such as air trapping, atelectasis, obstructive emphysema, asymmetric hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or consolidation. While a CT scan has high accuracy, it is not typically performed due to radiation risks.

The treatment of choice for a foreign body in the airway is its endoscopic removal with a rigid instrument, usually a bronchoscope, by a specialist otolaryngologist or pulmonologist. Bronchoscopy must be performed even if there is a high suspicion of an airway foreign body in spite of negative or inconclusive imaging.
questions.learning: Xray — The first investigation in a child with suspicion of foreign body aspiration is Xray. Food items (nuts, seeds hard candy, gum, bones raw fruits, and vegetables) account for the majority of choking cases in children.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the primary identification determined by a CBNAAT/ Gene-Xpert?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MTB + Rifampicin resistance

The Cartridge Based-Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (CBNAAT) is primarily done to check for Tuberculosis to detect DNA and rifampicin resistance.

CBNAAT (Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) is a rapid molecular test that detects the DNA of TB bacteria in HIV-positive individuals. It uses sputum or any other biological specimen (except blood and blood-contaminated specimens). It can give a result in less than 2 hours. It can also detect the genetic mutations in the rpoB gene associated with resistance to the drug rifampicin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 22 weeks of gestation presents to you with profuse vaginal bleeding. Her blood pressure and glucose levels are within normal limits. Placental implantation at which of the following sites can cause this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal os

Placenta previa occurs when the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, partially or completely covering the internal cervical os.

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Type I | Placenta in lower segment but not reaching os

| Type II | Placenta reaches os

| Type III | Placenta partially covers os

| Type IV | Placenta completely covers os

As pregnancy progresses:

• Lower uterine segment stretches
• Placental attachment disrupts
• Leads to painless vaginal bleeding

Painless bleeding in 2nd or 3rd trimester = placenta previa.

| Feature | Placenta previa | Abruptio placentae

| ------- | --------------- | ------------------

| Pain | Painless bleeding | Painful bleeding

| Uterus | Soft | Tender

| Cause | Placenta over os | Placental separation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal time for nuchal translucency evaluation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 11-14 weeks

Nuchal translucency evaluation, a component of first-trimester aneuploidy screening, is done between 11-14 weeks.

It represents the maximum thickness of the subcutaneous translucent area between the skin and soft tissue, overlying the fetal spine, at the back of the neck. When the nuchal translucency is increased, the risk of fetal aneuploidy and structural anomalies such as heart defects is significantly elevated.

First trimester aneuploidy screening combines two maternal serum analytes and a sonographic measurement:

1. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
2. Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)
3. Nuchal translucency (NT)

It is performed between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation. In cases of fetal Down syndrome, the first-trimester serum-free β-hCG level is higher and the PAPP-A level is lower. With trisomy 18 and trisomy 13, levels of both analytes are lower.

Note: Nuchal fold is a normal fold of skin seen at the back of the fetal neck during the second trimester of pregnancy. Increased nuchal fold thickness is associated with fetal aneuploidy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is acid-fast in nature?
questions.explanation: Acid-fast organisms are those that have a high concentration of mycolic acids in their cell walls, making them resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol during staining procedures (like Ziehl-Neelsen staining). The genus Mycobacterium is the classic group of acid-fast bacteria. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is an important opportunistic pathogen, especially in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS, and characteristically stains positive with acid-fast techniques. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) and Escherichia coli (Option B) are standard gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively, and are not acid-fast. Actinomyces (Option D) are filamentous branching bacteria that are typically gram-positive but not acid-fast (differentiating them from Nocardia, which is weakly acid-fast). Recognizing the acid-fast property is essential for the rapid laboratory diagnosis of mycobacterial infections. Clinically, finding acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum or tissue is a critical "red flag" that necessitates the initiation of targeted multi-drug therapy and, in many cases, respiratory isolation for the patient
questions.learning: Acid-fast organisms are those that have a high concentration of mycolic acids in their cell walls, making them resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol during staining procedures (like Ziehl-Neelsen staining).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young adult with gastric outlet obstruction presents with vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Normal saline

Normal saline is preferred in a patient with gastric outlet obstruction to rectify the electrolyte imbalance.

The recurrent vomiting secondary to the gastric outlet obstruction leads to dehydration and hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis. This abnormality has to be corrected and adequate rehydration ensured before the surgery is undertaken. The patient should be rehydrated with intravenous isotonic saline with potassium supplementation. Replacing the sodium chloride and water allows the kidney to correct the acid–base abnormality. (Normal saline has more chloride than Ringer lactate)

Surgery can be done once the electrolyte imbalance is corrected - Routine preoperative evaluation is conducted, oral feeding is discontinued and the stomach is emptied with a nasogastric tube. Intravenous fluids are given to replace the ongoing gastric losses.

Fluid Resuscitation

* Fluid resuscitation - 0.9% saline with KCl in 5% glucose provides maintenance and corrects deficits in most babies. As the chloride deficit is replaced, the kidneys correct the pH.

* The urine output should be monitored and the electrolyte levels must be checked every 6 hours.

* To ensure that rehydration has occurred, the urine output should be >2 cc/Kg/hr.
questions.learning: Normal saline Normal saline is preferred in a patient with gastric outlet obstruction to rectify the electrolyte imbalance. The recurrent vomiting secondary to the gastric outlet obstruction leads to dehydration and hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a flowchart illustrating the natural history of a disease, what is the term used for the time interval between points A and B?
questions.explanation: The flowchart shows: Disease Onset → A (First possible point of diagnosis) → B (Final critical point of diagnosis) → C (Usual time of diagnosis) → Outcome The interval between Point A and Point B represents Screening Time. Screening time is defined as the time interval between the first possible point of diagnosis (A) — when disease could earliest be detected through screening methods — and the final critical point of diagnosis (B) — beyond which treatment becomes less effective or irreversible damage occurs. This interval essentially represents the window period during which screening is beneficial and early intervention can meaningfully alter disease outcome. Clinical Significance: Screening time defines the optimal window for screening programs to be effective. A longer screening time means a disease is more suitable for mass screening programs as there is a wider window of opportunity for early detection and intervention. Why other options are wrong: (A) Lead time is incorrect because lead time refers to the interval between Point A and Point C — the difference between earliest possible diagnosis through screening and the usual time of clinical diagnosis. It represents the "head start" gained by screening over conventional diagnosis. (C) Generation time is incorrect because generation time refers to the time between receipt of infection and point of maximum infectivity in communicable disease epidemiology — completely unrelated to diagnostic intervals shown in this flowchart. (D) Lag time is incorrect because lag time refers to the delay between exposure to a risk factor and onset of disease, representing a pre-onset interval — not the interval between two diagnostic points as depicted here
questions.learning: The flowchart shows: Disease Onset → — A (First possible point of diagnosis) → B (Final critical point of diagnosis) → C (Usual time of diagnosis) → Outcome The interval between Point A and Point B represents Screening Time.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An image is shown with a structure marked “X,” representing a layer on the outer surface of the pharynx. Identify the structure indicated
questions.explanation: The marked structure is the buccopharyngeal fascia, a thin layer of the deep cervical fascia that covers the external surface of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles. It extends from the skull base to the esophagus and forms the anterior boundary of the retropharyngeal space. Prevertebral fascia (Option B) covers the vertebral column and prevertebral muscles, forming the posterior boundary of the same space. Pharyngobasilar fascia (Option C) is located on the inner surface of the pharyngeal muscles, attaching the pharynx to the skull. Alar fascia (Option D) is a separate component located between the buccopharyngeal and prevertebral layers. Understanding these facial planes is clinically vital for localizing deep neck infections and abscesses
questions.learning: The marked structure is the buccopharyngeal fascia, a thin layer of the deep cervical fascia that covers the external surface of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old farm worker from a remote village presents 8 hours after a snake bite that occurred early in the morning. He complains of headache, blurred vision, perioral tingling, dizziness, vertigo, and has had repeated vomiting since the bite. On examination, he shows respiratory depression and bradycardia (heart rate < 50/ min). The bite site has mild swelling and blistering without bleeding. He has already received 10 vials of antivenom. What should be the next step in management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient is displaying classic signs of neurotoxic snake envenomation, likely from a cobra or krait bite. Symptoms such as blurred vision (ptis), respiratory depression, and tingling are hallmark neurological effects. While Polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) has been started, the presence of respiratory distress requires adjunct therapy. Neostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, can transiently improve neuromuscular transmission in neurotoxic envenomation (particularly cobra bites). It must always be given with Atropine to block the muscarinic side effects, such as bradycardia and increased secretions. Checking the coagulation profile (Option A) is more relevant for vasculotoxic (Viper) bites where bleeding is prominent. Epinephrine (Option C) and hydrocortisone (Option D) are used to manage ASV-induced anaphylaxis, but not for the primary neurotoxic symptoms. Therefore, the neostigmine-atropine challenge is the critical next step to potentially reverse muscle paralysis and stabilize the patient
questions.learning: The patient is displaying classic signs of neurotoxic snake envenomation, likely from a cobra or krait bite. Symptoms such as blurred vision (ptis), respiratory depression, and tingling are hallmark neurological effects.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of cartilage?
questions.explanation: The histological image shows hyaline cartilage, identifiable by its glassy, homogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) rich in Type II collagen. Chondrocytes are seen residing within spaces called lacunae. Hyaline cartilage is the most common type and is found in articular surfaces, the respiratory tract, and the fetal skeleton. Elastic cartilage (Option B) contains dense networks of elastic fibers, making it more flexible, and is found in the outer ear and epiglottis. Fibrocartilage (Option C) contains thick bundles of Type I collagen, providing high tensile strength for intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. Calcified cartilage (Option D) is hyaline cartilage that has accumulated calcium salts, often seen during bone development or aging. The lack of visible fibers in the matrix confirms this as hyaline
questions.learning: The histological image shows hyaline cartilage, identifiable by its glassy, homogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) rich in Type II collagen. Chondrocytes are seen residing within spaces called lacunae.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the investigation performed in the condition shown below in the radiograph?
options: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
Micturating cystourethrography with psoriatic urethra stricture
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a minor anatomical discrepancy between the image provided and the options, as most strictures pictured in this set are bulbar. However, based on the options provided for this specific question...). The image shows a Retrograde Cystourethrogram (RGU), identified by the contrast being injected "upward" from the tip of the penis to visualize the urethra. This is the standard investigation for suspected urethral strictures. The image reveals a narrow, diseased segment of the penile (anterior) urethra. A Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) (Options C and D) is performed while the patient is voiding to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder neck. Membranous strictures (Option A) occur higher up at the level of the pelvic floor and are usually traumatic. There is no such thing as a "psoriatic" stricture (Option D). Therefore, based on the retrograde injection method and the location of the narrowing, RGU of a penile stricture is the correct identification

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can sit without support, turn diagonally, and babble bisyllables. Which of the following abilities is expected during this time?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Crawling

The described child is around 9 months of age, since sitting without support, turning diagonally(pivoting), and babbling bisyllables are key milestones of this age. At this stage, children typically start crawling, which is the expected gross motor milestone.

* Ability to sit unsupported(gross motor development): at 6-7 months

* To pivot while sitting(gross motor development): at 9-10 months

* Bisyllables(mama, baba, dada)(language milestone): at 8-10 months

Other options:

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women in her age group is called as __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total fertility rate

The average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women in her age group is called as total fertility rate.

Pearl PF0245: Fertility Indicators

* Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory.

* It is the number of live births per 1000 estimated mid-year population in a given year.

* Birth rate = No. of live births during the year x 1000/Estimated mid-year population

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

* General Fertility Rate

* It is the number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15 - 49 years) in a given year.

* GFR = Number of live births in an area in a year x 1000/Mid-year population of women in the reproductive age in the same area in the same year.

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

* Age-specific fertility rates

* It is the number of live births in a year to 1000 women in any specified age group.

* It is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

* ASFR = Number of live births in a particular age group x 1000/Mid-year female population of the same age group.

* Total Fertility Rate

* It represents the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women in each age group now.

* It is the sum of all age specific fertility rates multiplied by 5.

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size.

* Gross Reproductive Rate

* It is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

* Net Reproduction Rate

* It is the number of daughters a newborn girl will bear during her lifetime assuming age-specific fertility and mortality rates.

* NRR is a demographic indicator.

* NRR of 1 is equivalent of approximately the 2 child norm.

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate.
questions.learning: Total fertility rate — The average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive years bearing children at the same rates as the women in her age group is called as total fertility rate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old multiparous woman presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and absence of fetal movements. She has a history of occasional smoking. On examination, her pulse rate is 80/min, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg, and the abdomen feels tense on palpation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and a tense (couvelaire) abdomen on palpation is highly diagnostic of Abruptio Placenta. The lack of fetal movement suggests intrauterine fetal death, a common and severe complication of placental separation. Occasionally smoking and the elevated blood pressure (150/90 mmHg) are significant risk factors for this condition. Placenta previa (Option B) is classically associated with painless vaginal bleeding and a soft, non-tender uterus. Hydramnios (Option C) presents with an overdistended uterus but not acute painful bleeding. Preterm labor (Option D) involves regular contractions without the pathognomonic tenseness and severe hemorrhage seen in abruption. The combination of hypertension, smoking history, and a "wooden" or tense abdomen makes placental abruption the most probable and life-threatening diagnosis for both mother and fetus. Immediate management is required to stabilize the mother and proceed with delivery
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding during labor, and a tense (couvelaire) abdomen on palpation is highly diagnostic of Abruptio Placenta.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The given image is of an ulcer, identify the marked structure? (arrow pointing to the boundary between the margin and floor).
questions.explanation: In the anatomy of an ulcer, the "edge" is the boundary or transition zone between the outer margin and the inner floor. Its appearance is diagnostically significant: for example, an "undermined" edge is typical of tuberculosis, while a "raised or rolled-out" edge suggests malignancy. The margin (Option A) is the outer limit where the ulcer meets normal skin or mucosa. The floor (Option C) is the exposed surface of the ulcer, which may contain granulation tissue or slough. The base (Option D) is the deeper structure upon which the ulcer rests, such as muscle or bone. Accurate description of these parts is essential for classifying ulcers as venous, arterial, neuropathic, or malignant. The arrow specifically marks the slanting transition into the wound, confirming it is the edge

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fever and abdominal pain five days after a cholecystectomy, during which an injury to the common bile duct was identified. Imaging studies demonstrate a bile leak originating from the injured site. What is the most appropriate management approach for this postoperative complication?
questions.explanation: ERCP and stenting The patient is experiencing a post-cholecystectomy bile leak. In most cases where a minor injury or leak is identified in the postoperative period, the most appropriate and effective first-line management is Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and stenting. ERCP allows the clinician to place a stent that bypasses the site of injury and reduces the pressure in the biliary system. This "lowers the resistance" to bile flow, encouraging the leak to close spontaneously. Ultrasound-guided aspiration (Option A) may drain the resulting fluid collection (biloma) but does not fix the source. Re-exploration for primary repair (Option D) or hepaticojejunostomy (Option C) is reserved for severe, major bile duct resections or when endoscopic management fails. For an initial bile leak after a known injury, a minimally invasive endoscopic approach is the standard of care to achieve resolution with less morbidity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding ataxia-telangiectasia?
options: Follows autosomal dominant mode of inheritance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follows autosomal dominant mode of inheritance

Ataxia telangiectasia (AT) or Louis–Bar syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.

The defect in AT is in the ATM gene localized to chromosome 11q22-23. The ATM gene is involved in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to combined immunodeficiency (impaired immunoglobin isotype switching and association with thymic hypoplasia) and predisposition to an increased risk of lymphoreticular tumors such as lymphoma or leukemia.

AT is characterized by progressive ataxia (beginning during infancy), telangiectasia (initially on bulbar conjunctiva), sinopulmonary infections, hypogonadism, sensitivity to ionizing radiation, insulin resistance, and raised alpha-fetoprotein levels.
questions.learning: Follows autosomal dominant mode of inheritance Ataxia telangiectasia (AT) or Louis–Bar syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. The defect in AT is in the ATM gene localized to chromosome 11q22-23.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the following LV pressure-volume loop diagram, point C denotes ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic valve opens

The aortic valve will open at point C.

The volume-pressure curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle. The relationship between ventricular pressure (Y-axis) and volume (X-axis) throughout the cardiac cycle is represented by this loop.

* A - Mitral valve opens

* B - Mitral valve closes

* C - Aortic valve opens

* D - Aortic valve closes

Phase I: Period of filling

It begins at a ventricular volume of about 50 ml (end-systolic volume) and a diastolic pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg. As venous blood flows into the ventricle from the left atrium, the ventricular volume normally increases to about 120 ml, called the end-diastolic volume and the diastolic pressure rising to about 5 to 7 mm Hg.

Phase II: Period of isovolumic contraction

During isovolumic contraction, the volume of the ventricle does not change because all valves are closed. However, the pressure inside the ventricle increases to equal the pressure in the aorta (80 mm Hg) as depicted by point C.

Phase III: Period of ejection

During ejection, the systolic pressure rises even higher because of still more contraction of the ventricle. At the same time, the volume of the ventricle decreases because the aortic valve has now opened and blood flows out of the ventricle into the aorta.

Phase IV: Period of isovolumic relaxation

At the end of the period of ejection (point D), the aortic valve closes and the ventricular pressure falls back to the diastolic pressure level. The line labeled “IV” traces this decrease in intraventricular pressure without any change in volume. Thus, the ventricle returns to its starting point, with about 50 ml of blood left in the ventricle and at an atrial pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg.

The area subtended by this functional volume-pressure diagram (the shaded area, labeled “EW”) represents the net external work output of the ventricle during its contraction cycle.
questions.learning: Aortic valve opens — The aortic valve will open at point C. The volume-pressure curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Rigor mortis occurs first in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Myocardium

Rigor mortis occurs first in the myocardium.

The order of appearance of rigor mortis: Left chamber of heart is affected first. Other muscles are affected in the given order:

1. Involuntary muscles: Heart
2. Eyelids
3. Neck and lower jaw
4. Face
5. Chest
6. Upper extremities
7. Abdomen
8. Legs
9. Fingers and toes

Note- Rigor mortis first occurs in the myocardium but is first seen in eyelids. Here the question is first occurs in and the answer is myocardium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the stage of bed sore in the sacral region.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

The given image shows a pressure sore with extensive tissue destruction, including damage to the muscle layer and thus it belongs to stage 4.

Pressure sores also known as bed sores, pressure ulcers and decubitus ulcers are ulcers that occur due to prolonged pressure on certain sites thereby leading to tissue necrosis. The commonest sites involved are ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral >medial), and occiput. Paraplegic patients, elderly patients, and severely ill patients are at a higher risk of developing pressure sores.

Management is primarily proper skin care with pressure dispersion cushions, air-fluidized beds, and urinary or fecal diversion if required. Patients who are bed-bound should be turned once in 2 hours. Those in a wheelchair should lift themselves off the seat for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgery is the last resort and is done after a proper initial debridement and vacuum-assisted closure. Vacuum-assisted closure is a wound closure technique in which negative pressure is applied to the wound which leads to a decrease in edema. This hastens the debridement and formation of granulation tissue. Skin flaps with a muscle are also used for closure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following glucose transporter is present in skeletal muscles and adipose tissues?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GLUT 4

GLUT-4 is present in skeletal muscle cells and adipose tissues.

Glucose transporters, also referred to as GLUTs, are transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitative diffusion. Facilitative diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions through the cell membrane by them binding chemically to a carrier/ transport protein that is responsible for their movement across the cell membrane.

GLUT-4 is a transport protein present in adipocytes. When there is a rise in blood glucose level, insulin secreted by the pancreatic beta cells binds to its receptors on the plasma membrane of adipocytes. Upon binding of insulin to its receptor, activation of the receptor's tyrosine-kinase domain occurs. This activation starts a protein activation cascade leading to the translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane.

Once translocation occurs and GLUT4 is inserted into the plasma membrane, facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient into the cell occurs.

Other options:

Option B: GLUT-2 is found in the liver, pancreatic β cell, small intestine, and kidney. Its function is the rapid uptake or release of glucose.

Option C: GLUT-5 is present in the small intestine and is involved in the absorption of fructose.

Option D: SGLT-1 is a sodium-dependent unidirectional transporter present in the small intestine and kidney that is involved in the active uptake of glucose against a concentration gradient.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with the extension of MCP joint and flexion of IP joints. Which muscle is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Interossei and lumbricals

The lumbricals and interossei muscles are affected.

The lumbricals and interossei muscles through their attachments to the dorsal digital expansions, cause:

• Flexion of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints
• Extension of the interphalangeal (IP) joints

In cases of ulnar nerve injury, these muscles may get atrophied leading to the extension of MCP joints and flexion of IP joints.

Note: The ulnar nerve innervates all the intrinsic muscles of the hand, except for

• First and second lumbrical
• Abductor pollicis brevis
• Opponens pollicis
• Part of flexor pollicis brevis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The given chemical structure is of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chondroitin sulfate

The given chemical structure is of chondroitin sulfate.

Chondroitin sulfate is composed of repeating units of N-acetyl galactosamine with sulfate and glucuronic acid. Some important features of chondroitin sulfate are as follows:

• The most abundant GAG in the body.
• Location: Cartilage, CNS, bone
• They are located at sites of calcification in endochondral bone and are a major component of cartilage.
• They are found in high amounts in the ECM of the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are responsible for corneal transparency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

The glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for corneal transparency is keratan sulfate.

Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars and uronic acids. They may be attached to a protein molecule to form a proteoglycan.

Keratan sulfate is a mucopolysaccharide that does not contain uronic acid. It is constituted by repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

• Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.
• Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Keratin sulfate I and II differ in their linkage to the core proteins. Keratan sulfate I links to a core protein L-asparagine via N-acetylglucosamine and Keratan sulfate II to  L-Serine (or L-Threonine) via N-acetylgalactosamine.

The chemical structure of Keratan sulfate is shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option B: In chondroitin sulfates (chondroitin 4-Sulfate & chondroitin 6-Sulfate), the repeating disaccharide units are glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine.  They maintain the structure of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and are located in endochondral bone and cartilage. They are also found in the ECM of the central nervous system. They act as signaling molecules in the prevention of the repair of nerve endings after injury.

Option C: Heparan sulfate is found on many extracellular cell surfaces and contains glucosamine with fewer N-sulfates than heparin. The predominant uronic acid is d-glucuronic acid. In the plasma membrane of cells, they act as receptors and mediate cell growth and cell-cell communication. It is also found in the basement membrane of the kidney along with type IV collagen and laminin, where it determines the charge selectiveness of glomerular filtration.

Option D: Hyaluronic acid is present in synovial fluid. It is also found in skin, bone, cartilage, vitreous humor, and embryonic tissues. It contains repeating units of N Acetyl Glucosamine and glucuronic acid. It plays a role in morphogenesis and wound repair. The high concentrations of hyaluronic acid along with chondroitin sulfates in cartilage contribute to its compressibility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old pregnant G3P2L2 woman presents to you at 36+6 weeks. Ultrasound is done and shows the fetus is in a transverse lie. The liquor is adequate, the placenta is normal, and she has no risk factors. Both her previous deliveries were normal vaginal deliveries. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. External cephalic version

A pregnant woman G3P2L2 presenting at 36+6 weeks with a transverse lie without being in labor is managed with an external cephalic version (ECV), followed by vaginal delivery.

In a transverse lie, the fetus' long axis is perpendicular to the mother's. The shoulder is typically placed above the pelvic inlet when lying transversely. The head occupies one iliac fossa, and the other by the breech. This results in a shoulder presentation.

Management of transverse lie:

1. Before labor/early in labor - If the membranes are intact (like in this case), it is recommended that ECV should be offered and attempted whenever possible.

Prerequisites for ECV - Women who have reached 370/7 weeks of gestation. Multiparity, unengaged presenting part, nonanterior placenta, nonobese patient, and abundant amnionic fluid improves the chances of ECV.

Absolute contraindications - When vaginal delivery is contraindicated, e.g. placenta previa

Relative contraindications - Early labor, oligohydramnios or ruptured membranes, known nuchal cord, structural uterine abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, multifetal gestation, and prior abruption of the placenta

2. Active labor - A cesarean delivery is frequently necessary for such a scenario (Option A). The lower uterine segment is not occupied by the fetal feet or head in a dorsoanterior or back down position. A vertical hysterotomy incision is usually necessary for such a position. In a dorsoposterior or backup position, one or both feet can be gripped through a small transverse incision and delivered by breech extraction.

Expectant management refers to allowing vaginal delivery to happen. It is chosen when the version fails or is contraindicated. Vaginal delivery may be considered in the case of small fetuses with congenital malformations or dead fetuses (Option C).

Transverse lie (malpresentation) is a contraindication to induction of labor (Option D).
questions.learning: External cephalic version — A pregnant woman G3P2L2 presenting at 36+6 weeks with a transverse lie without being in labor is managed with an external cephalic version (ECV), followed by vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a past history of tuberculosis presents to the OPD with complaints of chronic cough, occasional hemoptysis, and persistent chest pain. Chest X-ray shows the following lesion. It has been observed that when the patient's position changes, the air within the lesion changes as well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergilloma

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a past history of tuberculosis with an X-ray showing Monod's sign is suggestive of aspergilloma. The gas/air surrounding a mobile fungal ball or mycetoma (usually an aspergilloma) in an already-existing lung cavity is referred to as the Monod sign.

Aspergilloma or fungal ball is a late manifestation of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) caused by Aspergillus species. A fungal ball is formed within the pulmonary cavity of CPA by the peeled-off inner layer of the cavity.

Patients present with chronic features of fatigue, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, and wheezing. However, clinical features such as foul-smelling sputum and night sweats are more commonly observed in Tuberculosis which helps in differentiating the two conditions.

Chest X-ray shows a spherical or ovoid mass within a cavity. The mass is mobile. CT demonstrates a rounded mass within a cavity.

Images below show chest x-ray and CT findings in aspergilloma.

Other options:

Option A: Lung abscess typically shows a thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level as shown below.

Option B & D: Hydatid cyst and bronchogenic carcinoma can also show cavitatory lesions with air crescent but a preformed cavity from the past history of tuberculosis suggests the diagnosis of aspergilloma.
questions.learning: Aspergilloma — The given clinical scenario of a patient with a past history of tuberculosis with an X-ray showing Monod's sign is suggestive of aspergilloma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The earliest detectable sign on a Barium Enema in patients with Ulcerative Colitis is: (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mucosal Granularity

Diffuse mucosal granularity is the earliest radiographic sign of ulcerative colitis on barium studies. This subtle finding represents the initial inflammatory changes that occur in the mucosa before more advanced signs develop. Mucosal granularity appears as fine irregularities on the normally smooth mucosal surface and is best visualized on double-contrast barium enema examinations.
questions.learning: Mucosal Granularity Diffuse mucosal granularity is the earliest radiographic sign of ulcerative colitis on barium studies. This subtle finding represents the initial inflammatory changes that occur in the mucosa before more advanced signs develop.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old patient is admitted following a road traffic accident with a GCS score of E2 M4 V2. CT imaging suggests the presence of a hematoma. Which treatment option is most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient has severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), as indicated by a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ≤ 8. In a patient with GCS ≤ 8 and a CT-confirmed intracranial hematoma such as an epidural hematoma (EDH) or subdural hematoma (SDH) causing mass effect, the definitive and most appropriate treatment is urgent craniotomy with evacuation of the hematoma. Early surgical decompression is essential to relieve raised intracranial pressure, prevent brain herniation, and limit secondary ischemic injury. Endotracheal intubation and ventilation (Option A) are mandatory supportive measures in severe TBI to protect the airway and optimize oxygenation but do not treat the underlying cause of neurological deterioration. Anticoagulants (Option C) are absolutely contraindicated as they would exacerbate intracranial bleeding. Corticosteroids (Option D) are contraindicated in acute TBI, as large trials (e.g., CRASH) have shown increased mortality. The cornerstone of management in severe TBI is rapid identification and surgical evacuation of mass lesions. Neurological outcome and survival depend critically on the time interval between injury and definitive surgical decompression

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following tests is done before performing an A-V fistula procedure? The image of the test is given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Allen's test

The image is suggestive of Allen's Test. It is usually done prior to radial artery cannulation and performing an A-V fistula procedure to test the adequacy of ulnar collateral blood flow to the hand.

Allen's test is performed by occluding the radial and ulnar arteries. The patient is asked to make a tight fist so as to exsanguinate the palm. Then the patient is asked to open the hand and the occlusion over the ulnar artery is released. As occlusion of the ulnar artery is released, the color of the open palm is observed. Normally, the color will return to the palm within 5 – 6 seconds. If the palm remains pale for more than 6-10 seconds, it indicates reduced ulnar collateral flow. The modified Allen’s test considers a threshold of 5-15 seconds.

In recent years, studies have shown that, although the Allen test is often used to identify patients at increased risk for ischemic complications from radial artery cannulation, the predictive value of this test is poor. It is also used for identifying patients acceptable for radial artery harvest or use for coronary angiography.

Other options:

Option B: Adson's test is a provocative maneuver for thoracic outlet syndrome. The test is performed by extending the patient’s neck and turning the head towards the affected side while they breathe in deeply. This compresses the interscalene space and will result in paraesthesia and obliteration of the radial pulse.

Option C: Elevated arm stress test or Roos test is a provocative test for the diagnosis of thoracic outlet syndrome. For this test, the patient abducts the shoulders to 90 degrees and flexes the elbow to 90 degrees. The patient is made to open and close the hand slowly for three minutes. The test is positive if the patient is unable to complete the test or experiences cramping, pain, or numbness on the affected side.

Option D: The reflex bradycardia and increase in blood pressure that immediately follows the sudden occlusion of an arteriovenous (A-V) fistula is known as the Nicoladoni-Branham sign.
questions.learning: Allen's test — The image is suggestive of Allen's Test. It is usually done prior to radial artery cannulation and performing an A-V fistula procedure to test the adequacy of ulnar collateral blood flow to the hand.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The typical lifespan for a Japanese woman is 87 years. Due to recent progress in cervical cancer testing, her life expectancy has risen by 15 years. With a healthcare utility value of 0.8, what can be determined based on these provided parameters?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. QALY

Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY) combine quantity of life gained with quality of life, expressed as a utility value.

Here, an increase of 15 life years with a utility of 0.8 directly fits the QALY framework (QALY = life years × utility).

DALY measures health loss, while HALE and DFLE are population-level expectancy measures, not used for individual intervention benefit.

| Indicator | Measures

| --------- | --------

| QALY | Benefit of health intervention

| DALY | Burden of disease

| HALE | Healthy life expectancy

| DFLE | Life expectancy without disability

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug can be used to treat both HIV and Hepatitis B?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir (available as TDF or TAF) is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is highly effective against both the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and the Hepatitis B virus (HBV). It is a foundational component of modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV and is also considered a first-line treatment for chronic Hepatitis B due to its high potency and low risk of resistance. Lamivudine and Emtricitabine also cover both viruses, making them useful in co-infected patients. Dolutegravir (Option A) is a highly effective integrase inhibitor but only works against HIV. Zidovudine (Option C) is an older HIV medication with no activity against HBV. Ritonavir (Option D) is a protease inhibitor primarily used as a "booster" to increase the levels of other HIV drugs. In patients co-infected with HIV and HBV, it is essential to use a regimen that targets both viruses to prevent HBV "flares" if treatment is interrupted or the HBV develops resistance
questions.learning: Tenofovir (available as TDF or TAF) is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is highly effective against both the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and the Hepatitis B virus (HBV).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman, 10 years post-mastectomy, reports gradual swelling and heaviness in her right upper limb without pain. Examination reveals bluish skin nodules without signs of infection. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: A patient who develops Lymphangiosarcoma in the setting of chronic, long-standing lymphedema following a radical mastectomy is suffering from Stewart-Treves Syndrome. This is a rare but highly malignant vascular tumor. It characteristically presents approximately 10 years after the initial surgery as a gradual worsening of the swelling and the appearance of bluish-red nodules or plaques on the skin of the lymphedematous arm. Thoracic outlet syndrome (Option B) and venous insufficiency (Option C) can cause swelling but do not explain the localized bluish skin nodules in a post-mastectomy patient. Recurrent breast cancer (Option D) usually presents as a discrete mass or skin thickening (peau d'orange) rather than widespread vascular nodules. Stewart-Treves syndrome has an extremely poor prognosis due to early metastasis. The definitive treatment usually involves radical amputation of the limb, although results are often suboptimal. This condition highlights the importance of long-term monitoring for chronic lymphedema
questions.learning: A patient who develops Lymphangiosarcoma in the setting of chronic, long-standing lymphedema following a radical mastectomy is suffering from Stewart-Treves Syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures passing via jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve passing through the jugular foramen has a separate canal.

The jugular foramen is formed by the occipital bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone. The spinal accessory nerve and vagus nerve also pass through this foramen.

The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the anteromedial part of the jugular foramen in a separate dural sheath.

The branches of the nerve are tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar and lingual branches.

Infection, malignancy and postoperative inflammation of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa will cause referred pain in the ear. This is conducted through the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

• All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
• All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate etc.

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx.

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

• Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
• By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following describes LD50?
options: 50% animal mortality in an experiment, after exposure to the drug
50% reduction of infection in the given population of experimental animals
Dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population.
Range of concentrations at which the likelihood of efficacy is high and the probability of adverse effects is low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 50% animal mortality in an experiment, after exposure to the drug

LD50 (median lethal dose) is the dose of the drug at which 50% of the experimental animals die, after exposure to the drug.

Larger the LD50, the safer the drug.

In humans, TD50 is considered. TD50 refers to the dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population.

Other options:

Option B: ED50 is the dose of the drug at which there is 50% reduction of infection in the given population of experimental animals, or the dose at which 50% of the experimental animals show the specific or desired effect.

Option C: TD50 is the dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population.

Option D: Therapeutic window refers to the range of concentrations at which the likelihood of efficacy is high and the probability of adverse effects is low.
questions.learning: 50% animal mortality in an experiment, after exposure to the drug LD50 (median lethal dose) is the dose of the drug at which 50% of the experimental animals die, after exposure to the drug.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents with a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. A radiograph is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor in children and adolescents. It typically presents as a painless, slow-growing lump near the growth plate of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia). The radiograph classically shows a bony outgrowth with a cortex and medulla continuous with those of the host bone, often described as "pedunculated" or "sessile." Enchondroma (Option A) is a benign cartilage tumor that grows within the medullary cavity, usually in the small bones of the hands. Osteosarcoma (Option B) is a highly malignant tumor presenting with deep-seated pain, night pain, and characteristic "sunburst" or "Codman's triangle" radiological features. Osteomyelitis (Option C) is an infection of the bone presenting with acute pain, fever, and local inflammatory signs. Given the adolescent age, painless clinical presentation, and pathognomonic radiological appearance of a bony outgrowth, osteochondroma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor in children and adolescents. It typically presents as a painless, slow-growing lump near the growth plate of long bones, especially around the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia).

questions.text: HDI is calculated by using: 1. Life expectancy at birth 2. Mean years of schooling 3. GNI (Gross National Income) per capita

| Health / Long & healthy life | Life expectancy at birth | Life Expectancy Index

| Knowledge / Education | Mean years of schooling (adults ≥25 y) + Expected years of schooling (children of school-entering age) | Education Index (arithmetic mean of the two sub-indices)

| Standard of living | GNI per capita (PPP $, log-transformed) | Income Index

HDI = geometric mean of the three dimension indices — ∛(Health × Education × Income).
