questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Sustaining a crush injury due to fall from a building during an explosion is classified under which type of blast injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tertiary blast injury

Tertiary blast injury occurs when the body is thrown by the blast wind and strikes a solid object, leading to blunt trauma and crush injuries.

• Mechanism: Blast wave → displacement of body → impact with ground/building

• Injuries include:

o Fractures

o Head injury

o Crush injuries

Blast injury classification:

• Primary: Pressure wave → ear, lung, bowel injury

• Secondary: Flying debris → penetrating injuries

• Tertiary: Body displacement → blunt/crush trauma

• Quaternary: Burns, inhalational injuries, toxins

• Medical Board composition typically includes:

• Obstetrician/Gynecologist
• Pediatrician

• Other specialists as required

•

The decision is based on medical opinion, not legal proceedings

•

Courts are involved only in exceptional or disputed cases

Why other options are required:

• Obstetrician: Performs and supervises MTP
• Pediatrician: Assesses fetal viability/anomalies
• Sonologist: Confirms congenital anomalies

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with contralateral weakness of the arm and leg, along with ipsilateral facial weakness. The NCCT brain shows evidence of intracerebral hemorrhage. What is the most likely location of the bleed? NCCT-Non contrast CT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pons

The clinical presentation of contralateral weakness of the arm and leg and ipsilateral facial weakness along with intracerebral hemorrhage in NCCT is a typical of a lesion in the pons.

Brainstem syndromes cause crossed hemiplegia with ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies and contralateral hemiplegia. Pontine syndromes occur due to the involvement of pontine branches of the basilar artery and anterior inferior cerebellar artery. They are

CNS lesion
Effects

Foville’s Syndrome/ Dorsal pontine syndrome

• Lateral gaze palsy
• Ipsilateral facial nerve palsy
• Contralateral hemiparesis

Millard–Gubler Syndrome/Ventral pontine syndrome

• Ipsilateral abducens nerve weakness
• Ipsilateral facial nerve palsy
• Contralateral hemiplegia

In Foville's syndrome, there is a dorsal pontine injury (lesion in the abducens nucleus) that causes lateral/ horizontal gaze palsy. In Millard-Gubler syndrome, there is a ventral pontine injury (lesion in the abducens fascicle) that causes lateral rectus weakness.

Locked-in syndrome occurs when a pontine stroke causes quadriplegia and paralysis of all voluntary muscles except vertical movements of the eyes and blinking. The vertical gaze nucleus, the rostral interstitial nucleus of medial longitudinal fasciculus, is located in the midbrain and is hence preserved.

Other options:

Option A: Basal ganglia → causes contralateral hemiplegia but does not cause ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy.
Option B: Midbrain → may cause oculomotor (III) palsy + contralateral weakness (Weber syndrome), but not isolated facial weakness.
Option C: Medulla → classically causes crossed findings (CN IX, X, XII) but not facial nerve involvement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs were not given for hypertension in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor and is strictly contraindicated during all stages of pregnancy. These drugs are highly teratogenic and can cause severe fetal complications, including renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, and intrauterine growth restriction. Methyldopa (Option A) is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist and has historically been the gold standard for long-term management due to its proven safety profile. Labetalol (Option C) is a combined alpha and beta-blocker frequently used as first-line therapy for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. Nifedipine (Option D) is a calcium channel blocker considered safe and effective for controlling blood pressure without affecting uterine blood flow. Because ACE inhibitors like Enalapril interfere with the vital fetal renin-angiotensin system, they must be discontinued immediately upon the recognition of pregnancy in favor of the safer alternatives mentioned

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of Condyloma Acuminata?
questions.explanation: Condyloma Acuminata, also known as anogenital warts, are benign epithelial tumors of the skin and mucosa. The absolute most common cause, responsible for over 90% of all genital warts, is infection with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 6 and 11 (Option B) . These are classified as "low-risk" HPV types because they have a minimal association with the development of invasive cancer. In contrast, HPV 16 and 18 (Option C) are "high-risk" types most strongly linked to cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinomas. HPV 31 and 33 (Option A) are also high-risk types but are less common than 16 and 18. Recognizing the difference between these serotypes is vital for understanding the rationale behind HPV vaccines (like the quadrivalent or nonavalent versions) which target both the high-risk types for cancer prevention and the low-risk types for wart prevention. Therefore, HPV 6 and 11 are the definitive causative agents

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the red marked area in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The third rib is a typical rib, having a head, neck, and body. It is attached posteriorly to the thoracic vertebrae and curves around the chest wall to reach the anterior side near the sternum. The posterior part of the third rib is located close to the vertebral column and is thicker and stronger, as it supports articulation with the spine. This portion includes the head, neck, and the region near the tubercle. It plays an important role in forming the rib cage, which protects the thoracic organs. Additionally, it provides attachment sites for muscles and ligaments that are essential for breathing movements and maintaining the stability of the upper body

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a patient presenting with a blister on the hand and axillary lymphadenopathy, which specific history-related questions should be asked based on the findings of the clinical examination?
options: History of similar complaint in family members
questions.explanation: The combination of a primary inoculating lesion (hand blister) and regional lymphadenopathy (axillary) is highly suggestive of Cat Scratch Disease (CSD). CSD is caused by the bacterium Bartonella henselae, which is typically transmitted to humans through the scratch or bite of an infected cat, particularly kittens. Asking about "exposure to cats" is the most specific and relevant history to confirm this clinical suspicion. Exposure to rats (Option A) would suggest conditions like rat-bite fever or leptospirosis, which present differently. Family history (Option C) is less relevant for this acute infectious process. A tick bite (Option D) could suggest Lyme disease or Rickettsial infections, but the classic presentation of CSD focuses on the regional nodes draining a feline-induced skin lesion. Therefore, identifying contact with a cat provides the crucial epidemiological link for the diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of a primary inoculating lesion (hand blister) and regional lymphadenopathy (axillary) is highly suggestive of Cat Scratch Disease (CSD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with chronic cough and shortness of breath. Bronchoscopy reveals increased neutrophils and macrophages within the airways. Which of the following enzymes released by these inflammatory cells is primarily responsible for the tissue destruction seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elastase

Cigarette smoking recruits neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs, where they release elastase, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades alveolar elastic fibers. In smokers, oxidative stress also inactivates α₁-antitrypsin, the major inhibitor of elastase, resulting in unopposed elastase activity and progressive destruction of alveolar walls, leading to emphysema (COPD).

• AAT deficiency: Causes panacinar emphysema (predominantly lower lobes) and may be associated with liver disease.
• Smoking-related emphysema: Centrilobular (centriacinar) emphysema, predominantly affecting the upper lobes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Elastin: A structural protein of the extracellular matrix, not an enzyme.
• B. Peroxidase: Enzyme involved in microbial killing by neutrophils; it does not cause alveolar destruction.
• D. Collagenase: Degrades collagen and contributes to tissue remodeling, but elastase is the principal enzyme responsible for emphysematous destruction.
questions.learning: Elastase Cigarette smoking recruits neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs, where they release elastase, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades alveolar elastic fibers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old boy was admitted to the casualty with a history of breathlessness following massage by his mother. He had a history of hairline ankle fracture and was on a below-knee cast which was removed recently. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary thromboembolism

The given clinical history of immobilization after the application of the cast is a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Massaging the leg may dislodge the thrombus causing pulmonary embolism (PE). It is the commonest complication of DVT leading to death.

PE and DVT are part of the same spectrum of venous thromboembolism. PE occurs due to obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation by deep venous thrombi that detach from their site of formation and embolize to the vena cava, right atrium, and right ventricle. Virchow’s triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, leading to recruitment of activated platelets, provides the ideal environment for thrombus formation.

DVT presents with pain and swelling of the calf (the most common symptom), tenderness and edema. Clinical examination is unreliable and the elicitation of signs such as Homan's or Mose's signs is not recommended owing to the risk of clot dislodgement. Patients with symptoms of PE present with fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis. On examination, they can have cyanosis, jugular venous distension, fixed split-second heart sound and pleural rub, but may be subtle or absent. Some patients are asymptomatic.

Depending on the clinical presentation, patients with PE can be stratified as:

• High-risk (massive) PE is characterized by systemic hypotension. Patients can have dyspnea and syncope and may present in cardiogenic shock.
• Intermediate-risk PE is characterized by right ventricle (RV) dysfunction but normal blood pressure. RV dysfunction can be diagnosed with echocardiography and ECG.
• Low-risk PE is characterized by normal blood pressure and the absence of any RV dysfunction.

Investigations:

• Venous duplex ultrasound to look for thrombi in the leg.
• Chest x-ray in PE shows hyper lucency in an area of oligemia (Westermark sign). D-dimer levels are elevated and ECG will show sinus tachycardia (the most common ECG abnormality) and an S1Q3T3 sign (an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III, and an inverted T wave in lead III).
• Definitive diagnosis of PE is by a CT-Pulmonary Angiography.

The management of PE will vary according to the risk stratification:

• A patient with high-risk PE will primarily be treated with anticoagulation and thrombolysis or catheter/surgical embolectomy.
• A patient with low-risk PE will be treated with anticoagulation alone, or an IVC filter as secondary prophylaxis.
• Patients with intermediate-risk PE require individualized treatment.

Anticoagulation can be done with the classical strategy of low-molecular-weight heparin followed by warfarin, or by low-molecular-weight heparin for 5 days, switched to novel oral anticoagulant like Dabigatran after that. Fibrinolysis, if indicated, is done with recombinant TPA administered over 2 hours. It can be done up to 14 days after the PE has occurred.

Management of DVT:

• Anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and unfractionated heparin (UFH) if renal impairment is present.
• After treatment with heparin, patients should be commenced on oral anticoagulants for at least 3 months with either factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban and apixaban) or direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran).
• Other measures such as rest, limb elevation and compression stockings are also used.
questions.learning: Pulmonary thromboembolism — The given clinical history of immobilization after the application of the cast is a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery? * Patient selection * Primary exploration * ICU care * Secondary exploration * Abdominal closure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3,4,5

The correct answer is option C: 1,2,3,4,5

The correct sequence  of five stages of damage control surgery are:

* Patient selection

* Control of haemorrhage and control of contamination(primary exploration)

* Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit

* Deﬁnitive surgery(secondary exploration)

* Abdominal closure

Damage control surgery is minimal intervention done to stabilize the patient and do the definite surgery later. It centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries. The aim of the DCS is to restore physiology over anatomy. It is applied to trauma patients with combined vascular and visceral injuries.

The phases are:

*

Phase 1 involves recognition of the severity of the injury. Here,rapid-sequence induction of anesthesia and intubation is done. This is followed by early rewarming and prompt movement of the patient to the operating theatre.

*

Phase 2 involves performing immediate laparotomy. Here, the focus is to control bleeding and contamination. Abdominal packing and temporary wound closure are done.

*

Phase 3 involves movement to the intensive care unit (ICU). The aim is to normalize the biochemical and physiological parameters.

*

Phase 4 involves re-exploration in the operating theatre. Here, definitive repair of all injuries is done. Multiple procedures on multiple occasions may be required.

Pearl PF2177: Damage Control Surgery

Five stages of damage control surgery:

1. Patient selection
2. Control of hemorrhage and control of contamination
3. Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit
4. Deﬁnitive surgery
5. Abdominal closure

Phases of Damage Control Surgery:

Phase 0: Identification of patient for damage control surgery in emergency room
Phase 1: Emergency laparotomy to stop bleeding and prevent contamination
Phase 2: ICU care for resuscitation
Phase 3: Re-laparotomy for definitive repair
Indications for damage control surgery:
Anatomical

* Inability to achieve haemostasis

* Complex abdominal injury, e.g. liver and pancreas

* Combined vascular, solid and hollow organ injury, e.g. aortic or caval injury

* Inaccessible major venous injury, e.g. retrohepatic vena cava

* Demand for non-operative control of other injuries, e.g. fractured pelvis

* Anticipated need for a time-consuming procedure

Physiological (decline of physiological reserve)

* Temperature <34ºC

* pH <7.2

* Serum lactate >5 mmol/L (normal is <2.5 mmol/L)

* Prothrombin time (PT) >16 s

* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) >60 s

* Blood transfusion approaching 15 units

* Blood pressure <70 mmHg

Environmental

* Operating time >60 min

* Inability to approximate the abdominal incision

* Desire to reassess the intra-abdominal contents (directed relook)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient taking metronidazole for diarrhea consumed alcohol at a party. Subsequently, he developed red rashes, generalized itching, and a headache. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Several medications, most notably metronidazole, inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is responsible for breaking down the toxic metabolite of alcohol. When a patient on these drugs consumes even a small amount of alcohol, acetaldehyde accumulates in the blood, leading to a highly unpleasant syndrome called a disulfiram-like reaction. Symptoms include intense flushing ("red rashes"), headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, and palpitations. Methanol poisoning (Option A) is characterized by metabolic acidosis and visual disturbances. The "cheese reaction" (Option C) occurs when patients on MAO inhibitors eat tyramine-rich foods, leading to a hypertensive crisis. To prevent this reaction, patients prescribed metronidazole must be strictly counseled to avoid all alcohol during treatment and for at least 48-72 hours after the last dose. Other drugs causing this reaction include certain cephalosporins and sulfonylureas
questions.learning: Several medications, most notably metronidazole, inhibit the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is responsible for breaking down the toxic metabolite of alcohol.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presented with seizures. His past history is significant for an episode of fever with rash at 1 year of age which resolved spontaneously. What is the most helpful investigation to diagnose his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgG measles in CSF

The clinical scenario of a child with a previous history of fever with rash at 1 year, now presenting with seizures, is highly indicative of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare chronic complication of measles. Anti-measles antibodies are elevated in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (IgG >IgM); hence, it is the most helpful investigation to diagnose this condition.

SSPE is a fatal progressive demyelinating disease caused by chronic CNS infection with the genetically altered variant of the measles virus. It occurs several years after primary measles infection and is more common in males.

Clinical manifestations progress through four stages:

• Stage I: involves mild symptoms like irritability and poor school performance.
• Stage II: is characterized by myoclonic seizures.
• Stage III:choreoathetosis, immobility, dystonia, lead-pipe rigidity, and cognitive decline are seen.
• Stage IV: leads to coma and death.

Diagnosis of SSPE is established by documentation of a compatible clinical course along with one of the following supporting findings: elevated measles antibody (IgG >IgM) in CSF analysis or characteristic electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns, suppression-burst episodes (high voltage sharp slow waves) or typical histological findings or isolation of virus from brain tissue.

CT and MRI show evidence of multifocal white matter lesions, cortical atrophy, and ventricular enlargement. Increased T2 signaling in the white matter of the brain is seen as the disease progresses (shown below):

Treatment is mainly supportive. Isoprinosine along with interferons is said to have additional effects. Carbamazepine is found to be useful in controlling myoclonic jerks in the early stages of the illness.

In measles, after an incubation period of 8-12 days, the prodromal phase starts with mild fever and is followed by conjunctivitis, photophobia, coryza, cough, and increasing fever. Koplik spots, appearing 1-4 days prior to the rash, are a characteristic sign of measles. The rash (shown below) appears on the 4th day of fever and typically begins on the forehead (around the hairline), and behind the ears, as a red maculopapular eruption.

The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media. The most common cause of death in measles is pneumonia. Low serum retinol levels in children with measles are associated with higher morbidity and mortality and hence Vitamin A therapy is indicated for all patients with measles.

Other options:

Option B: A common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy is mesial (medial) temporal sclerosis. It is the most common cause of surgically remediable partial epilepsy in adolescents and adults. It is often preceded by febrile seizures. Pathologically, these patients have atrophy and gliosis of the hippocampus. MRI shows hippocampal sclerosis (shown below).

Option D: C1Q4 antibodies in the CSF are seen in neuromyelitis optica. Neuromyelitis optica, also known as Devic’s disease, is an aggressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis.
questions.learning: IgG measles in CSF — The clinical scenario of a child with a previous history of fever with rash at 1 year, now presenting with seizures, is highly indicative of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare chronic complication of measles.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Relative bradycardia is seen in:
questions.explanation: Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, occurs when the pulse rate does not increase proportionally with the body temperature during a febrile illness. This clinical phenomenon is a classic feature of certain infections, most notably Enteric (Typhoid) fever and Brucella. While several other conditions can manifest this sign, Brucella is a primary choice among the listed options. Dengue (A) typically presents with high-grade fever and tachycardia, although a transient bradycardia may occur during the convalescent phase. Bordetella pertussis (C) primarily affects the respiratory tract with paroxysmal coughing and does not typically exhibit Faget's sign. Leptospirosis (D) is associated with high fever and conjunctival suffusion; while it can have cardiac complications, it is not the defining clinical association for relative bradycardia in standardized medical testing. Recognizing this pulse-temperature dissociation is a valuable diagnostic tool in evaluating undifferentiated tropical fevers. Therefore, Brucella is the most accurate answer for this characteristic physiological finding in the context of these options
questions.learning: Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, occurs when the pulse rate does not increase proportionally with the body temperature during a febrile illness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of a category III dog bite and reports having received post-exposure prophylaxis for a dog bite six months ago. What should be the next step in management?
options: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 &3
Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0,3 & 7
Wound cleaning + intramuscular (IM) vaccine + rabies immune globulin (RIG)
questions.explanation: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) management depends on the patient's prior vaccination status. For a person who has previously completed a full course of pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis (as this patient did six months ago), the protocol is streamlined. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and national guidelines, such individuals do NOT require Rabies Immune Globulin (RIG), even for Category 3 bites. Instead, they require immediate wound cleaning with soap and water for 15 minutes and a booster series of two doses of the modern rabies vaccine, administered intramuscularly or intradermally on day 0 and day 3. Options C and D are incorrect because the additional dose on day 7 and the administration of RIG are only necessary for previously unvaccinated (naive) individuals. Option A is incorrect because wound cleaning alone is insufficient to prevent rabies, which is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear. This simplified two-dose "re-exposure" regimen is effective due to the immunological memory established by the previous vaccination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive limb weakness over the past year. Examination reveals muscle fasciculations and increased muscle tone, with preserved sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the simultaneous involvement of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN). The presence of hypertonia (a UMN sign) and muscle fasciculations (an LMN sign) in the same limb, while the sensory system remains intact, is pathognomonic for ALS. Spinal Muscular Atrophy (Option B) is a pure LMN disease and would not present with UMN signs like hypertonia. Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (Option C) typically presents with pure LMN weakness that is often asymmetric and lacks UMN features. Becker Muscular Dystrophy (Option D) is a genetic myopathy that causes proximal muscle weakness but does not involve motor neurons, meaning it lacks fasciculations and UMN signs. Because ALS relentlessly destroys both sets of motor neurons in the motor cortex and spinal cord while sparing sensory pathways, it is the only viable diagnosis for this clinical picture
questions.learning: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the simultaneous involvement of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. During evaluation, the physician reviews the functional roles of the intestinal epithelium. Which of the following functions is NOT a primary function of the intestinal epithelium?
questions.explanation: The secretion of bile salts is a primary function of the liver (hepatocytes), not the intestinal epithelium. Bile is synthesized in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum to aid in the emulsification and absorption of fats. The other functions listed are key roles of the intestinal epithelium. The epithelium is highly specialized for the absorption of ions (Option A), water, and nutrients via various transporters. Mucous secretion (Option C) is performed by goblet cells interspersed within the epithelium to protect the mucosal surface and facilitate the passage of contents. The formation of digestive enzymes (Option D), such as disaccharidases and peptidases, occurs at the brush border of the enterocytes, allowing for the final stages of carbohydrate and protein digestion. While the intestine is vital for the reabsorption of bile salts in the terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation), their initial secretion is exclusively a hepatic process
questions.learning: The secretion of bile salts is a primary function of the liver (hepatocytes), not the intestinal epithelium. Bile is synthesized in the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum to aid in the emulsification and absorption of fats.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following ultrasound findings is diagnostic of polycystic ovarian morphology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ≥20 follicles in one ovary

The international diagnostic guidelines for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)—specifically the updated consensus recommendations—define Polycystic Ovarian Morphology (PCOM) by the presence of 20 or more follicles (measuring 2–9 mm) in at least one ovary when using high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound transducers (>8 MHz). Alternatively, an ovarian volume of >10 mL in at least one ovary satisfies the definition. It does not require both ovaries to meet the threshold simultaneously

High-Yield Points

• Current cutoff: ≥20 follicles in one ovary (using high-frequency transvaginal ultrasound ≥8 MHz).
• Older Rotterdam criterion (2003): ≥12 follicles and/or ovarian volume >10 mL.
• Only one ovary needs to meet the criterion.
• PCOM alone does not diagnose PCOS; diagnosis requires fulfillment of accepted PCOS diagnostic criteria after excluding other causes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Macrophages play an important role in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation. Which of the following cells perform the same function in the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages located in the liver that form part of the mononuclear phagocyte system. These are present, lining the walls of the sinusoids, not the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse).

Macrophages can be divided into:

* Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.

* Tissue macrophages survive for months.

2 main functions of macrophages:

* Phagocytosis.

* Antigen presentation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Up to what time after delivery can an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) be safely inserted in the postpartum period??
questions.explanation: Postpartum Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (PPIUCD) insertion is a highly effective strategy for preventing unintended pregnancies. According to standard protocols, the device can be inserted immediately after the delivery of the placenta (within 10 minutes) or up to 48 hours following delivery. After this 48-hour window, the risk of device expulsion and infection increases significantly due to the rapid involution of the uterus. If insertion does not occur within the first 48 hours, the patient is usually advised to wait at least 6 weeks (Option C) until the puerperium is complete and the uterus has returned to its normal size. Options A, C, and D are either incomplete or describe intervals outside the specific "immediate postpartum" window. PPIUCD provides long-term, reversible contraception that does not interfere with breastfeeding, making it an ideal choice for many women during the hospital stay following delivery

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the respiratory burst in neutrophils?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NADPH oxidase

The deficiency of NADPH oxidase is responsible for the respiratory burst in neutrophils.

NADPH + 2O2 → NADP+ + 2·O2− + 2H+

NADPH oxidase in the inflammatory cells (neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and macrophages) produces superoxide anion by reducing oxygen by a process of respiratory burst during phagocytosis.

There are multiple sources of oxygen radicals in the body:

* Ionizing radiation (x-rays and UV) causes lysis of water, leading to the formation of hydroxyl radicals.

* Transition metal ions (Cu+, Co2+, Ni2+, and Fe2+) can react nonenzymatically with oxygen or hydrogen peroxide to form hydroxyl radicals.

* Nitric oxide can react with superoxide to yield peroxynitrite, which decays to form hydroxyl radicals.

* NADPH oxidase in the inflammatory cells produces superoxide radicals.

Other options:

Options A: Catalase is involved in protecting cells from oxidative damage by removing hydrogen peroxide, it is not involved in the generation of reactive oxygen species during the respiratory burst.

Option C: Defensin is an anti-bacterial compound that plays a role in the defense mechanism of the cell.

Option D: Myeloperoxidase is an enzyme found in the granules of neutrophils that uses hydrogen peroxide to produce more potent antimicrobial agents.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Patient experiences softening of the cervix in early pregnancy. This sign is called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Goodell

Goodell's sign refers to the softening of the cervix, which is observed during early pregnancy. This sign occurs due to increased vascularization and changes in the connective tissue of the cervix, making it feel softer compared to the non-pregnant state, where the cervix feels firm like the tip of the nose.

| Piscacek’s sign | Asymmetrical uterine enlargement in lateral implantation

| Hegar’s sign | On bimanual exam, the abdominal and vaginal finger appose below the body of the uterus

| Palmer’s sign | Rhythmic uterine contractions elicited on bimanual exam

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding androgen insensitivity syndrome? 1. Inherited as X-linked recessive disorder 2. Karyotype is 46 XXY 3. It is also called testicular feminization 4. Confirmation of diagnosis by gonadal biopsy Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

• 1. Inherited as X-linked recessive disorder. ✓

• AIS is caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome and follows X-linked recessive inheritance.

• 2. Karyotype is 46 XXY. ✗

• The karyotype is 46,XY, not 47,XXY (which is Klinefelter syndrome).

• 3. It is also called testicular feminization. ✓

• Complete AIS is classically referred to as testicular feminization syndrome.

• 4. Confirmation of diagnosis by gonadal biopsy. ✓

• Histopathological examination of the gonads (showing testes) confirms gonadal tissue. In current practice, diagnosis is primarily established by 46,XY karyotype, hormonal profile, and genetic testing for androgen receptor mutations, but gonadal biopsy has traditionally been used for confirmation in examination contexts.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A smoker who was given an interscalene block for an arthroscopic acromioclavicular joint reconstruction 2 days ago was followed up by a Chest x-ray which showed as below. He is asymptomatic at present and is comfortably resting on the bed. What is the next step in management?
options: Insert chest drain as soon as possible
Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed

The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax.

As the patient is asymptomatic with no symptoms of dyspnoea or respiratory distress the best way to manage is to wait and watch.

Postoperative pneumothorax is seen mostly in patients with pre existing lung conditions like asthma or in chronic smokers. The pre-existing blebs or bullae in the individuals rupture due to pressure gradients created by the positive pressure from ventilation or the arthroscopic pump and shaver system used during surgery.

The pressure gradient from the positive pressure of anesthesia and the ipsilateral lung is highest in the lateral decubitus position.

The other complications that can occur are subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum.
questions.learning: Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During a preoperative assessment, a 45-year- old patient undergoes evaluation of the airway to predict the likelihood of difficulty during endotracheal intubation. On inspection, the soft palate, uvula, fauces (pillars), and tonsils are all fully visible without any obstruction. Based on these findings, which Mallampatti score does this airway correspond to?
questions.explanation: The Mallampati classification is used by anesthesiologists to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. A Mallampati Score of 1 is assigned when there is complete visualization of the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars. This score indicates that intubation is likely to be straightforward. Score 2 (Option B) involves visualization of the soft palate and the majority of the uvula, but the pillars are obscured. Score 3 (Option C) allows for the visualization of the soft palate and the base of the uvula only. Score 4 (Option D) is assigned when the soft palate is not visible at all, and only the hard palate can be seen; this score predicts a "difficult airway." Accurate assessment requires the patient to sit upright, open their mouth wide, and protrude the tongue without phonating. Identifying a Score 1 allows the surgical team to proceed with standard intubation protocols, while higher scores necessitate preparation for advanced airway management techniques
questions.learning: The Mallampati classification is used by anesthesiologists to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. A Mallampati Score of 1 is assigned when there is complete visualization of the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with complaints of hair loss. Based on the findings observed during clinical examination, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition characterized by non-scarring hair loss that typically presents as "well-demarcated, smooth, circular patches" on the scalp or body. The provided image shows the classic focal patch without inflammation, scaling, or scarring. A characteristic clinical finding at the margins of these patches is "exclamation mark hairs"—short hairs that are narrower at the base. Tinea capitis (Option A) is a fungal infection that usually features scaling, erythema, and "black dots" (broken hairs). Kerion (Option B) is a severe, inflammatory form of tinea capitis that presents as a boggy, pus-filled mass. Options C and D are identical in the source text, both correctly identifying the condition. Alopecia areata has an unpredictable course; while many patients experience spontaneous regrowth, others may progress to total scalp hair loss (alopecia totalis). First-line treatment often involves intralesional corticosteroid injections to suppress the localized immune response and encourage hair regrowth
questions.learning: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition characterized by non-scarring hair loss that typically presents as "well-demarcated, smooth, circular patches" on the scalp or body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 20-year-old man reports to the emergency room after falling from a ladder. Physical examination reveals an inability to abduct the arm and flex the elbow, as shown in the image below. There is sensory loss from the shoulder to the lateral arm. Which nerve roots are affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C5 and C6

The image shows a typical presentation of a policeman's tip, waiter's tip or porter's tip deformity seen in Erb’s palsy, and the nerves affected are the C5 and C6 roots.

The Erb’s point in the brachial plexus is in the upper trunk, where the six nerves meet. The nerves are the C5 and C6 roots, the suprascapular nerve, the nerve to subclavius, and the anterior and posterior divisions of the upper trunk.

Given below is a diagram depicting the location of the Erb's point:

Anatomically, the brachial plexus consists of roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches.

The common causes of Erb's palsy are the undue separation of head and neck, i.e., falling on the shoulder, and birth injuries. The resulting muscle weakness results in the depicted deformity, which includes the following features:

* The arm is adducted and medially rotated at the shoulder joint

* The elbow joint is extended

* The radioulnar joint is pronated

* Sensory loss along the outer aspect of the arm

Aeroplane splint is used in the treatment of brachial plexus injury (Erb’s palsy). Here, the shoulder is maintained in abduction and external rotation, the elbow in flexion, the forearm in supination, and the wrist in extension.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with bluish-black discoloration of the sclera and pinna for the past six months and reports that his urine has turned black on standing since childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical features described are classic for alkaptonuria, a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. It is caused by deficiency of the enzyme homogentisate oxidase, which is involved in the degradation of the amino acids phenylalanine and tyrosine. As a result, homogentisic acid accumulates in the body. When homogentisic acid is excreted in urine and exposed to air, it oxidizes and turns the urine black—often noticed since childhood. With time, the pigment deposits in connective tissues, leading to bluish-black discoloration of the sclera and ear cartilage (pinna), a condition known as ochronosis. Phenylketonuria presents with intellectual disability and a “mousy” odor, tyrosinemia causes liver and kidney failure, and maple syrup urine disease produces urine with a burnt sugar smell. The combination of black urine on standing and ochronosis is pathognomonic of alkaptonuria

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a case of face presentation during labor, which diameter is seen?
questions.explanation: In face presentation, the fetal head is in a state of complete extension, making the face the presenting part with the chin (mentum) as the denominator. The engaging diameter in a fully extended head is the submentobregmatic diameter, which measures approximately 9.5 cm. This diameter allows for a favorable vaginal delivery if the mentum is in an anterior position. Mentobregmatic (Option A) refers to a 13.5 cm diameter seen in brow presentation, which is the largest diameter and often leads to obstructed labor. Suboccipitobregmatic (Option B) is the 9.5 cm diameter associated with a well-flexed vertex presentation, which is the most common and favorable for normal delivery. Occipitofrontal (Option C) is a 11.5 cm diameter found in a deflexed vertex presentation. Consequently, the submentobregmatic diameter is the specific anatomical landmark for a face presentation
questions.learning: In face presentation, the fetal head is in a state of complete extension, making the face the presenting part with the chin (mentum) as the denominator.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior nucleus

The structure marked in the above image is mamillary body and the fibers from the mamillary body end in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

The mammillary bodies are two small hemispherical, pea-sized eminences, lying side by side, forming the floor of the third ventricle. The fibres from medial mammillary nucleus project to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

The anterior thalamic nuclei have 3 subdivisions—anteroventral nucleus, anteromedial nucleus, and anterodorsal nucleus.

• Major input: Mamillothalamic tract from the mammillary nuclei of the hypothalamus.
• Major cortical output: Anterior limbic area, cingulate, and the parahippocampal gyrus
• Major function:

• Regulation of alertness and attention
• Acquisition of memory
questions.learning: Anterior nucleus — The structure marked in the above image is mamillary body and the fibers from the mamillary body end in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70 year old male presents with neck nodes. Examination of left ear reveals a dull tympanic membrane, deafness and tinnitus. On tympanogram, a Type B curve is obtained. Most probable diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis is nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Points in favour:

* 70yr old with neck nodes pointing towards malignancy (can be either due to infection but no other signs of infection given plus the age points more towards malignancy).

* On examination ear shows dull tympanic membrane and audiometry shows curve B which means  fluid is present in left ear ruling out option d (Sensorineuronal hearing loss).

* Type B tympanogram seen in serous otitis media. Presence of unilateral serous otitis media in an adult should raise the suspicion of a nasopharngeal growth.

* Age of the patient (most common age 5th -7th decade).

* sex of the patient (most common in males).

Other options:

Option a: On examination either cholesteotoma granulation or perforation will be seen.

Option b: On examination, otoscopy shows a red reflex through intact tympanic membrane. “Rising sun” appearance is seen when tumour arises from the floor of middle ear.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

* Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is also called Guangdong tumor.

* Commonest site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmüller.

* Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV) is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Presenting symptoms and signs of nasopharyngeal cancer in order of frequency are:

* Cervical lymphadenopathy (most common) (60–90%)

* Hearing loss

* Nasal obstruction

* Epistaxis

* Cranial nerve palsies -Cranial nerves V and VI are the most commonly involved among all the cranial nerves. (V more than VI)

* Headache

* Earache

* Neck pain

* Weight loss

Nasopharyngeal cancer can cause:

* Conductive deafness (eustachian tube block)

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal/facial neuralgia (involvement of CN V) and

* Palatal paralysis (CN X)

This is collectively called Trotter’s triad.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal cancer.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone.

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dacryocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) as it re-establishes the lacrimal drainage.

One of the sequelae of chronic dacryocystitis is mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy.

Streptococcus hemolyticus and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common etiological agents for acute and chronic dacryocystitis

Initially, the inflammation is controlled with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents. Sequelae of acute dacryocystitis is a lacrimal fistula, which is treated with is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Nebulized salbutamol is used in the management of which of the following electrolyte abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperkalemia

Nebulized salbutamol (β₂-adrenergic agonist) is used as an adjunct in the emergency management of hyperkalemia. It lowers serum potassium by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump, thereby shifting potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells. It acts rapidly but does not remove potassium from the body.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Hypernatremia: Managed with free water replacement or hypotonic fluids, not salbutamol.
• C. Hyponatremia: Treated according to severity with fluid restriction, hypertonic saline, or vasopressin antagonists, depending on the cause.
• D. Hypomagnesemia: Treated with oral or intravenous magnesium replacement.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to you with an irregularly irregular pulse of 120/minute and a pulse deficit of 20. Which of the following would be the JVP finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent a wave

Pulse deficit = difference between:

• Apical heart rate
• Peripheral pulse rate

In AF:

• Some ventricular contractions are too weak to produce a peripheral pulse

Thus, pulse deficit occurs. An irregularly irregular pulse with pulse deficit indicates atrial fibrillation.

In AF, organized atrial contraction is absent, leading to loss of the ‘a’ wave in JVP.

Cannon ‘’ waves occur with AV dissociation, not AF.

Thus, the characteristic JVP finding is an absent ‘a’ wave.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which substrate accumulates in type IX Mucopolysaccharidosis (Natowicz Syndrome)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyaluronic acid

The substrate that is accumulated in Mucopolysaccharidosis type IX (Natowicz syndrome) is hyaluronic acid.

Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IX (MPS IX), also known as Natowicz Syndrome, is an extremely rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of the hyaluronidase (HYAL1) enzyme. This enzyme is responsible for breaking down hyaluronic acid, and its deficiency leads to its accumulation in tissues, resulting in joint stiffness, soft tissue masses, and mild skeletal abnormalities.

Unlike other MPS types, MPS IX does not significantly affect cognitive function or major organs, and patients generally have a normal life expectancy. The condition follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern due to mutations in the HYAL1 gene. Diagnosis is confirmed through elevated hyaluronic acid levels in urine, enzyme activity tests, and genetic analysis. While there is no specific cure, treatment focuses on symptom management, pain relief, and physical therapy to maintain mobility.

Other options -

Option B: Dermatan sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) found in the skin, blood vessels, and connective tissues, playing a role in cell signalling and wound healing. Its accumulation occurs in mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., MPS I, II, and VI), leading to tissue damage and organ dysfunction.

Option C: Heparan sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) found on cell surfaces and in the extracellular matrix, involved in cell signalling and coagulation. Its accumulation occurs in mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., MPS I, II, and III), leading to neurological and systemic dysfunction.

Option D: Keratan sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) found in the cornea, cartilage, and connective tissues, playing a role in hydration and structural integrity. Its accumulation occurs in mucopolysaccharidosis type IV (Morquio syndrome), leading to skeletal and joint abnormalities.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. Skin grafting was done wherein the graft was taken from the same person. Which type of graft is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autograft

The given image shows a split skin graft obtained from the same person. This type of graft is autograft.

Skin grafting is the transfer of skin from the donor area to the recipient area. The most preferable donor site is the buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

Autograft is the transfer of tissue from one location to another location on the same patient.

Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories:

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing).

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction.

Other options:

Option B:Xenograft is tissue transfer from a donor of one species to a recipient of another species. It is also known as heterograft.

Option C: Allograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically different members, e.g. kidney transplantation (human to human). It is also known as homograft.

Option D: Isograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically identical individuals, i.e. between two identical twins.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)
questions.learning: Autograft — The given image shows a split skin graft obtained from the same person. Skin grafting is the transfer of skin from the donor area to the recipient area.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the graph given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Line graph

The given image depicts a line graph.

A line graph depicts a time-trend and has time as the x-axis. In the given graph above, the x-axis is the value of Hb concentration.

Pearl PF1736: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following image shows a histogram.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ECG finding is characteristically found in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wide QRS

Characteristic ECG findings in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is Wide QRS interval.

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a form of atrioventricular reentry phenomenon characterized by the presence of accessory conducting pathways between the atria and ventricles that are separate from the AV node and Purkinje tissue.

The tachycardia is usually produced by the conduction of a normal impulse from the ventricles to the atria via the accessory pathway (bundle of Kent). This is the orthodromic pathway. Less often, a premature atrial beat travels down the accessory pathway (while AV Node is still in refractory period) leading to premature ventricular activation. This is the antidromic pathway.

The classic ECG features in WPW are as follows:

*

A shortened PR interval (typically <120 ms)

*

A slurring and the slow rise of the initial upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave)

*

A widened QRS complex (total duration >0.12 seconds)

*

ST-segment–T wave (repolarization) changes, generally directed opposite the major delta wave and QRS complex, reflecting altered depolarization

Pearl PF1816: Wolff Parkinson White Syndrome

Wolff Parkinson White Syndrome (WPW) is characterized by an abnormal accessory pathway in the heart leading to arrhythmias.

Pathology- Born with an accessory pathway, the bundle of Kent which connects the atria and ventricle. The electrical impulses from the SA node reach the ventricles earlier via the accessory pathway as there is no AV nodal delay in this pathway. This leads to the preexcitation of the ventricle and initiation of ventricular contraction. This ventricular contraction is prolonged when the impulse via the AV nodal pathway reaches the ventricles.

Most common location of the accessory pathway- between the left atrium and free wall of the left ventricle

ECG changes:

Shortened PR interval- because of the early initiation of ventricular depolarization

Prolonged QRS duration- because of the AV nodal impulse reaching the ventricles after the aberrant impulse.

Delta waves- slurred upstroke of QRS complex

The given ECG shows delta waves marked with red arrows:

Treatment:

* Catheter ablation is the treatment of choice.

* Anti-arrhythmic drugs like procainamide, amiodarone, quinidine, propafenone, dofetilide are used in slowing conduction in the accessory pathway (prolong refractory period).

* IV procainamide is the drug of choice in a hemodynamically stable WPW presenting with atrial fibrillation.

* DC cardioversion is done in hemodynamically unstable patients.
