questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman with a past history of spontaneous abortion now presents with amenorrhea. Her serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level is 6 mIU/mL. Based on her clinical history and hormonal findings, what is the most likely cause of her amenorrhea?
questions.explanation: Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following a vigorous dilation and curettage (D&C) performed for a spontaneous abortion. The adhesions obliterate the uterine cavity, leading to secondary amenorrhea despite normal hormonal function. The provided FSH level of 6 mIU/ml is within the "normal" range (typically 5–20 mIU/ml), which indicates that the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is intact. Sheehan's syndrome (Option A) involves pituitary infarction after postpartum hemorrhage and would show "low" gonadotropins. Premature ovarian failure (Option B) would be characterized by a "very high" FSH (usually >40 mIU/ml) as the ovaries fail to respond. PCOS (Option C) typically presents with irregular periods and metabolic signs, not sudden amenorrhea following a procedure, and usually shows a high LH:FSH ratio. The clinical history of a procedure followed by amenorrhea with a normal FSH is pathognomonic for an "outflow tract" obstruction like Asherman syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by hysteroscopy
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following a vigorous dilation and curettage (D&C) performed for a spontaneous abortion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in which of the following vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B6

Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), a coenzyme required by kynureninase enzyme to convert 3-OH kynurenine to 3-OH anthranilic acid during tryptophan metabolism.

Other options-

Option A: Riboflavin or Vitamin B2 deficiency manifests as angular stomatitis, magenta tongue, seborrhea, corneal vascularization. It is seen in alcoholism, and individuals with a poor diet and decreased intake of dairy products.

Option B: A patient with thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency presents either dry Beriberi with predominantly neurological symptoms like neuropathy, muscle weakness, and wasting or wet Beriberi with predominant cardiac symptoms like cardiomegaly, tachycardia, high output congestive cardiac failure.

Option C: Vitamin B12 or cobalamin deficiency presents as anemia, fatigue, and pallor symptoms. Other presenting complaints may include peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, diarrhea, headaches, neuropsychiatric disturbances like dementia, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SACD) leading to ataxia. A peripheral smear shows macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
questions.learning: Vitamin B6 Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in deficiency of vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate), a coenzyme required by kynureninase enzyme to convert 3-OH kynurenine to 3-OH anthranilic acid during tryptophan metabolism.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Anuj has been diagnosed with diphtheria and is being treated in the ward. His 3-year-old brother, Ajay who lives in the same house has received vaccination against diphtheria about 16 months back. What is the next best step for the management of the younger sibling, Ajay?
options: Nothing as the child is already exposed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythromycin only

In the given clinical scenario, a 3-year-old child is likely to have received the 4th dose (1st booster) of the diphtheria vaccine between 16–24 months of age according to National Immunization Schedule (i.e., 16 months ago). Since he has received a booster dose within 5 years, only erythromycin is indicated in case of close contact with the diphtheria patient.

All household contacts with diphtheria patients should be closely monitored for 7 days. Culture should be taken from both the throat and nose. All contacts should receive antibiotic prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G or erythromycin), regardless of immunization status.

Children who have not received a booster dose of the diphtheria toxoid vaccine within 5 years should be given the vaccine in an age-appropriate form. Children who have not yet received their 4th dose should be vaccinated accordingly.

If fewer than three doses of diphtheria toxoid have been given, or vaccination history is unknown, an immediate dose of diphtheria toxoid should be given and the primary series completed according to the current schedule.

Asymptomatic carriers of diphtheria are treated with antimicrobial prophylaxis for a period of 10-14 days. If an individual has not received a booster dose of diphtheria toxoid within 1 year, an age-appropriate preparation of the vaccine should be administered promptly.

Droplet precautions (respiratory colonization) or contact precautions (cutaneous colonization) of cases and carriers are maintained until two consecutive negative cultures (collected 24 hours apart) are obtained after cessation of therapy.
questions.learning: Erythromycin only — In the given clinical scenario, a 3-year-old child is likely to have received the 4th dose (1st booster) of the diphtheria vaccine between 16–24 months of age according to National Immunization Schedule (i.e., 16 months ago).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following factors is not considered in the FRAX score assessment?
questions.explanation: The FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score is used to calculate the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture based on individual clinical risk factors. While Body Mass Index (BMI) (Option C) is a core component, it is calculated using weight and height; however, absolute height (Option A) is not a standalone factor in the risk calculation. Smoking status (Option B) and current or past glucocorticoid intake (Option D) are well-established clinical risk factors included in the tool. Other factors considered include age, sex, prior fracture history, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, and alcohol intake. The tool is designed to identify patients who may benefit from pharmacological intervention to prevent fractures. While height is measured to calculate BMI, it does not serve as an independent predictor of bone mineral density or fracture risk within the FRAX algorithm. Therefore, "height" is the correct choice as the factor not directly assessed as an independent risk variable
questions.learning: The FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score is used to calculate the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture based on individual clinical risk factors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old male with a history of respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago is unable to stand or walk for the past 2 weeks and the weakness is progressive, ascending, and symmetrical in nature. The lower limbs were involved before and gradually the upper limbs were also affected. On examination you note areflexia. Pain and proprioception are preserved. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Guillain-Barré syndrome

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS).

GBS is an acute, fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. GBS is caused when immune response/antibodies against external antigens like infections, vaccines, etc target similar proteins present in the person's nervous tissue.

Clinical features are rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis with or without sensory disturbance. Respiration is compromised when it involves respiratory muscles. In such cases, ventilatory support is needed.

High-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) or plasmapheresis are equally effective for typical GBS. IVIg is the initial therapy chosen because of its ease of administration and good safety record.

Other options:

Option B: Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disorder due to autoimmune damage to the acetylcholine receptors. It is characterized by weakness and muscle fatiguability. Weakness increases with usage. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can be seen. Proximal limb weakness is also present.

Option C: Polymyositis is one of the inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric and proximal muscle weakness. This weakness usually worsens over several weeks to months. It is more common in women. Most patients improve with immunotherapies, but they require lifelong treatment.

Option D: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease characterized by multiple episodes of neurological deficits due to patchy white matter lesions that involve various sites of the brain. It is caused by an autoimmune response directed against components of the myelin sheath. The demyelinated plaques are the hallmark of MS

Pearl PF1047: Mechanism of Immunopathogenesis of Guillain-Barre Syndrome

The following sequence of events, takes into consideration, the development of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) associated with Campylobacter jejuni infection.

* B cells recognize glycoconjugates on jejuni (Cj) that cross-react with ganglioside present on Schwann cell surface and subjacent peripheral nerve myelin.

* Most of the B cells are activated via a partially T cell–dependent route and secrete primarily IgG autoantibodies. Some B cells, activated via a T cell–independent mechanism, secrete primarily IgM

* The activated B cells escape from Peyer’s patches into regional lymph nodes.

* Activated T cells also function to assist in the opening of the blood-nerve barrier, facilitating penetration of pathogenic autoantibodies.

* The earliest changes in myelin consist of edema between myelin lamellae and vesicular disruption of the outermost myelin layers.

* These effects are associated with activation of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex and mediated by calcium entry; it is possible that the macrophage cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF) also participates in myelin damage.
questions.learning: Guillain-Barré syndrome — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the thickened nerve marked in the arrow in the image shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Great auricular nerve

The thickened nerve marked with the arrow in the above image is the great auricular nerve and the thickened nerve visible below the great auricular nerve is the transverse cervical nerve.

Nerve thickening in this case is likely to be due to leprosy.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of cervical plexus and arises from the second and the third cervical spinal nerves.

It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

• Anterior branch - supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.
• Posterior branch - supplies the skin over the mastoid process, posteroinferior part of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

• Leprosy - Nerve thickening is present. The nerve is palpable over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image)
• Frey's syndrome - An aberrant connection between the auriculotemporal nerve and great auricular nerve causes gustatory sweating.
questions.learning: Great auricular nerve — The thickened nerve marked with the arrow in the above image is the great auricular nerve and the thickened nerve visible below the great auricular nerve is the transverse cervical nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the definitive treatment of intractable vertigo due to Meniere’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Labyrinthectomy

The definitive treatment of intractable vertigo due to Ménière’s disease is labyrinthectomy.

Labyrinthectomy involves uniform destruction of hearing and vestibular function. Ideal candidates have no functional hearing and have failed more conservative treatments, such as gentamicin injection. Despite this morbidity, labyrinthectomy has the highest rate of vertigo control (>95%), more than vestibular neurectomy (78-90%), and is considered the single definitive treatment.

The step-by-step management approach for Ménière's disease consists of dietary modifications and vestibular suppressants as the initial measures, followed by intratympanic gentamicin ablation, and finally, surgical intervention.

Primarily, the management of Menier's disease involves a sodium restricted diet and diuretics like acetazolamide (Option A). They are more useful for short-term control.

Gentamicin (Option D) is a selective vestibulotoxic aminoglycoside antibiotic that is preferentially taken up by type I hair cells. It is opted for only if dietary modifications and vestibular suppressants have failed to control the symptoms. If used judiciously, hearing is preserved.

The options for surgical management include - Endolymphatic sac surgery, vestibular neurectomy, and labyrinthectomy. Endolymphatic sac surgery is currently declining in popularity due to lack of evidence of vertigo control.

Vestibular neurectomy (Option C) refers to selective ablation of the vestibular nerve. Even though it is considered a hearing sparing surgery and carries comparable rates of vertigo control as labyrinthectomy, it is an intradural procedure and carries a greater risk of complications. Hearing loss will still progress as it would have in the natural course of illness.
questions.learning: Labyrinthectomy — The definitive treatment of intractable vertigo due to Ménière’s disease is labyrinthectomy. Labyrinthectomy involves uniform destruction of hearing and vestibular function.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with chronic heart failure presents to the emergency department in shock, with hypotension and reduced urine output. The physician starts low-dose dopamine therapy. Based on the pharmacological effects of dopamine at low doses, which beneficial effect is most likely to be achieved in this patient?
questions.explanation: Dopamine has dose-dependent effects on various receptors. At "low doses" (typically <5 mcg/kg/min), it primarily stimulates dopaminergic ( and ) receptors, which causes vasodilation in the renal, mesenteric, and coronary vascular beds. This leads to an "increase in renal blood flow" and improved urine output, which is the intended benefit in a patient with heart failure and low perfusion. "Intermediate doses" (5–10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors to increase cardiac contractility (Option A). "High doses" (>10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors, leading to significant vasoconstriction (Option B) and potential tachycardia (Option C). While the concept of a specific "renal-dose" dopamine is debated in modern critical care, physiologically, the low-dose stimulation of dopaminergic receptors is responsible for the selective vasodilation of the renal arteries
questions.learning: Dopamine has dose-dependent effects on various receptors. At "low doses" (typically 10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors, leading to significant vasoconstriction (Option B) and potential tachycardia (Option C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with 6 kg weight loss over three months and difficulty swallowing. His history includes treatment for esophageal cancer one year ago. What is the most likely explanation for his current symptoms?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a prior history of esophageal cancer who presents with significant weight loss and new-onset dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) within a year of treatment, Esophageal cancer recurrence must be the first and most likely differential diagnosis. Malignant recurrence often presents with rapidly progressive dysphagia, initially for solids and then liquids, accompanied by systemic signs like cachexia. Fibrosis (Option B) can occur post-radiation but is less likely to cause a massive 6 kg weight loss in just three months. Achalasia cardia (Option C) typically presents in younger patients and is a motility disorder, not a late-onset sequel of cancer treatment. GERD (Option D) causes heartburn and regurgitation but is not a primary cause of profound weight loss and obstructive dysphagia. Management requires an urgent Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (UGIE) with biopsies and a CT or PET scan for restaging. Unfortunately, the prognosis for recurrent esophageal malignancy is generally poor, and management often shifts toward palliative care interventions
questions.learning: In a patient with a prior history of esophageal cancer who presents with significant weight loss and new-onset dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) within a year of treatment, Esophageal cancer recurrence must be the first and most likely differential diagnosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The numerator of perinatal mortality rate includes ___________
options: Early neonatal death of fetus > 1000 g
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Early neonatal death of fetus > 1000 g

Early neonatal death of fetus > 1000 g is included in the numerator of perinatal mortality rate .

Perinatal mortality rate is described as late foetal and early neonatal deaths weighing over 1000 grams at birth expressed as a ratio per 1000 live births weighing over 1000 gram at birth.
questions.learning: Early neonatal death of fetus > 1000 g Early neonatal death of fetus > 1000 g is included in the numerator of perinatal mortality rate . Perinatal mortality rate is described as late foetal and early neonatal deaths weighing over 1000 grams at birth…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following are seen in iron deficiency anemia?

1. Reduced serum iron level
2. Reduced transferrin saturation
3. Increased total iron binding capacity
4. Reduced ferritin level
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 4

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by reduced serum iron level, reduced transferrin saturation, increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and reduced ferritin level.

Serum iron level represents the amount of circulating iron bound to transferrin. When the iron stores become depleted in IDA, the serum iron level begins to fall.

TIBC is an indirect measure of the circulating levels of the iron-transporting protein, transferrin. IDA is characterized by more free transferrin (not bound to iron) available in circulation. This increases the TIBC. Transferrin saturation is calculated as: (serum iron ÷ TIBC) x 100. Normal transferrin saturation is 25-50%. Iron deficiency states show low transferrin saturation. A transferrin saturation >50% indicates a large amount of iron being delivered to the tissues, and can cause tissue iron overload. This is seen in hemochromatosis.

Serum ferritin is the most useful laboratory test to assess the levels of iron stores in the body. As iron stores are depleted, serum ferritin levels fall. Levels <15 μg/L are diagnostic of completely absent iron stores.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by reduced serum iron level, reduced transferrin saturation, increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and reduced ferritin level.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with headache and thick nasal discharge. On examination, the inferior turbinate appears hypertrophied with a characteristic mulberry-like appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic Hypertrophic rhinitis is a condition of permanent, irreversible thickening of the nasal mucosa, most commonly involving the inferior turbinates. On physical examination, the posterior end of the inferior turbinate characteristically exhibits a "mulberry appearance"—pitted and irregular due to chronic edema and fibrosis. This leads to persistent nasal obstruction, headache, and thick discharge. Atrophic rhinitis (Option A) involves the thinning of the mucosa and a spacious cavity with foul-smelling crusts. The common cold (Option B) is an acute viral infection. A nasal polyp (Option D) is a smooth, greyish-white, insensitive mass that arises from the ethmoid sinuses, not a primary hypertrophy of the turbinate itself. Management of hypertrophic rhinitis initially involves nasal steroid sprays, but definitive treatment often requires surgical reduction of the turbinate tissue (e.g., partial turbinectomy or radiofrequency ablation). Identifying the "mulberry" turbinate is a classic clinical task for diagnosing the end-stage results of chronic rhinitis or allergic rhinosinusitis
questions.learning: Chronic Hypertrophic rhinitis is a condition of permanent, irreversible thickening of the nasal mucosa, most commonly involving the inferior turbinates.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which condition is the reservoir sign seen along with mastoid tenderness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute mastoiditis

Reservoir sign along with the tenderness of the mastoid is seen in acute mastoiditis.

Reservoir sign is seen in acute mastoiditis/coalescent Mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.

Mastoiditis is a complication of otitis media.

Other signs of acute mastoiditis:

The light-house effect is seen is acute mastoiditis. It is described as a pulsatile mucopurulent or purulent discharge, coming through a central pin-hole perforation of pars tensa. It suggests a reservoir of infection in the mastoid and middle ear.

Note: In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose is also called reservoir sign.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following clinical features: 1. Raised ICP 2. Seizures 3. Focal deficit 4. Headache Which of the above clinical features are related to most brain tumours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Why is A correct?

• 1. Raised ICP ✓

• Brain tumors increase intracranial pressure by mass effect, cerebral edema, or obstruction of CSF pathways, leading to headache, vomiting, papilledema, and altered consciousness.

• 2. Seizures ✓

• Seizures are a common presenting feature, especially in supratentorial tumors, due to cortical irritation.

• 3. Focal deficit ✓

• Depending on the tumor location, patients may develop hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field defects, cranial nerve palsies, or cerebellar signs.

• 4. Headache ✓

• Headache is one of the most frequent symptoms, typically worse in the early morning or aggravated by coughing, sneezing, or straining due to raised ICP.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A one-and-half-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. On examination, respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
No need of treatment only home remedies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

From the given clinical scenario, it can be easily inferred that the child has pneumonia. The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.
questions.learning: Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home From the given clinical scenario, it can be easily inferred that the child has pneumonia. The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Many GPCR receptors act via an increase in cAMP. The steps involved in this mechanism are given below. Which of the following is the correct sequence of events in the cAMP signal transduction pathway? 1. Activation of adenylate cyclase 2. Activation of PKA 3. Conversion of ATP to cAMP 4. Phosphorylation of target proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 2 and 4

Correct answer is B because GPCR activation first stimulates adenylate cyclase (1), which converts ATP to cAMP (3).

cAMP then activates protein kinase A (PKA) (2).

Activated PKA phosphorylates downstream target proteins (4), producing the cellular response.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 2 and 4 Correct answer is B because GPCR activation first stimulates adenylate cyclase (1), which converts ATP to cAMP (3). cAMP then activates protein kinase A (PKA) (2).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine pediatric examination, a 4-year-old child is incidentally found to have a painless abdominal lump. Further assessment reveals a large, mobile mass confined to one side of the abdomen that does not cross the midline. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the core pediatric oncology pattern from Q.233. In a 4-year-old child, a large, painless, smooth abdominal mass that does not cross the midline is the classic clinical description of a Wilms tumor. Wilms tumor typically remains confined to the renal fossa of one side. In contrast, Neuroblastoma (Option A) often presents in younger children with a mass that is "knobby" and characteristically crosses the midline because it arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain. Angiomyolipoma (Option B) is rare and often associated with tuberous sclerosis. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) is extremely uncommon in this age group. Pediatricians must handle abdominal masses very gently during palpation to avoid the rare but possible risk of rupturing the tumor capsule, which could seed the peritoneum. Wilms tumor has a very good prognosis with modern multi-modal treatment consisting of nephrectomy and chemotherapy
questions.learning: This question reinforces the core pediatric oncology pattern from Q.233. In a 4-year-old child, a large, painless, smooth abdominal mass that does not cross the midline is the classic clinical description of a Wilms tumor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use and smoking presents with repeated episodes of vomiting and sudden, sharp epigastric pain. The symptoms began shortly after heavy alcohol intake. He is now febrile and tachycardic. Bedside imaging reveals the presence of free air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with recurrent vomiting and sudden sharp epigastric pain, along with a history of chronic alcohol consumption and smoking, which are strong risk factors for peptic ulcer disease (PUD). The X-ray shows a key diagnostic feature: free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). This indicates perforation of a hollow viscus, most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer. When an ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the stomach or duodenal wall, air escapes into the peritoneal cavity, producing this classic radiological sign. Clinically, perforation presents with: 1. Sudden severe epigastric pain (“stabbing”) 2. Vomiting 3. Signs of peritonitis (guarding, rigidity) 4. Possible fever and tachycardia Why other options are incorrect: 1. Tension pneumothorax → Chest findings, not abdominal free air 2. Boerhaave syndrome → Esophageal rupture, shows mediastinal air 3. Mallory-Weiss tear → Causes bleeding, not perforation
questions.learning: The patient presents with recurrent vomiting and sudden sharp epigastric pain, along with a history of chronic alcohol consumption and smoking, which are strong risk factors for peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 75 year old woman with complaints of mass per vaginum, as shown in the below image was posted for operative repair. During the pre-anaesthetic check-up, she was found to be unfit for major surgery. Which of the following procedures is recommended for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Le Fort’s repair

The given scenario and the image is suggestive of severe uterine prolapse in elderly women. Le Fort’s repair is recommended in this case.

This repair is done in patients who satisfy the following criteria:

* Very elderly menopausal patient with an advanced prolapse

* Do not wish to retain sexual function

* Medically unfit for major surgeries

This procedure can be performed under sedation and local anesthesia, or epidural anesthesia. The vaginal flaps from the anterior and posterior vaginal walls are excised, the raw areas are apposed in the midline with catgut sutures. This prevents the uterus from prolapsing.

This operation limits marital functions; hence, it should not be advised in women who wish to retain sexual function.

Other options

Abdominal sling operations are designed for women with type II or III degree prolapse and who are desirous of retaining childbearing function and menstrual function.

Sling operations are best suited to nulliparous prolapse. It includes,

* Abdominal wall cervicopexy (Option A)

* Shirodkar’s abdominal sling operation (Option B)

* Khanna’s abdominal sling operation (Option D)

Pearl PF2112: Management of Uterine prolapse

Category
Treatment

Nulliparous or congenital prolapse

Abdominal sling operations:

• Abdominal wall cervicopexy
• Shirodkar’s abdominal sling operation
• Khanna’s abdominal sling operation

Pregnancy and postnatal period

• Ring pessary (up to 16 weeks period of gestation)
• Pelvic floor exercises

<40 years

• Fothergill's repair (Manchester operation)
• Shirodkar's procedure

>40 years - with completed family
Vaginal hysterectomy and pelvic floor repair

>60 years - unfit for surgery

• Le Fort's repair
• Colpocleisis

These are done if the patient doesn't want to retain sexual function
questions.learning: Le Fort’s repair — The given scenario and the image is suggestive of severe uterine prolapse in elderly women. Le Fort’s repair is recommended in this case.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following receptors is used by the HIV virus to enter host cells?
questions.explanation: The entry of the HIV virus into host cells is a multi-step process involving specific surface receptors. The primary receptor for HIV-1 is the CD4 molecule, found on T-helper cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells. However, entry also requires the binding of a co-receptor. CCR5 (Option B) is the most critical co-receptor for the initial infection and is utilized by R5-tropic strains of the virus. Another common co-receptor is CXCR4, used by X4-tropic strains in later stages of the disease. CD8 (Option D) is a marker for cytotoxic T-cells, which are not the primary targets for HIV entry. CD6 and CCR7 (Options A and C) are involved in other immune functions like cell adhesion or lymph node homing but are not the primary entry co-receptors for HIV. Mutations in the CCR5 gene (such as the CCR5-delta 32 mutation) provide resistance to HIV infection, highlighting its essential role in viral entry
questions.learning: The entry of the HIV virus into host cells is a multi-step process involving specific surface receptors. The primary receptor for HIV-1 is the CD4 molecule, found on T-helper cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with heartburn and chest pain described as a burning sensation, worsened after meals and when lying down, along with occasional regurgitation of acidic fluid into the throat. What is the most common condition causing these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of "burning" retrosternal pain, "heartburn," and "acidic regurgitation" that worsen after meals and with recumbency are pathognomonic for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD). The most prevalent underlying clinical condition or complication resulting from chronic acid reflux that actually causes this perceived pain and heartburn is esophagitis (Option D). Esophagitis is the inflammation of the esophageal lining due to gastric acid exposure. While myocardial infarction (Option C) is a critical life-threatening differential for chest pain, it would not typically be triggered by lying down after a meal. Pneumonia (Option B) involves fever and productive cough. Barrett's esophagus (Option A) is a premalignant metaplastic change resulting from chronic reflux, but the acute burning sensation itself is directly caused by the inflammatory state of esophagitis. Therefore, esophagitis is the definitive condition responsible for the patient's acute symptoms. Treatment involves lifestyle changes and proton pump inhibitors
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of "burning" retrosternal pain, "heartburn," and "acidic regurgitation" that worsen after meals and with recumbency are pathognomonic for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the true nature of health propaganda?
options: It aids in developing a reflective behavior
questions.explanation: Health communication can be classified into health education and health propaganda. Health propaganda is characteristically defined by the fact that it appeals to emotions rather than logic or reason to achieve rapid behavioral change. It is often a one-way communication ("top-down") that provides pre-packaged "truths" to the public. In contrast, health education is actively acquired (Option A) by the learner, it is behavior-centered (Option C), and it aids in developing a reflective behavior (Option D) where individuals make informed choices based on scientific understanding. Propaganda aims for immediate obedience (e.g., "Don't spit") without necessarily explaining the underlying biological reasons. While propaganda can be useful for mass communication during emergencies (like "Wear a mask" during a pandemic), it is generally less sustainable than education for long-term health behavior modification. Understanding this distinction is vital for public health workers to choose the right communication strategy to empower communities and ensure lasting improvements in health outcomes
questions.learning: Health communication can be classified into health education and health propaganda. Health propaganda is characteristically defined by the fact that it appeals to emotions rather than logic or reason to achieve rapid behavioral change.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with cough and weight loss. Chest X-ray reveals a lung mass, and biopsy demonstrates chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity. Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SIADH

Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity indicate a neuroendocrine tumor, most commonly small cell carcinoma of the lung in chronic smokers.

Small cell carcinoma classically causes SIADH due to ectopic ADH secretion.

Hypercalcemia is linked to squamous cell carcinoma, gynecomastia to β-hCG–secreting tumors, and clubbing is a nonspecific finding.

| Option | Associated Condition | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | -------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Hypercalcemia | Squamous cell carcinoma | PTHrP secretion | ❌ Not neuroendocrine tumor | Squamous hallmark

| B. SIADH ✅ | Small cell carcinoma | ✔ ADH secretion | ✔ Correct | Most common SCLC syndrome

| C. Gynecomastia | hCG-producing tumors | Germ cell tumors | ❌ Not lung NE tumor | Seen in testicular cancer

| D. Clubbing | Chronic lung disease | ILD, lung cancer | ❌ Not specific paraneoplastic | Non-specific finding

| Cancer Type | Syndrome

| ----------- | --------

| Small cell carcinoma | SIADH, Cushing (ACTH)

| Squamous cell carcinoma | Hypercalcemia (PTHrP)

| Adenocarcinoma | Clubbing (rarely)

| Large cell | Variable
questions.learning: SIADH Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity indicate a neuroendocrine tumor, most commonly small cell carcinoma of the lung in chronic smokers. Small cell carcinoma classically causes SIADH due to ectopic ADH secretion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child is noted to have micrognathia and low- set ears on clinical examination. These features are most commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
questions.explanation: Chromosomal deletion is the most common genetic abnormality associated with micrognathia (small jaw) and low-set ears. These features are classic hallmarks of several deletion syndromes, such as Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) and DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion). Translocations (Option B) typically involve the fusion of different chromosomes and are more commonly associated with specific cancers, like CML, rather than these distinct congenital dysmorphisms. Amplification (Option C) refers to an increase in gene copy numbers and is primarily linked to oncogenesis (e.g., N-MYC in neuroblastoma) rather than structural anomalies. Inversions (Option D) involve the reversal of a chromosome segment and rarely lead to major structural congenital defects unless a critical gene is directly disrupted. Therefore, given the specific presentation of facial hypoplasia and low-set ears, a chromosomal microdeletion is the most probable underlying genetic mechanism
questions.learning: Chromosomal deletion is the most common genetic abnormality associated with micrognathia (small jaw) and low-set ears. These features are classic hallmarks of several deletion syndromes, such as Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) and DiGeorge syndrome…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines are given through the intramuscular route? 1. BCG vaccine 2. Hepatitis B vaccine 3. Pentavalent vaccine 4. Inactivated Polio vaccine Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3 and 4

The following vaccines are administered by the intramuscular (IM) route:

• Hepatitis B vaccine ✔️
• Pentavalent vaccine (DPT-HepB-Hib) ✔️
• Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) ✔️ (full-dose IPV)

• 1. BCG vaccine❌: Given intradermally.
• 2. Hepatitis B vaccine✔️: Given intramuscularly.
• 3. Pentavalent vaccine✔️: Given intramuscularly.
• 4. Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)✔️: Given intramuscularly (fractional IPV is given intradermally).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man developed abdominal pain for which he was being evaluated. You notice the following in his CECT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horse shoe kidney

The given image shows a horseshoe kidney. It is prone to obstruction, reflux, and stone formation (the likely cause of pain in this case)

Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital anomaly of the kidneys with male preponderance

Horseshoe kidney is caused due to the fusion of the lower poles of the kidney. The lower border of the kidneys usually lies in front of the L3 vertebra due to the arrest of ascent.

The common associations of horseshoe kidney are:

* Vesicoureteral Reflux

* Wilms Tumor

* Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

* Turner’s Syndrome

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correctly matched?

1. Pre-contemplation phase - A person is thinking about commencing morning walks due to their increased health benefits.

2. Contemplation phase - A smoker is considering giving up his habit of smoking.

3. Maintenance phase - A person who quit smoking one year back and has abstained from smoking ever since

4. Action -  A person who is overweight says he can't do anything as his entire family is overweight
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Statement 2,3

True statements are:

• Contemplation phase - A smoker is considering giving up his habit of smoking. (Recognizes his problem and thinks about to bring about a change)
• Maintenance phase - A person who quit smoking one year back and has abstained from smoking ever since. (He has sustained his abstinence from smoking)

Motivation enhancement therapy (MET) is a systematic intervention approach for bringing about change in the addictive behaviour seen in people with substance use disorders. It is based on the principle of motivational psychology and aims to enable the patient to deal with his addiction by producing internally motivated change.

Addictive behaviors do not change abruptly, and go through gradual stages. The stages of motivation enhancement therapy (MET) include:

Precontemplation - individuals in this stage are often unaware that their behaviour (eg. alcohol abuse) is problematic or is producing negative consequences.

Contemplation - individuals in this stage recognize their problems and begin to think about changing their behaviour. They weigh the pros and cons of change. They may still feel ambivalent about changing their behaviour.

Preparation or determination - individuals in this stage make decisions to change their habits and are ready to take action. They start to take small steps toward behaviour change.

Action - individuals in this stage change their behaviour and intend to keep moving forward with this change in behaviour

Maintenance - individuals in this stage sustain their change in behaviour for a while and intend to maintain this change going forward. People work to prevent relapse to earlier stages.

Other statements:

Statement 1: This statement is false as people in the pre-contemplation stage are unaware that their behaviour is problematic.

Statement 4: This statement is also false as people in the action stage make strides to change their behaviour.
questions.learning: Statement 2,3 True statements are: • Contemplation phase - A smoker is considering giving up his habit of smoking. (Recognizes his problem and thinks about to bring about a change) • Maintenance phase - A person who quit smoking one year back and has…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to the casualty after a road traffic accident (RTA) with chest trauma. He is conscious and speaks single words. He has a respiratory rate of 44 cycles per min and a BP of 90/40 mmHg. There is a hyper-resonance on percussing the right side of his chest. What will be your next, immediate step?
options: Insert needle in appropriate intercostal space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Insert needle in appropriate intercostal space

The given clinical scenario of chest trauma with a hyper resonant note on the right side suggests pneumothorax. Hemodynamic instability in this patient suggests tension pneumothorax and this is managed by immediate decompression by insertion of a needle in the appropriate place.

Pneumothorax refers to the presence of excess air in the pleural space. Entrapment of air occurs by:

1. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax - Due to the spontaneous rupture of apical pleural blebs or cystic spaces immediately below the visceral pleura.
2. Secondary pneumothorax - Due to the rupture of dilated cystic spaces in lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
3. Tension pneumothorax - Due to a one-way valve mechanism that directs airflow into the pleural space leading to a higher than atmospheric pressure environment. This leads to the affected lung being unable to expand appropriately and leads to hemodynamic instability.

Tension pneumothorax is a surgical emergency and the excessive pressure has to be immediately relieved. A chest X-ray is not required before emergency decompression as it is a clinical diagnosis, but an X-ray should be done following chest tube insertion (option D). Tension pneumothorax is managed by immediate needle decompression in the 5th ICS (adults), followed by definitive management with a chest tube inserted in the same space.

Other options:

Option A: Intubation is performed when the patient is unresponsive post chest tube insertion.

Option C: While IV fluids are a part of the resuscitation protocol, the management of tension pneumothorax takes higher precedence as the next immediate step.

Note: According to ATLS 10th edition

• In adults, needle thoracostomy or needle decompression location is changed to the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line from the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.
• In the pediatric age group, the needle thoracostomy location remains at the 2nd ICS midclavicular line.
questions.learning: Insert needle in appropriate intercostal space — The given clinical scenario of chest trauma with a hyper resonant note on the right side suggests pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complications after undergoing an illegal attempt to terminate her pregnancy. Which of the following methods used for inducing abortion is considered abnormal and unlawful?
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act in India, abortion must be performed by a registered medical practitioner using approved medical or surgical methods. Standard, legal methods include pharmacological agents like Mifepristone (Option B) and surgical procedures such as vacuum aspiration (Option D) or dilatation and curettage (Option A). An abortion stick (Option C) is a traditional, highly dangerous, and unlawful method used by unauthorized persons ("quacks"). It involves inserting a wooden or bamboo stick coated with an irritant paste (like marking nut or arsenic) into the cervix to induce uterine contractions or local necrosis. This method is "abnormal" as it carries an extreme risk of sepsis, uterine perforation, and death. Therefore, because it is an improvised, non-medical device specifically associated with criminal abortion, the abortion stick is the correct answer
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act in India, abortion must be performed by a registered medical practitioner using approved medical or surgical methods.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In patients with diabetes mellitus, cataract formation occurs mainly due to the accumulation of which substance within the lens?
questions.explanation: In patients with diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia activates the polyol pathway, where glucose is converted into sorbitol by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is only slowly metabolized into fructose, leading to its accumulation within the lens. Because sorbitol is osmotically active, its presence causes a significant influx of water, resulting in lens swelling and osmotic stress. This process, along with subsequent oxidative damage to lens proteins, leads to the formation of "snowflake cataracts" in younger diabetics or accelerated senile cataracts in older patients. Dulcitol and Galactitol (Options B and D) are identical substances that accumulate in cases of galactosemia, not diabetes. Mannitol (Option C) is an exogenous osmotic diuretic that does not accumulate in the lens. Therefore, sorbitol accumulation is the direct biochemical cause of lens opacification in the setting of elevated blood glucose levels
questions.learning: In patients with diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia activates the polyol pathway, where glucose is converted into sorbitol by the enzyme aldose reductase.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a population of 10,000, what is the minimum land area needed to implement the trench method of controlled waste tipping effectively?
questions.explanation: The trench method of controlled tipping (a type of sanitary landfill) is commonly used for solid waste disposal in small towns or rural areas. In this method, trenches are dug, waste is deposited, compacted, and then covered with soil daily. For planning purposes in community medicine/public health, standard guidelines suggest that for a population of 10,000, a minimum of about 5 acres of land is required to ensure proper functioning of the trench method over a reasonable period. This land requirement considers: 1. 1. Daily waste generation 2. 2. Space for trench digging and covering 3. 3. Future expansion and rotation of trenches 4. 4. Safe distance from habitation and water sources Why other options are incorrect: (A) 4 acres: Slightly inadequate for long-term use (C) 2 acres: Too small → leads to overcrowding and improper disposal (D) 1 acre: Grossly insufficient
questions.learning: The trench method of controlled tipping (a type of sanitary landfill) is commonly used for solid waste disposal in small towns or rural areas. In this method, trenches are dug, waste is deposited, compacted, and then covered with soil daily.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 67-year-old female is brought to the OPD in a poor general condition. On examination, she was found to have a right ovarian mass. Her CT scan indicated peritoneal caking. Her CA-125 levels were 1200 IU/L. What would be the management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chemotherapy followed by debulking surgery

In the given scenario, the patient presents with poor general condition and the presence of peritoneal metastases is suggestive of Stage III ovarian cancer. The preferred management would be to initiate neoadjuvant chemotherapy with three cycles of paclitaxel + carboplatin over three weeks, followed by debulking/cytoreductive surgery, and then continue another three cycles of chemotherapy.

Epithelial ovarian cancers are treated with a multimodality approach. The usual approach in Stage I and II disease where the patient is fit for surgery, is to perform cytoreductive surgery, which also helps in determining the extent of disease, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy (Option A). However, patients with advanced disease and poor general condition are unfit for anaesthesia and surgery at the time of presentation and have a higher operative risk, hence neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to surgery is preferred and has been shown to reduce morbidity in such patients.

Other options:

Option C: Ovarian tumors are not radiosensitive and radiotherapy does not form part of the protocol for treatment of ovarian cancers.

Option D: Staging laparotomy is the term used to describe the procedure of surgically exploring patients with early-stage disease and would not be the approach in a patient with advanced disease in whom chemotherapy followed by debulking surgery is indicated.
questions.learning: Chemotherapy followed by debulking surgery — In the given scenario, the patient presents with poor general condition and the presence of peritoneal metastases is suggestive of Stage III ovarian cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male on digital rectal examination was found to have a rectal mass raising the suspicion of rectal carcinoma. His bowel habits are normal and he visited the outpatient department for a routine check-up. Which of the following should be recommended as the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Full Colonoscopy and biopsy

As the patient is elderly with a rectal mass, presenting to an outpatient department, colorectal carcinoma has to be ruled out and the investigation of choice is a colonoscopy along with a biopsy.

A colonoscopy can be used to view 100–160 cm from the anal verge while a sigmoidoscopy can only see up to 60 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy rules out any associated proximal lesions as well.

Moreover, a rigid sigmoidoscopy procedure requires the rectum to be empty and thus a barium enema has to be given prior to the procedure.

Colonoscopy can also be therapeutic in the case of proximal adenomas which are snared via the colonoscope. In case of sensing cancer, a CT colonography or barium enema can be used.

The other investigations used in rectal cancer include:

* Digital rectal examination - for assessing the depth of penetration

* Endorectal ultrasound or MRI - provides an accurate assessment of the extent of invasion of the bowel wall

* MRI with an endorectal coil - is the investigation of choice to assess the 'T' and 'N' stages

* CECT - for evaluation of metastasis.

Screening for colorectal malignancy:

* Start screening at 50 years of age in an average risk patient

* Yearly stool occult blood testing

* Colonoscopy every 10 year

* Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 year
questions.learning: Full Colonoscopy and biopsy As the patient is elderly with a rectal mass, presenting to an outpatient department, colorectal carcinoma has to be ruled out and the investigation of choice is a colonoscopy along with a biopsy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient with h/o chicken pox comes to the clinic with the findings shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Herpes Zoster Ophtalmicus

The given image along with the past history of chicken pox is suggestive of a case of herpes zoster ophtalmicus which involves the face and the eyes.

Herpes zoster Opthlamicus:

It is the term used for shingles  involving the dermatome supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

Pathogenesis: Varicella zoster causes both chicken pox and shingles. Usually after chicken pox, the organism travels in a retrograde fashion to the dorsal root and cranial sensory nerve ganglia and remains dormant until it is activated again. During this time, it travels in an antegrade fashion to the skin and eyes to cause the typical manifestations

Mechanisms of ocular involvement:

* Direct viral inflammation leads to conjunctivitis and epithelial keratitis.

* Secondary and occlusive vasculitis may cause uveitis, keratitis, epicleritis and scleritis. Optic neuritis and cranial nerve palsies may also be seen.

* Cicatrizing processes may occur following severe eyelid, particular skin and conjunctival involvement. Reactivation causes necrosis and inflammation the sensory ganglia causes corneal anaesthesia and neurotrophic keratopathy.

The spread is airborne and through fomites and the lesions cease to be infectious when they crust.

Age and immunocompromised status are the two most important predisposing factors for this condition because of the diminishing T-cell immunity.

Ocular manifestations:

Hutchinson’s rule is related to herpes zoster ophthalmicus. It states that if the tip of the nose is involved, there will be a significant risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the involvement of the nasociliary nerve.

Corneal lesions in herpes zoster ophthalmicus: zoster keratitis

Epithelium

* Superficial punctate keratitis

* Pseudo-dendritic/micro-dendritic ulcer

Stroma:

* Nummular keratitis

* Disciform keratitis (Associated with endothelitis)

Other ocular lesions in herpes zoster:

Uveitis

Episcleritis and scleritis

* Conjunctivitis

* Acute retinal necrosis

* Secondary glaucoma

* Anterior segment necrosis and phthisis bulbi
questions.learning: Herpes Zoster Ophtalmicus — The given image along with the past history of chicken pox is suggestive of a case of herpes zoster ophtalmicus which involves the face and the eyes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Van Nuys grading system for ductal carcinoma in situ does not include:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hormone receptor staining

Staining for estrogen and progesterone receptors is not part of the Van Nuys system used for grading DCIS.

The components of the Van Nuys prognostic index (VNPI) are as follows:

• Size of the tumor
• Extent of resection margin
• Histological variant of DCIS - based on nuclear grade, presence of necrosis, presence of microcalcification
• Age of the patient

Patients with a high score in this grading system benefit from radiotherapy after excision, whereas those with low-grade and completely excised tumors, need no further treatment.

A score ranging from 1 (lesions with the best prognosis) to 3 (lesions with the worst prognosis) is given for each of the four prognostic predictors. Total scores range from 4 (least likely to recur) to 12 (most likely to recur).

• Scores 4-7 with >3mm margin: Excision alone
• Score 7 with < 3 mm margin, score 8 with > 3mm margin, score 9 with >5mm margin: Excision with RT
• Score 9 with < 5mm margin & score 10,11,12: Mastectomy

Note: The type of microcalcification seen on imaging, helps in determining the nuclear grade of DCIS. While the linear branching type of microcalcification is associated with high nuclear grade, fine granular type is associated with low nuclear grade.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with right-sided visual field defects in both eyes while central vision remains unaffected. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Visual field defect involving the right sides of each eye with central vision preserved is called bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. It occurs in lesions of the occipital lobe.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries.

HH may be either complete or incomplete.

* A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes.

* An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively.

Other Options:

Option A: Optic Chiasm Lesion: Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma.

Option B: Optic Tract Lesion : Lesions at the occipital lobe, optic tract and optic radiation would all cause homonymous hemianopia, but macular sparing will occur in the setting of optic lobe damage.

Option C: Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia.

Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.
questions.learning: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing Visual field defect involving the right sides of each eye with central vision preserved is called bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought by a lady police sub-inspector with an alleged history of sexual violence 2 days back. She was accompanied by her mother. The registered medical practitioner should do which of the following as the next step?
options: Documentation of injuries and examination findings
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Take a detailed history

The registered medical practitioner should take a detailed history as the next step.

The registered medical practitioner must take a detailed history and then take informed consent for examination. In case of refusal, an informed refusal is to be documented after explaining to them the consequences of choice. As part of the examination, they should collect specimens, preserve clothing, and document injuries and examination findings. Medical treatment and testing for pregnancy have to be done for all victims of sexual assault free of cost and police should be informed as per section 357-C of CrPc.

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 considers all individuals (both male and female) below the age of 18 years as children and protects them from sexual abuse. It defines various forms of sexual offenses which include:

• Sexual harassment: A person is said to commit sexual harassment upon a child when such person with sexual intent,

• Carries out any act with sexual connotations
• makes a child exhibit his/her body
• shows any object to a child in any form/media for pornographic purposes.

• Sexual assault

• Any act with sexual intent that involves physical contact without penetration.

• Aggravated sexual assault

• Similar to sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term "aggravated".

• Penetrative sexual assault

• An act with sexual intent that involves physical penetration.

• Aggravated penetrative sexual assault

• Similar to penetrative sexual assault along with the criteria explained under the term "aggravated".

• Pornography

The term aggravated is used for those assaults done:

• by a person in a position of trust or authority such as police officer, security forces, relative, doctor.
• in the course of communal violence.
• on mentally & physically disabled.
• gang sexual assault.
• using deadly weapons.
• causing grievous hurt

The Act prescribes stringent punishment graded as per the gravity of the offense, with a maximum term of rigorous imprisonment for life and fine. Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act, 2012 requires mandatory reporting of cases of child sexual abuse to law enforcement authorities and applies to everyone including parents, doctors, and school personnel. Failure to report a suspicion of child abuse is an offense under the Act.
questions.learning: Take a detailed history — The registered medical practitioner should take a detailed history as the next step. The registered medical practitioner must take a detailed history and then take informed consent for examination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Distension of the right atrium leads to an increase in heart rate due to activation of which reflex?
questions.explanation: The Bainbridge reflex, also called the atrial reflex, is an increase in heart rate due to an increase in central venous pressure. When the right atrium is distended by increased blood volume, stretch receptors in the atrial wall are activated, sending signals to the brainstem to increase sympathetic tone and heart rate. This reflex helps to move excess blood out of the venous system into the arterial system. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (Option A) causes bradycardia and hypotension in response to noxious stimuli in the ventricles. The Cushing reflex (Option C) is a triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations seen in increased intracranial pressure. The J reflex (Option D) or juxtacapillary reflex is triggered by pulmonary congestion, leading to apnea followed by rapid breathing. The Bainbridge reflex is physiological and works in opposition to the baroreceptor reflex to maintain circulatory balance

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of Valsalva maneuver is due to_________
options: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to left ventricular pressure
Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure

Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of the Valsalva maneuver is due to increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure.

Valsalva maneuver involves the performance of forced expiration against a closed glottis. It occurs during coughing, defecation, and heavy lifting. At the onset of straining, the blood pressure is raised because the increase in intrathoracic pressure is added to the pressure of the blood in the aorta. The pressure then falls as the high intrathoracic pressure compresses the veins and decreases the cardiac output.

When the glottis is opened and intrathoracic pressure returns to its normal state, cardiac output is regained, but there is constriction in the peripheral vessels. As a result, blood pressure elevates beyond the normal range, which triggers the baroreceptors, leading to bradycardia and a subsequent decrease in pressure back to normal levels.
questions.learning: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of the Valsalva maneuver is due to increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A psychiatrist prescribes lithium for a patient who is diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding lithium?
options: Lithium is teratogenic if given to pregnant females
Lithium toxicity is exacerbated with thiazide
Lithium can decrease thyroid hormone levels
Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose

Option D is the incorrect statement regarding lithium. Haemodialysis is used in lithium overdose.

Lithium is a small monovalent cation. It is used in the treatment of acute mania and the prevention of recurrences of bipolar disorder in adults or adolescents. Lithium is a mood stabiliser with suicide reduction in bipolar patients and is also efficacious in unipolar depressive patients who respond inadequately to antidepressant therapy.

Lithium toxicity occurs with the concomitant use of

* Thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone)—Diuretics cause Na⁺ loss, which promotes proximal tubular reabsorption of Na⁺ as well as Li⁺. Hence, plasma levels of lithium rise. (Option B)

* Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors

* Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

* Tetracyclines

* Loop diuretics (furosemide)

These act by increasing the tubular reabsorption of lithium, resulting in decreased excretion of lithium and thereby increasing the serum lithium levels, causing toxicity.

Adverse effects—Serum lithium levels greater than 1.5 mEq/L are considered toxic.

* Acute intoxication is characterised by vomiting, profuse diarrhea, coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, and convulsions.

* Central nervous system: Lithium at therapeutic levels causes fine tremors, and at toxic levels causes coarse tremors. Incoordination, ataxia, and slurred speech can occur at peak serum concentrations.

* With long-term use, some patients develop renal diabetes insipidus. Patients present with polyuria and polydipsia.

* Lithium therapy causes significant weight gain.

* Lithium therapy is associated with hypothyroidism. This is due to interference with the release of thyroid hormone, which leads to a fall in circulating T3 and T4 levels and a subsequent increase in TSH secretion from pituitary enlargement and stimulation of the thyroid. (Option C)

* Lithium is contraindicated in pregnancy. Early pregnancy causes Ebstein anomaly in the foetus. Foetal lithium exposure is associated with neonatal goitre, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur. (Option A)

Treatment of lithium overdose—There is no specific antidote. Osmotic diuretics and sodium bicarbonate infusion promote lithium excretion. Haemodialysis is indicated if serum levels are > 4 mEq/L.

Pearl PF0735: Lithium in bipolar disorder

Guidelines for Lithium therapy

Indications:

Mania, hypomania, bipolar disorder, etc.

Blood levels of lithium:

For therapeutic purpose (treatment of acute mania) : 0.8-1.2 mEq/L

For prophylaxis (to prevent relapse of bipolar disorder): 0.5-0.8 mEq/L

Toxic levels of lithium: >/= 1.5 mEq/L

Contraindications:

• CKD
• Heart disease
• Hyponatremia or diuretic use

Baseline studies:

• BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen), Creatinine, Calcium, Urine analysis
• Thyroid function test
• ECG in patients with coronary risk factors

Acute adverse effects:

• Tremor, ataxia, weakness
• Polyuria, polydipsia
• Vomiting, diarrhea
• Cognitive impairment

Chronic adverse effects:

• Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
• Thyroid dysfunction
• Hyperparathyroidism

Pearl PF0744: Teratogenic drugs and the birth defects
