questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the given structure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreatic islet cells

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas.

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

• Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:

• α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon
• β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin
• δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin
• PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.

• Minor cell types:

• D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.
• Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes.

The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node.

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles. Lymphocytes surrounding the arteriole are called peri-arterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) and contain T cells. Follicles in white pulp contain B cells.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids.

The image given below shows the histology of the spleen.
questions.learning: Pancreatic islet cells — The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which region of the brain regulates and coordinates the vomiting reflex?
questions.explanation: The vomiting reflex is a complex process coordinated by the vomiting center located in the medulla oblongata. A critical component of this system is the Area Postrema (Option C), situated on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The Area Postrema functions as the Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ); it lacks a functional blood-brain barrier, allowing it to detect circulating toxins, drugs, or metabolic waste products in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Once triggered, it sends signals to the vomiting center to initiate the emetic response. The apneustic and pneumotaxic centers (Options A and B) are located in the pons and regulate the rhythm of breathing. The hypothalamus (Option D) regulates temperature, hunger, and thirst but does not directly control the vomiting reflex. The Area Postrema is a primary target for antiemetic medications, making it a vital structure in clinical pharmacology and neurology
questions.learning: The vomiting reflex is a complex process coordinated by the vomiting center located in the medulla oblongata. A critical component of this system is the Area Postrema (Option C), situated on the floor of the fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following disorders are caused by enzymatic defects in the heme biosynthesis pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Porphyrias

Porphyrias are a group of inherited or acquired disorders caused by deficiency of enzymes involved in the heme biosynthesis pathway, leading to the accumulation of porphyrins or their precursors in tissues. Clinical manifestations depend on the site of accumulation and are characterized by neurovisceral symptoms, photosensitivity, or both.

• A. Porphyrias: Caused by enzyme defects in the heme synthesis pathway, resulting in accumulation of toxic heme precursors.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Myelodysplastic syndrome: A clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder causing ineffective hematopoiesis; unrelated to heme biosynthesis.
• C. Hemophilias: Inherited coagulation factor deficiencies (Factor VIII or IX), not disorders of heme synthesis.
• D. Plasma cell disorders: Disorders of monoclonal plasma cell proliferation (e.g., multiple myeloma), unrelated to the heme pathway.
questions.learning: Porphyrias Porphyrias are a group of inherited or acquired disorders caused by deficiency of enzymes involved in the heme biosynthesis pathway, leading to the accumulation of porphyrins or their precursors in tissues.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the diagnostic investigation shown below that is considered the preferred method for evaluating distal small bowel tumors.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enteroclysis

Enteroclysis, which is the investigation of choice in patients with small bowel tumors.

Enteroclysis is a barium study in which the contrast agent is put directly into the duodenum through a nasogastric tube.

Continued infusion of 500 to 1000 mL of thin barium sulfate and methylcellulose suspension is done and then viewed continuously with the use of either fluoroscopy or radiographs taken at frequent intervals. This technique is a double-contrast procedure that allows detailed imaging of the entire small intestine.

Enteroclysis has a sensitivity of over 90% in the detection of small bowel tumors and is the investigation of choice, particularly for tumors located in the distal small bowel.

Advantages of enteroclysis:

* The contrast is administered at a controlled rate directly in the small bowel, bypassing the regulatory action of the pylorus.

* The entire small bowel is demonstrated in a distended state, allowing better diagnosis. As a result of the dilatation, the following can be visualized:

* Mild strictures

* Small sinus tracts and fistulas

* Minimal extrinsic compressions

* Skip lesions

* Proximal and distal extent of diffuse diseases.

* The examination can be completed in 15–30 minutes, thus reducing patient waiting time.

Pearl PF1589: Barium Studies

Barium swallow: Used to assess the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.

The image below is a barium swallow showing eosinophilic esophagitis and associated stricture:

Barium meal: Used to assess stomach and duodenum.

Barium meal followthrough: Used to assess the small intestine

Barium enema: Used to assess the large intestine
questions.learning: Enteroclysis Enteroclysis, which is the investigation of choice in patients with small bowel tumors. Enteroclysis is a barium study in which the contrast agent is put directly into the duodenum through a nasogastric tube.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with diabetes mellitus presents with severe ear pain and persistent otorrhea that has not responded to antibiotic therapy. On examination, granulation tissue is seen in the external auditory canal, along with facial nerve paralysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa, also known as Necrotizing Otitis Externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external ear canal and skull base. It occurs almost exclusively in elderly diabetic or immuno compromised patients. The hallmark clinical features include excruciating ear pain (disproportionate to findings), persistent otorrhea, and the presence of granulation tissue at the junction of the cartilaginous and bony canal. The involvement of cranial nerves, most commonly the facial nerve (CN VII) resulting in paralysis, indicates advanced disease and osteomyelitis of the temporal bone. Otomycosis (Option A) involves fungal growth but is not necrotic. Serous otitis media (Option B) involves painless fluid behind the drum. Eczematous otitis externa (Option D) is an itchy, skin-surface inflammation without deep invasion. Therefore, the combination of diabetes, granulation tissue, and nerve paralysis makes Malignant Otitis Externa the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa, also known as Necrotizing Otitis Externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external ear canal and skull base. It occurs almost exclusively in elderly diabetic or immuno compromised patients.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A prospective cohort study evaluates the association between high dietary salt intake and hypertension. During follow-up, 25% of participants are lost, and most of those lost belong to the high-salt intake group. Which bias is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Selection bias

Differential loss to follow-up causes attrition (selection) bias, making the remaining sample unrepresentative.
questions.learning: Selection bias Differential loss to follow-up causes attrition (selection) bias, making the remaining sample unrepresentative.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During a field visit, an epidemiologist observes mosquito larvae resting parallel to the water surface, without a siphon tube, and having palmate hairs on their abdominal segments. Based on these characteristics, which mosquito species do these larvae most likely belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anopheles

Anopheles mosquito larvae characteristically rest parallel to the water surface due to the absence of a siphon tube.

They possess palmate hairs on abdominal segments, which help maintain this horizontal position.

In contrast, Aedes and Culex larvae have siphon tubes and hang at an angle, while Mansonia larvae attach to aquatic plants for respiration.
questions.learning: Anopheles Anopheles mosquito larvae characteristically rest parallel to the water surface due to the absence of a siphon tube. They possess palmate hairs on abdominal segments, which help maintain this horizontal position.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman comes with complaints of fatigue which worsens towards the end of the day. She also complains of double vision while watching television. The physician suspects a case of myasthenia gravis. Which of the following tests has the highest sensitivity in diagnosing this condition?
options: Acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase antibodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Single-fiber electromyography

Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) has the highest sensitivity in the clinical diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

During single-fibre electromyography, action potentials of two muscle fibres innervated by one motor axon are recorded, and the variability in the interval between them, called jitter, is increased in myasthenia gravis. It is the most sensitive test used for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder associated with a decrease in postsynaptic depolarization due to the blocking of acetylcholine receptors by autoantibodies. It is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can also be seen. When it becomes generalized, the proximal muscles of the limbs are affected first.

Despite the muscle weakness, the deep tendon reflexes remain normal. The snarling expression on smiling (facial weakness), nasal timbre of speech (weakness of palate and tongue), and difficulty swallowing may be seen. Bulbar weakness and respiratory depression are seen more frequently in MuSK antibody–positive myasthenia gravis. Treatment includes anticholinesterase drugs like pyridostigmine and immunosuppression.

Other options:

Option B: The acetylcholine receptor antibody (AChR-Ab) test should be done in all patients (most specific). If negative, test for MuSK antibodies.

Option C: Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) is considered abnormal if there is a decremental response of >10%.

Option D: CT scan of the chest is likely to show thymic hyperplasia and thymoma which are frequently associated in patients with myasthenia gravis.
questions.learning: Single-fiber electromyography Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) has the highest sensitivity in the clinical diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. During single-fibre electromyography, action potentials of two muscle fibres innervated by one motor axon are…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The image below depicts which of the following types of cell-to-cell signaling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paracrine

The given image shows the paracrine cell-to-cell signaling mechanism. In paracrine signaling, the signaling molecules released by a cell only affect target cells in close proximity to it.

An example of paracrine signaling is the release of endothelin-1, a potent vasoconstrictor released by the endothelial cells.

Synaptic signaling is a special case of paracrine signaling (for chemical synapses) between neurons and target cells.

Other options:

Option B: In the autocrine signaling mechanism, the cells respond to the signaling molecules that are released by themselves, which is the site of release and action within the same cell. Note that the signaling molecules are first secreted out of the cell and then act on the same cell through receptors. An example is the proliferation of activated T-cells by IL-2 released by the same cell after it interacts with antigen-presenting cells.

Option C: In endocrine signaling, a signaling molecule, a hormone (for example insulin, FSH, LH), is usually carried by the blood from its site of release to act on its target at a distance.

The below image shows the different types of extracellular cell-to-cell communication mechanisms.

Option D: Merocrine is a type of glandular secretion and not an extracellular signaling mechanism. In this, the secretions are poured out by exocytosis and the cell remains intact. An example of the merocrine gland is the goblet cell and eccrine sweat gland.

An illustration depicting this mechanism is given below.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Delayed hypersensitivity is due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Interferon gamma

Delayed hypersensitivity is due to interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma).

Delayed hypersensitivity is also called cell-mediated/type 4 hypersensitivity reaction. It is mediated by T cells and occurs by 2 mechanisms:

1. CD4+ T helper cells mediated
2. CD8+ T helper cells mediated

CD4+ T helper cells mediated pathway:

Antigen peptides recognized by CD4+ T cells secrete interluekin -2. Interleukin -2 helps in further proliferation of T cells that respond to the antigen peptide. These T cells differentiate into Th1 or Th17 cells as a result of the cytokines produced from the antigen presenting cells (APC).

APCs also secrete interleukin - 12 which enhances differentiation of the T cells to the Th1 subset. Inflammatory cytokines like interluekins -1, 6, 23 induce differentiation of T cells to the Th17 subset. These responses lead to the release of interferon gamma that alters the macrophages in several ways to ensure eliminating the antigen.

Interferon-gamma-induced changes in the macrophages:

1. Augmented ability of the macrophages to phagocytose and kill micro-organisms.
2. Increased expression of class 2 MHC molecules to enhance antigen presentation.
3. Increased secretion in presence of tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, and other inflammatory chemokines.
4. Amplification of the Th1 response by producing more interleukin-12.

CD8+ T helper cells mediated pathway:

CD8+ T cells destroy antigen-presenting target cells using perforins and granzymes. These mediators are preformed in the lysosomes of a cell. The perforin-granzyme complex enters the target cell by endocytosis. Granzymes cause the activation of caspases inducing apoptosis of the target cell. CD8+ T cells also produce interferon gamma following viral infections and contact allergens. Interferon-gamma then proceeds to stimulate the production of inflammatory mediators and bring about the hypersensitivity reaction.

Examples of delayed hypersensitivity reactions include the tuberculin reaction and contact dermatitis.

Interferon-gamma is an important effector involved in both immune mechanisms of delayed hypersensitivity reactions and hence is the best answer for this question.
questions.learning: Interferon gamma Delayed hypersensitivity is due to interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma). Delayed hypersensitivity is also called cell-mediated/type 4 hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma associated with it. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The most probable diagnosis is Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Adolescent male presenting with recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx points towards angiofibroma. The consistency of the tumor is firm but the digital palpation should never be done until at the time of operation, because of the risk of profuse bleeding.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head with contrast enhancement is now the investigation of choice. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus often called antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomonic of angiofibroma.

Surgical excision is the treatment of choice though radiotherapy and chemotherapy monotherapy or in combination have also been used.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common non-pancreatic site for tumour distribution in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duodenum

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma). The most common site overall is the duodenum, followed by the pancreas. Thus, the most common non-pancreatic site is the duodenum.

Why not the other options?

• B. Ovaries: Extremely rare site for gastrinoma.
• C. Stomach: Gastrinomas do not commonly arise in the stomach.
• D. Liver: The liver is the most common site of metastasis, not the primary tumor.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with a 0.3-cm nodule on the left nasolabial fold. It was excised and a pathological examination was done. The image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Basal cell carcinoma

The given clinical scenario of a nodule on the nasolabial fold and the histopathological image showing peripheral palisading is likely to be basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

Basal cell carcinoma is a slow-growing malignant tumor, with locally invasive characteristics. It affects the pilosebaceous skin.

Ultraviolet radiation exposure is the strongest predisposing factor. Other risk factors include exposure to arsenic, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and ionizing radiation.

It mainly affects the elderly or middle-aged men who are excessively exposed to sun, common in the age group 40-80 and white-skinned people.

Macroscopically, it is categorized as localized and generalized. Nodular, nodulocystic (nodular and nodulocystic together account for 90% of BCC), pigmented, and nevoid are the localized cancers while superficial multifocal and superficial spreading, infiltrative, and cicatrizing are the generalized types. Nodular type is described as pearly waxy nodules at the margins. A central depression with umbilication or ulceration and rolled-out edges are characteristic of BCC.

The below gross image shows pearly, rolled-out borders suggestive of basal cell carcinoma.

Histopathologic features show ovoid cells in nests with a single palisading layer. The outer layer of cells is in the active division and thus incomplete excision can lead to being more aggressive. The below image shows the histopathology of BCC.

Sites near the eye, nose, and ear and size >2 cm are considered to be high risk. Direct invasion at these sites can reach the cranium.

Management is by Moh's microscopic surgery. Non-surgical measures such as topical 5-fluorouracil, and imiquimod are useful. Metastasis is extremely rare.

Other options:

Option B: Melanoma is a malignancy, commonly seen in young adults, arising from melanocytes and involves the skin, mucosa, retina, and leptomeninges. Microscopically, malignant changes are seen in the basal epidermis with breach and invasion of the dermis as shown below.

Option C: Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common malignant tumor, seen more commonly in men. Microscopically, the proliferation of irregular masses of squamous epithelium is seen. The image is shown below.

Option D: Nevus are aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or dermo-epidermal junction. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.
questions.learning: Basal cell carcinoma — The given clinical scenario of a nodule on the nasolabial fold and the histopathological image showing peripheral palisading is likely to be basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: New A 33-year-old male comes with complaints of dry cough, fever, and shortness of breath for 2 days along with a loss of taste and smell. He is a social worker who has been traveling a lot. What would be the investigation of choice for this patient to confirm the diagnosis of COVID-19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

The patient with the above clinical scenario is most likely suffering from COVID-19. RT-PCR (reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction) is the investigation of choice to confirm an acute infection of COVID-19.

There are two major types of tests for COVID-19:

* Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs; eg, RT-PCR) –
RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 is the primary test used to diagnose active COVID-19. The test is typically performed on nasopharyngeal swabs, but can also be performed on other respiratory tract specimens (eg, oropharyngeal swabs, lower respiratory tract samples).

* Serology –
Serologic tests measure antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 and are primarily used to identify patients who have had COVID-19 in the past. While some serologic assays can help identify patients with acute infection, they are not as reliable as RT-PCR and not recommended for this purpose.

Basic protective measures against the new coronavirus: (SARS CoV 2)

* Wash your hands frequently for at least 20 seconds.

* Maintain social distancing- Maintain at least 1-meter distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing

* Avoid touching eyes, nose, and mouth

* Practice respiratory hygiene- cover your mouth and nose with your bent elbow or tissue when you cough or sneeze, then dispose of the used tissue immediately.

* If you have fever, cough, and difficulty breathing, seek medical care early

* Stay informed and follow the advice given by your healthcare provider

Treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment recommended for COVID-19. People with COVID-19 should receive supportive care to help relieve symptoms. For severe cases, treatment should include care to support vital organ functions.
questions.learning: RT-PCR — The patient with the above clinical scenario is most likely suffering from COVID-19. RT-PCR (reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction) is the investigation of choice to confirm an acute infection of COVID-19.

questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 46-year-old man presents with fatigue and arthralgia involving the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints. He is found to have mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests show: • Hemoglobin: normal • Serum ferritin: elevated • Transferrin saturation: 68% His younger brother is asymptomatic. The physician decides to evaluate the brother for the same condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test for screening the asymptomatic sibling?
options: Liver biopsy with Prussian blue staining
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transferrin saturation

This question tests the correct screening strategy for hereditary hemochromatosis, especially in asymptomatic first-degree relatives.

Earliest biochemical abnormality:

• ↑ Transferrin saturation (>45%)
• Occurs before ferritin rises

Best initial screening test:

• Transferrin saturation
• Preferred in:

• Asymptomatic individuals
• Family members of affected patients

• Ferritin is an acute phase reactant
• Can be elevated in:

• Infection
• Inflammation
• Liver disease

→ Less specific for early screening

Stepwise approach:

• Screen → Transferrin saturation
• Confirm → HFE gene mutation
• Assess severity → MRI / biopsy
questions.learning: Transferrin saturation — This question tests the correct screening strategy for hereditary hemochromatosis, especially in asymptomatic first-degree relatives.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An RTA patient has received 4 packed RBC within a few hours. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.explanation: Stored packed red blood cells (PRBCs) contain citrate as an anticoagulant. During rapid or massive blood transfusions, the large volume of citrate enters the recipient's bloodstream and binds to ionized calcium. This chelation leads to acute hypocalcemia. While the liver normally metabolizes citrate, this process is often impaired in trauma patients due to shock or hypothermia. Clinical manifestations include paresthesia, muscle cramps, and a prolonged QT interval. Hypernatremia (Option A) and hyponatremia (Option B) are not typical complications of PRBC transfusion as the sodium content in the preservative is minimal. While hyperkalemia (Option D) can occur due to potassium leakage from older stored cells, hypocalcemia resulting from citrate toxicity is a more classic and specifically tested metabolic complication of rapid PRBC administration. Therefore, monitoring ionized calcium levels is essential during emergency resuscitation involving multiple units of blood
questions.learning: Stored packed red blood cells (PRBCs) contain citrate as an anticoagulant. During rapid or massive blood transfusions, the large volume of citrate enters the recipient's bloodstream and binds to ionized calcium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A renal biopsy section is provided in the image. Identify the type of cells indicated by the marked area in this histological specimen.
questions.explanation: The marked cells in the renal biopsy are Lacis cells, also known as extraglomerular mesangial cells or Goormaghtigh cells. These cells are a critical component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and are located in the triangular space between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa. Their primary role is to facilitate signal transmission between the macula densa and the JG cells, thereby regulating renin secretion and blood pressure. Macula densa cells (Option A) are specialized tubular cells in the distal tubule that sense sodium concentration. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (Option B) are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that produce renin. Podocytes (Option D) are epithelial cells covering the glomerular capillaries, forming the filtration barrier. Given the specific anatomical location between the arterioles, the marked cells are Lacis cells

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Calabar swelling, which is a short-lived, inflammatory, oedematous swelling close to a limb joint, is characteristically seen in infection caused by which of the following nematodes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loa loa

Loiasis is a filarial infection caused by Loa loa, transmitted by the Chrysops (deer fly or mango fly). It is characterized by transient, localized, non-pitting subcutaneous edema (Calabar swellings), which result from a hypersensitivity reaction to migrating adult worms. Migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva (“African eye worm”) is a classic clinical feature.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Onchocerca volvulus: Causes river blindness, subcutaneous nodules, and dermatitis; transmitted by the blackfly (Simulium).
• B. Mansonella perstans: Usually causes mild or asymptomatic filariasis without characteristic Calabar swellings.
• D. Brugia malayi: Causes lymphatic filariasis with recurrent lymphangitis and lymphedema/elephantiasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a food adulteration disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorosis

Fluorosis is not classified as a disease caused by food adulteration.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India- Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Prakasam), Telangana(Nalgonda), Punjab, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

* Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L).

* Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L).

* Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L)

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

The given images show dental fluorosis and skeletal fluorosis (interosseous-membrane-calcification), respectively:

Other options:

Option A: Neurolathyrism is a neurological disorder caused by excessive consumption of Lathyrus sativus (grass pea), leading to spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. It results from the neurotoxin β-ODAP, primarily affecting populations dependent on the legume during famine.

Option B: Epidemic dropsy is a toxic disease caused by consuming adulterated mustard oil contaminated with Argemone mexicana seeds. It leads to symptoms like oedema, gastrointestinal issues, and cardiovascular complications.

Option D: Aflatoxicosis is a toxic condition caused by ingesting food contaminated with aflatoxins, which are produced by Aspergillus fungi in stored grains and nuts. It can lead to acute liver damage, jaundice, and an increased risk of liver cancer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with breast carcinoma develops right upper limb lymphedema after mastectomy as a result of axillary lymph node dissection. 10 years later, she presents with multiple confluent, hemorrhagic, necrotic, and elevated purple-black papules over the right upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lymphangiosarcoma

The most likely diagnosis in this setting is lymphangiosarcoma.

Angiosarcoma may develop in areas affected by lymphedema, classically in the ipsilateral upper extremity, several years after radical mastectomy with lymph node resection for breast cancer known as Stewart–Treves syndrome (STS). Lymphatic vessels are most likely the source of the tumour.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the first step in the management of an 18-month-old child with both eyes deviated medially:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Refractive error testing

In children, who present with a convergent squint, the first step is to check the visual acuity and estimate the error of refraction.

Convergent squint also known as Esotrpia is commonly seen in children with hyperopia (also known as hypermetropia) of which the accomdative type of esotropia is more common in the age group below 3 years.

The first line of management in the treatment of esotropia includes refractive error correction with glasses.

If a child with accomdative issues, is unable to use spectacles (such as a child ≤ 2 years) or is non compliant with wearing glasses we can eliminate accommodation by temporarily treating him with miotic drugs such as echothiophate.

Further treatment may include orthoptic training with specific exercises or surgical correction when the angle of squint is 10° or more with correcting lenses and when orthoptic training doesnt help in reasonable correction of the squint.

Mnemonic:

The algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

• R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics
• O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia
• O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component
• P: Prism correction: for remaining error

Classification of Accomdative esotropia:

Type
Criteria

Refractive

• Associated with high hypermetropia (+4 to +7 D)
• Typically esotropia is for both near and distance.
• Fully correctable by spectacles

Non-refractive

• Occurs independent of refractive errors
• Abnormal accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio
• Typically esotropia is greater for near than for distance
• Fully corrected by bifocal glasses

The below image shows accomdative esotropia before and after correction.

Option A: Forced Duction Test (FDT) is performed to differentiate between the paralytic and restrictive type of inconcomitant squint.

FDT is positive in restrictive squint where a resistance is encountered during passive rotation.
questions.learning: Refractive error testing — In children, who present with a convergent squint, the first step is to check the visual acuity and estimate the error of refraction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following radiological image was taken to access the urinary tract, identify the investigation shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)

The radiological image shown above is that of an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), also known as Intravenous Urography (IVU).

IVP is an X-ray with special contrast injected into the veins to visualize the kidneys, ureter, and bladder.

Normal Structure seen in IVP:

Renal arteries → Nephrogram (cortex > medulla) → Calyces (~1 min) → Pelvicalyceal system (~15 min with compression) → Ureters → Postmicturition KUB shows normal drainage.

Indications of IVP:

* Calculi: size, location

* Obstruction: level, effects on renal excretion

* Functional versus mechanical obstruction (post-diuretic IVU)

* Ureteric fistula or Ureteric stricture

* GU Tuberculosis

* Collecting system integrity: trauma/intervention

* Congenital anomalies

* Upper tract urothelial lesion

It is a cheaper, readily available alternative to CT in resource-limited settings

Other options:

Option A: X-ray KUB: It is used to specifically visualize KUB (kidney, Ureter, Bladder). The X-ray KUB image below shows a thimble bladder caused due to TB of the bladder.

Option C: Retrograde Pyelogram is an X-ray test in which a special contrast is inserted into the urethral orifice of the penis via a catheter to visualize more distal urinary tract abnormalities. It is used to diagnose urethral strictures, injuries, blockage, and diverticula ( it is for the urethra, not the ureter). RGP Image below shows a bulbar urethral stricture.

Option D: Micturating CystoUrethrogram, also known as a voiding cystourethrogram (VCU). In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foley's catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It helps diagnose posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve. The following image shows a voiding cystourethrogram in a patient with grade V VUR.
questions.learning: Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) — The radiological image shown above is that of an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), also known as Intravenous Urography (IVU). IVP is an X-ray with special contrast injected into the veins to visualize the kidneys, ureter, and bladder.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 39-year-old man presents with symptoms of stress and difficulty coping with work– life balance. On evaluation, he is found to have a blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg and elevated blood glucose levels. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
questions.explanation: This patient has Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) and coexisting hyperglycemia. In this scenario, Telmisartan—an Angiotensin II Receptor Blocker (ARB)—is the preferred treatment. Telmisartan lowers blood pressure by reducing peripheral resistance and provides essential renal protection by lowering intraglomerular pressure. Crucially, unlike some other classes, ARBs do not negatively affect glucose metabolism; some evidence even suggests they improve insulin sensitivity. Glucocorticoids (Option A) are contraindicated as they raise both blood pressure and glucose. Thiazide diuretics (Option C) can cause hyperglycemia, making them less ideal for patients with already elevated blood sugar. Advising rest only (Option D) is insufficient management for Stage 2 hypertension. Immediate pharmacological therapy combined with lifestyle modifications is required to reduce the patient's heightened cardiovascular and metabolic risks
questions.learning: This patient has Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) and coexisting hyperglycemia. In this scenario, Telmisartan—an Angiotensin II Receptor Blocker (ARB)—is the preferred treatment.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the correct order of End plate potential at the neuromuscular junction:
options: Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential
Na+ channel opens → Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release
Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal
Action potential → Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ca2+ entry in Axon Terminal → Ach Release → Na+ channel opens → Action potential

Ca²⁺ entry in Axon Terminal → ACh Release → Na⁺ channel opens → Action potential

The Full Sequence

| Step | Event | Location

| ---- | ----- | --------

| 1 | Motor nerve AP arrives | Axon terminal

| 2 | Ca²⁺ enters via VGCC | Axon terminal

| 3 | ACh released into synaptic cleft | Presynaptic

| 4 | ACh binds nicotinic receptors | Motor end plate

| 5 | Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx | Postsynaptic membrane

| 6 | End plate potential generated | Motor end plate

| 7 | If EPP reaches threshold → muscle AP | Muscle fiber

Key Conceptual Point

The question asks specifically about end plate potential — this is a postsynaptic event that begins with ACh binding, NOT with the muscle action potential.

The EPP is the graded potential at the motor end plate caused by Na⁺ influx. It is what leads to the muscle action potential, so the action potential comes last in this sequence.

Why Other Options Fail

B — Starts with Na⁺ channel opening before ACh release. Na⁺ channels open because ACh binds — can't happen first.

C — Starts with ACh release, skipping Ca²⁺ entry. ACh cannot be released without the Ca²⁺ trigger — this is the step that couples electrical signal to vesicle fusion.

D — Starts with action potential. This confuses the muscle AP with the nerve AP. The sequence being asked is what happens after the nerve AP arrives — the nerve AP is the trigger, not part of the EPP sequence itself.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Graft from identical twin is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isograft

A graft from an identical twin is called isograft.

Isograft is defined as an organ or tissue that is taken from an individual (donor) and is placed on another individual (recipient) who has the same genetic constitution as of the donor. Example, graft between identical twins.

Transfer of cells/tissues/organs within the same species.

Xenotransplant
Transfer of cells/tissues/organs in a different species.

Isograft
Transfer of organ or tissue within genetically identical individuals. Eg: Identical twins
questions.learning: Isograft — A graft from an identical twin is called isograft. Isograft is defined as an organ or tissue that is taken from an individual (donor) and is placed on another individual (recipient) who has the same genetic constitution as of the donor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with history of having ingested a button battery. What is your next course of action?
options: Reassure and to check whether passed in stools
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Remove endoscopically

This case should be managed by removing the button battery endoscopically after confirming its position on X-Ray.

Button battery ingestion causes alkaline caustic injury, more in the areas surrounding the negative pole.

Management :

• The child is to be kept NPO until the oesophageal position of the battery is ruled out by X-ray scan. Vomiting should never be induced since the battery, which has passed through the esophagus, might lodge back again into it. Reassurance can be done only if the position of the battery is confirmed and if there are no symptoms.
• Since the question does not mention that the child is asymptomatic, the management of choice would be removing the battery endoscopically.
• Management also depends on battery life. Fresh batteries need to be removed as soon as possible as they have a higher concentration of injurious substances.
questions.learning: Remove endoscopically — This case should be managed by removing the button battery endoscopically after confirming its position on X-Ray. Button battery ingestion causes alkaline caustic injury, more in the areas surrounding the negative pole.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The treatment given to the patient presenting with a history of binge alcohol intake and symptoms of convulsions, altered sensorium, and plasma glucose level of 45 mg/dL is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiamine followed by dextrose

In a chronic alcoholic with hypoglycemia (glucose 45 mg/dL) and altered sensorium, the correct management is thiamine administration before glucose.

• Chronic alcoholics are commonly thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficient
• Thiamine is required for glucose metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase, etc.)
• Giving glucose first increases metabolic demand and can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy

Correct sequence: Thiamine first → then dextrose

• Thiamine deficiency → impaired cerebral energy metabolism
• Glucose without thiamine → accumulation of lactate → neuronal injury

Why other options are incorrect:

• 25% dextrose alone: Can worsen neurological damage
• Fomepizole: Used in methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning
• Thiamine alone: Does not correct hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Thiamine followed by dextrose — In a chronic alcoholic with hypoglycemia (glucose 45 mg/dL) and altered sensorium, the correct management is thiamine administration before glucose. • Chronic alcoholics are commonly thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficient •…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presents to the emergency department. The arterial blood gas report is as follows: pH, 7.2; pCO2, 81mm Hg; and HCO3, 40 meq/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory acidosis

The arterial blood gas values suggest a likely diagnosis of respiratory acidosis.

The various buffering systems present in the body maintain the systemic arterial pH between 7.35-7.45. The most common acid-base disorders are metabolic acidosis or alkalosis and respiratory acidosis or alkalosis.

Normal values in an arterial blood gas are as follows:

• pH: 7.35-7.45
•

PaCO2: 35-45 mmHg

•

HCO3: 22-26 mEq/L

•

PaO2: 75-100 mmHg

Respiratory changes (changes in PCO2) promote a corresponding change in metabolic response (changes in HCO3-) and vice versa as a compensatory mechanism. In general, PCO2 and HCO3- move in the same direction for compensation in metabolic and respiratory acid-base disorders respectively. A change in the two parameters in opposite directions points to a mixed acid-base disturbance.

Respiratory acidosis can be secondary to severe pulmonary disease, respiratory muscle fatigue, or ventilatory control abnormalities. It is marked by an increase in PaCO2 and a decrease in pH. A compensatory rise of HCO3- can also be seen.

A rapid rise in PCO2 (acute hypercapnia) can present with dyspnea, confusion, and psychosis. It can be seen in severe asthma secondary to bronchospasm, anaphylaxis, or inhalational burns. Chronic hypercapnia causes sleep disorders, memory loss, and daytime somnolence. It is commonly seen in end-stage obstructive lung disease.

Acute respiratory acidosis may need tracheal intubation and assisted mechanical ventilation. Rapid correction of hypercapnia should be avoided as it can trigger cardiac arrhythmias and seizures. Chronic respiratory acidosis is difficult to manage and improvement in lung function is the primary aim.

Other options:

Option A: Respiratory alkalosis arises due to alveolar hyperventilation and can be due to salicylates, high altitude states, cardiac failure, and anemia.

Option B: Metabolic acidosis arises due to an accumulation of endogenous acids. Examples include lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, and starvation. It can also be seen in renal failure.

Option D: Metabolic alkalosis can be seen in Liddle's syndrome, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, massive blood transfusion, and cystic fibrosis. It is marked by elevated pH and HCO3- values. A rise in PaCO2 indicates a compensatory respiratory response.
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis — The arterial blood gas values suggest a likely diagnosis of respiratory acidosis. The various buffering systems present in the body maintain the systemic arterial pH between 7.35-7.45.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl is not compliant with spectacles for her myopic astigmatism. What would be the appropriate management in her case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spherical equivalent spectacles

The appropriate management for myopic astigmatism in a 15-year-old girl (<18 years) would be spherical equivalent spectacles.

Prescription in astigmatism has 3 components:

• Power of the spherical component: Convex (+) or concave (-) in dioptre sphere (DS)
• Power of the cylinder: Convex (+) or concave (-) dioptre cylinder (DC)
• Axis or orientation of the cylinder

The cylinder power and axis are correcting the astigmatic part of the refractive error. If an astigmatic eye were to be corrected with a spherical lens alone, the result would be a blur circle on the retina, called the circle of least confusion.

The spherical lens power places the circle of least confusion on the retina and is called the spherical equivalent. It is defined as the spherical power whose focal point coincides with the circle of least confusion, where one would see minimal blurring in their vision. To calculate the spherical equivalent, add half the cylinder power to the sphere power:

Spherical equivalent= spherical power + 1/2 (cylindrical power)

For example, for spherical power +2 and cylindrical power +3,

+2.00 +(+3.00 /2) = +3.50.

Spherical equivalent spectacles are given if one has to give less cylinder power than was measured.

Other options:

Options A and C - LASIK and Femto LASIK should be done in patients above 18 years of age.

Option D - Implantable Collamer lens is indicated for patients 21-45 years of age.

The image demonstrates the steps of LASIK
questions.learning: Spherical equivalent spectacles — The appropriate management for myopic astigmatism in a 15-year-old girl (<18 years) would be spherical equivalent spectacles.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A person is performing weightlifting and attempts to lift the dumbbells overhead. Which of the following changes will be seen in the sarcomere during this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I band decreases

During skeletal muscle contraction, sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of the 'I' band.

Key Changes in the Sarcomere During Contraction:

* Overall sarcomere length decreases – causing muscle contraction.

* During contraction, the Z lines come closer to each other reducing the length of the sarcomere.

* The A band remains constant and the M line becomes prominent.

* H-zone (only myosin region) decreases – as actin filaments slide inward.

* I-band (only actin region) shortens – due to increased overlap with myosin

Pearl PF1350: Microanatomy of Muscle Fibres

* Each muscle consists of numerous muscle fibres.

* Each skeletal muscle fibre is multi nucleated, bonded by sarcolemma, enclosing sarcoplasm, smooth muscle and cardiac muscles are uninucleated.

* Within the sarcoplasm, there are several hundreds of nuclei arranged in the periphery just beneath the sarcolemma.

* The sarcoplasm also consists of evenly distributed, longitudinal threads called myofibrils.

* Each myofibril consists of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments overlapping each other.

* The portion of myofibril which consists of thick filaments is known as A band or dark band, and the portion of a myofibril between two A bands consisting of only thin filaments is known I band or Light band.

* Thus the A band consists of both thick and thin filaments, where as I band consists of only thin filaments.

* In the middle of ‘A’ band, there are only thick filaments with no overlapping thin filaments. This zone is known as ‘H’ zone. In the middle of H zone, there is a dark band known as ‘M’ band.

* In the middle of I band, there is a dark ‘Z’ disc or Krause's membrane.

* The segment of the myofibril between two Z discs is known as the sarcomere.
questions.learning: I band decreases During skeletal muscle contraction, sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of the 'I' band.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following opioids is a partial agonist at mu and a full agonist at kappa receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pentazocine

Pentazocine is a partial agonist at mu and a full agonist at kappa receptors.

Analgesia produced by pentazocine is predominantly mediated by the κ receptor.

Pentazocine is a mixed agonist-antagonist opioid agent. It is a full agonist at the κ receptor and a partial agonist or weak antagonist at the µ receptor

Note: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu receptors but an antagonist at kappa receptors
questions.learning: Pentazocine Pentazocine is a partial agonist at mu and a full agonist at kappa receptors. Analgesia produced by pentazocine is predominantly mediated by the κ receptor.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The most appropriate expansion of Apgar is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration

The parameters to consider while calculating APGAR score in newborn babies are:

1. Appearance
2. Pulse rate
3. Grimace
4. Activity(muscle tone)
5. Respiratory effort

The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life. It gives a maximum score of 10 which indicates the newborn is in the best possible condition.

Changes in the Apgar scores denote the response of the infant to resuscitation. Apgar scores should not be used to determine the need for resuscitation or to guide the steps of resuscitation. Apgar score alone should not be interpreted as evidence of asphyxia.

A score from 7-10 is considered normal. Scores between 0-3 require immediate resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

Causes for false positive APGAR score are:

• Prematurity
• Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
• Acute cerebral trauma
• Precipitous delivery
• Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)
• Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
• Hemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.
questions.learning: Appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration — The parameters to consider while calculating APGAR score in newborn babies are: 1. Respiratory effort The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life.
